0.title: The Letter of Joy: Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
0.overview:
Philippians is the most personal and warmest of Paul’s letters — a love letter to the church that had been his closest partner in the gospel from the very beginning of the European mission. He wrote it from prison, most likely in Rome, facing the real possibility of execution. And yet the letter’s dominant note is joy. “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice” (4:4). The word “joy” or “rejoice” appears sixteen times in four chapters. This is not the forced cheerfulness of a man in denial; it is the deep, settled gladness of a man who has found that Christ is sufficient for every circumstance, including chains, including death.

Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia — the first European city Paul evangelized (Acts 16), where the gospel arrived through a riverside prayer meeting, a wealthy cloth merchant named Lydia, a slave girl freed from a spirit of divination, and a jailer shaken to conversion by an earthquake. The church that emerged from these unlikely beginnings remained Paul’s most generous supporter: “no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving except you only” (4:15). When Paul was imprisoned, they sent Epaphroditus with a gift — and now Paul sends this letter back with him, full of gratitude, theology, and pastoral instruction.

Where was Paul imprisoned when he wrote? Three places have been suggested. Some argue for Ephesus, because it was near enough to Philippi for the several journeys the letter implies; others for Caesarea, where Paul was held for two years (Acts 24:27). The more likely answer is Rome, around AD 60–62. Paul mentions the whole imperial guard (1:13) and those of Caesar’s household (4:22), and he faces a verdict that could end in death with no further appeal, which fits Rome, where he had already appealed to Caesar, better than either alternative.

The letter’s theological heart is the great Christ hymn of chapter 2 (vv. 6–11), which may be the earliest christological poem in the New Testament — pre-Pauline in origin, perhaps already sung in the churches before Paul wrote. It traces the arc of the Son of God from the heights of divine equality, through the descent of incarnation and the depths of a slave’s death on a cross, to the exaltation at which every knee bows and every tongue confesses. This is not merely doxology; it is the pattern of Christian existence. The community that sings this hymn is called to embody it: the same self-emptying, other-serving, glory-surrendering mind that was in Christ Jesus is to be in them.

The letter’s other great passage is the biographical testimony of chapter 3 (vv. 4–11), where Paul lists his impressive Jewish credentials — circumcised on the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, blameless under the law — and then counts them all as loss, as rubbish, as dung (skybala) compared to “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.” This is the gospel of grace arriving at personal address: not the abstract doctrine of justification but the lived reality of a man for whom Christ has become everything, and everything else has become nothing by comparison.

Philippians is the answer to the question: what does a life shaped by the gospel actually look like? It looks like partnership rather than rivalry, like humility rather than self-promotion, like contentment rather than anxiety, like pressing forward rather than dwelling on the past, like the peace of God that passes understanding rather than the turmoil of the person whose security rests on circumstances. It is the most beautiful portrait of mature Christian life in Paul’s letters — and it was painted by a man in chains, who could see the executioner’s sword, and who wrote: “to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”

1.title: To Live Is Christ: Partnership, Prison, and the Advance of the Gospel
1.overview:
Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, settled by retired soldiers, and the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16): a businesswoman named Lydia, a converted jailer, and a few others. About ten years later Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, to thank them for a gift and to steady them under opposition. It is the warmest of his letters, full of joy.

Chapter 1 thanks God for their partnership in the gospel and states a great certainty: God, who began a good work in them, will finish it. Paul prays that their love will grow in knowledge and discernment. Then he reports from his cell: his chains have advanced the gospel through the imperial guard, other believers have grown bolder, and even rivals who preach to spite him are preaching Christ, so he rejoices. Facing a possible death sentence, he writes, “to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain,” yet expects to stay for their sake. He ends by calling them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing together, unafraid, knowing that suffering for Christ is itself a gift of grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and Timothy greet the whole church at Philippi, including its overseers and deacons. Paul thanks God with joy every time he remembers them, because they have been his partners in the gospel from the first day, and he is sure that God, who began his work in them, will bring it to completion on the day of Christ. He carries them in his heart; they share in God’s grace with him in prison and in defending the gospel. His prayer is that their love will grow, guided by knowledge and discernment, so that they choose what matters most and are found pure and full of the fruit of righteousness on the last day, to God’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Finishes What He Starts

Philippians 1:6 is among the strongest statements of perseverance in the New Testament, and its whole force lies in the subject of the two verbs. God began the good work; God will complete it. The believer is the field, not the farmer. Reformed theology has always insisted that perseverance is not the Christian’s achievement but God’s gift — the same grace that opens a heart keeps it, and the same power that raised Christ is at work in everyone united to him.

This is not a doctrine that makes effort pointless; it is what makes effort reasonable. Paul will command the Philippians to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, and in the same breath tell them that it is God who works in them both to will and to work (2:12–13). The two sentences are not in tension. A Christian labours precisely because the outcome is guaranteed by someone else, which is the only ground on which anyone has ever laboured with hope. Assurance rests not on the strength of our grip but on the certainty of his (John 10:28–29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had every reason for anxiety. Their apostle was in chains, their city was a Roman garrison town where the imperial cult was a civic expectation, opposition was real (v.28), and the congregation had a quarrel in it that Paul will have to name by the end of the letter (4:2). His answer is not to reassure them about their circumstances or to praise their track record, but to point them to the character of the God who started the work.

Now: The Christian who lies awake wondering whether his faith will last is asking a question about the wrong grip. If perseverance depends on the tenacity of the believer, the honest answer is bleak; every one of us has already discovered how quickly we let go. Verse 6 puts the question the other way round — will God let go? — and answers it with “I am sure of this.” And verse 9 supplies the prayer to pray for the people you love: not that their week would be easy, but that their love would grow eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Meaning first. Philippians is Paul’s most joyful letter, written from prison to the church he loved most. Its great theme is joy in Christ whatever the circumstances, and partnership in the gospel. Chapter 1 opens with warm thanksgiving for the Philippians’ partnership from the first day, confidence that God will finish the good work he began in them, and a prayer that their love will abound in knowledge and discernment (vv. 1–11). Then Paul explains his situation: his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel, spreading it through the imperial guard and emboldening other believers. Even those who preach out of rivalry are preaching Christ, so he rejoices (vv. 12–18). He faces possible death with calm: for to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. To depart and be with Christ would be far better, but remaining is better for them, and he expects to stay (vv. 19–26). Finally, he calls them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel, united, unafraid of opponents, knowing that God has granted them not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him (vv. 27–30). Over the whole chapter stands one name: Christ is mentioned again and again, as the one Paul serves, the one he longs for, the one he lives for and the one he will be with.

The setting. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16:11–40). Founded by Philip II of Macedon and refounded as a colony for Roman army veterans after the battle of Philippi in 42 BC, it was proud of its Roman citizenship. Some ten years before this letter, Paul had walked into the city and found, apparently, no synagogue. So he went down to the river on the Sabbath and spoke to the women who had gathered there to pray. The church that resulted began with people who had nothing whatever in common. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth with a household and money of her own, whose heart the Lord opened (Acts 16:14). A slave girl whom Paul delivered from the spirit that made her somebody’s income (Acts 16:16–18). And the jailer who fastened Paul and Silas in the stocks and then, in the night, washed their wounds (Acts 16:33). A businesswoman, a slave and a prison officer: that is the kind of congregation reading these words. Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, though some suggest Ephesus or Caesarea. The Philippians had sent Epaphroditus with a gift (4:18), and this letter is, among other things, a thank-you letter.

Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus. Paul’s first word about himself is douloi, slaves. Not “apostle”. He claims that title elsewhere when his authority is under attack, and he is perfectly willing to use it; here, with a church that loves him and needs no persuading, he sets it down. And the word he chooses instead is the very word he will use of Christ in the letter’s great hymn: Jesus emptied himself, “by taking the form of a servant” (2:7), the form of a doulos. The letter’s opening line is already the letter’s argument. Before Paul asks the Philippians to have the mind of Christ, he shows them a man who has begun to. A slave in that world owned nothing, not even his time; whatever came into his hands belonged to his master. Paul and Timothy wear that status as a title, because the Master is the one who first took it on himself.

Why is Timothy named, if Paul wrote the letter? Timothy was with Paul when the church was founded (Acts 16:1–3, 12), so the Philippians knew and loved him, and Paul is about to send him to them (2:19–23). Naming him shows that the letter comes from the gospel team, not from one celebrated man. But Timothy is a co-sender rather than a co-author: from verse 3 the letter is written in Paul’s own “I”, and in chapter 2 Paul speaks about Timothy in the third person. Notice too that Paul calls them both servants. The older apostle and his younger helper stand on the same footing before Christ.

To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi. Hagioi, holy ones, and we should be clear what it does not mean, because the English word has drifted. It is not a rank awarded for exceptional godliness, and it is not a description of how these people are doing. It is a statement of where they are: in Christ Jesus. They are set apart because he has laid hold of them. Every believer in Philippi is a saint on the same grounds, the jailer no less than Lydia. And notice the word “all”. Paul will say it again and again in this letter (1:4, 7, 8, 25; 2:17), in a letter that will eventually have to name two women who cannot get along (4:2). He loves them all, and he will not let any party in the church imagine he belongs to them more than to the others.

Two addresses. Every Christian in Philippi had two addresses, and Paul writes both on the envelope: in Christ Jesus, and at Philippi. The first is where they live; the second is where they are stationed. The first does not change when they move house or are thrown out of the city, and it is the one that decides who they are. The second is where they are to show it, in that particular street, with those particular neighbours. A Christian who forgets the first address becomes anxious and worldly. A Christian who forgets the second becomes otherworldly and useless. Paul keeps both in one sentence.

Am I a saint if I do not feel holy? Yes, if you are in Christ. Saint is not a feeling or an achievement; it is what God has made you by joining you to his Son (1 Corinthians 1:2, 30). The Corinthians were called saints in the same breath as they were rebuked for quarrels and immorality. What you feel is not the measure; what God has done is. But the name is also a calling. Because you are set apart for God, you are now to live like it, and the rest of this letter will show what that looks like: humble, joyful, united, pressing on. You do not become a saint by living a holy life. You live a holy life because you are one.

With the overseers and deacons. No other letter Paul wrote greets the church’s officers in the address. It tells us the Philippian church had grown into settled order, with recognised men leading and serving. The overseers (episkopoi, from which comes the word bishop) were the elders who led and taught (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). The deacons (diakonoi, servants) served the practical needs of the church (1 Timothy 3:8–13). Two offices, both plural. And the order of the sentence tells us something about how Paul thinks: he addresses the whole body first and the leadership second, inside the same sentence. The officers are not over the saints; they are among them. They may also have been the ones who organised the gift Epaphroditus brought, which would explain why they are mentioned here.

Where Christians differ: church government. Some churches have a bishop over many congregations, distinct from elders. Others have a single pastor with no elders. Verdict: in the New Testament, overseer and elder are the same office: Paul calls the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:17) overseers (Acts 20:28), and uses the two words of the same men in Titus 1:5–7. Each church was led not by one man but by a plurality of qualified men, with deacons serving alongside. The New Testament pattern is two offices, elders and deacons, with elders sharing leadership. Churches may organise their wider fellowship in various ways, and godly believers in other traditions serve Christ faithfully, but this local pattern is biblical.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church leaders are superior Christians. They are servants among servants, and the letter begins by calling even the apostle a slave. Nor does it mean that the people who are not officers are spectators. The whole letter is addressed to all the saints, and every one of them is a partner in the gospel (v. 5).

What do elders and deacons actually do, and how should I treat them? Elders shepherd the church: they teach the word, pray, watch over souls and give account to God for them (Acts 20:28; Hebrews 13:17; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Deacons serve the practical needs of the body so that the word is not neglected: care for the poor and sick, the church’s money and property, and much quiet work that keeps a congregation running (Acts 6:1–6). Scripture tells you to respect and love those who labour among you (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), to pray for them, to make their work a joy and not a groan, and to bring a concern to them directly and graciously rather than complaining behind their backs. They are not above correction; they are also not your staff.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The order never varies in Paul, and it cannot. Grace is God’s unearned favour reaching down; peace is what that favour creates when it lands. Not a mood, but the end of the war: since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). You cannot have the second without the first, and a great deal of religion is the attempt to do exactly that: to manufacture peace of mind while leaving the question of grace unsettled. Paul puts them in the only order in which they come. And notice where they come from: the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together, one source, one gift. Only God gives grace, and Paul names the Son beside the Father without a pause. A man in chains, writing to a church under pressure, begins by giving away the two things no prison can confiscate.

In a sentence. From Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all God’s holy people in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of the people in your church who have nothing in common with you: the one from a different class, a different generation, a different past. Paul’s first readers were a merchant, a former slave and a prison officer, and the only thing that held them together was the first address on the envelope, in Christ Jesus. Thank God this week for one such person by name, and speak to them on Sunday. Pray too for your elders and deacons by name: not that they would be impressive, but that they would be servants, like the men who wrote this letter.

For worship. The Lord of glory took the form of a slave, and so the apostle is glad to be called one. The Father and the Son together pour out grace and peace on a riverside congregation of the most unlikely people in a garrison town, and call every one of them holy. He sets apart a dealer in purple, a girl who had been owned, and a jailer with blood on his hands, and writes over them all the same name: saints, in Christ Jesus. Nothing about them made it so. Everything about him does.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.

I thank my God in all my remembrance of you. In all of it: every memory, with none set aside. Stop and measure that against your own recollection of any group of people you have worked closely with for ten years. Paul had been beaten with rods in this city and put in the stocks. He knew this church’s quarrels; he will address one by name in chapter 4. And still there is no memory of Philippi that he has to step around in order to give thanks. And notice to whom the thanks go. Not to the Philippians, though he is grateful to them, but to God, because everything good in them is God’s work (v. 6). “My God” is personal. Paul is not thanking a distant power; he is speaking to the God he knows.

Always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy. Here joy (chara) appears for the first time in a letter where joy and rejoicing come back again and again, sixteen times in all, from a man in chains. Praying for other people is often felt as a duty and performed as one. Here it is the thing Paul enjoys. If you want a test of whether someone is a partner or merely an acquaintance, this is a fair one: does bringing them to God gladden you, or is it an item on a list? And notice the order of his prayer: the thanksgiving comes before the request, verses 3–5 before verses 9–11. He gives thanks for what God has already done in them before he asks for anything more.

Because of your partnership in the gospel. The reason for the joy is in this phrase. The word is koinōnia: sharing, having something in common, going in together on a venture. It is not merely a warm word for friendship. In ordinary Greek it could describe a business partnership, two men with capital in the same ship, and that is nearer to Paul’s meaning than sentiment is. The Philippians had put money into the gospel enterprise from the start (4:15–16), and they had put themselves in: their prayers, their messenger, their own suffering. They were not Paul’s audience or his donors. They were shareholders in the same undertaking.

What it cost them. Philippi was not a wealthy church. Writing to Corinth about the Macedonian congregations, Philippi chief among them, Paul says that in a severe test of affliction their joy and their deep poverty overflowed in a wealth of generosity: they gave beyond their means, of their own accord, begging earnestly for the favour of taking part (2 Corinthians 8:1–5). That is the koinōnia Paul is thanking God for: poor people who had to be talked out of giving more than they could afford. When he says the word, that is what he can see. Set that against the way we usually measure a church’s part in the gospel. Paul is not thanking God for their capacity. He is thanking God for what they did with what little they had, and he remembers it a decade later.

From the first day until now. The first day was a riverbank and a handful of praying women, and Lydia’s first act as a believer was to open her house to the missionaries (Acts 16:15). Between that day and this one lie an earthquake, a jail, a magistrate’s apology, and years of gifts carried up and down the Egnatian Way, the great Roman road that ran through the city. Paul remembers the whole arc. History matters between Christians; a relationship that has cost something and survived is not the same as a new acquaintance, and Paul does not pretend otherwise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only financial support counts as partnership. Prayer, encouragement, hospitality, sending workers and shared suffering are all part of it, and Paul names several of them in this one letter. Nor does it mean that gospel partnership is for a committed inner circle. The partnership Paul thanks God for belongs to them all.

What if there are people in my church I cannot thank God for? Begin where Paul begins: not with what they are like, but with what God has done. If they are in Christ, God has begun a good work in them (v. 6), and you can thank him for that even when you cannot yet thank him for their manner. Name one thing in them that is plainly his grace, however small: their faithfulness in turning up, their love for their children, a gift they use. Thank God for it specifically. Thanksgiving does not pretend there are no faults; Paul will deal frankly with a quarrel in chapter 4. But it changes the eyes you see them with, and it is very hard to go on resenting someone you pray for with thanks every week.

How can I be a partner in the gospel if I have little to give? The Philippians were poor, and they are the model. Partnership is not measured by size but by sharing: you go in with the work. Pray regularly and by name for missionaries and gospel workers, and tell them you do. Give what you can, proportionately and gladly (2 Corinthians 9:7). Open your home. Write to someone who is labouring in a hard place. Stand with believers who suffer. And above all, live and speak the gospel where you are. The widow’s two coins (Mark 12:41–44) were counted in heaven as the largest gift in the treasury.

In a sentence. Paul thanks his God every time he remembers them. In all his prayers for all of them, he always prays with joy because of their partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.

On a Tuesday. Take a list of five people you pray for, and before you ask anything for them, thank God for one specific thing he has done in each of them. Do it for a week and notice whether praying for them becomes a joy rather than a chore. Then ask which gospel work you are a shareholder in, not merely an admirer of. If the answer is none, choose one this week: a missionary, a church plant, a struggling congregation nearby. Learn their names and put something in.

For worship. God does not merely save individuals and leave them alone; he binds them into a fellowship, and makes poor people rich enough to give. The same God who opened Lydia’s heart opened her purse and her door, and kept that riverside church giving for ten years. He gives a man in prison so many good memories that he cannot pray without joy. Every partnership in the gospel is his gift, and every gift given for his Son is remembered by him far longer than by us.

verseByVerse.quote: And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.

And I am sure of this. This is one of the great sentences of the New Testament, and it repays being exact about what it says. “Sure” (pepoithōs) means persuaded, settled, confident. Paul’s confidence is not in the Philippians. It does not say the Philippians will finish what they started. It says God will finish what he started.

That he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion. There are two verbs, began (enarxamenos) and will bring to completion (epitelesei), and they share one subject. He opened the account; he will close it. Both verbs could be used of a religious rite, of beginning a sacrifice and carrying it through to its finish. Whether or not Paul meant to sound that note, the shape is right: a work commenced by God upon a person is not an experiment, and it will not be abandoned half-done. He is not a builder who runs out of money at the second storey.

A good work in you. Which work? The whole of it: the moment the light came on, the verdict of not guilty pronounced over you in Christ, and the slow, unglamorous business of being made new that is going on in you now, usually more visibly to others than to yourself. In Philippi it began with a heart opened at a riverbank (Acts 16:14) and a jailer trembling in the night and asking what he must do to be saved (Acts 16:30). Neither of them started it. And the same God who began it in them includes their partnership in the gospel (v. 5): their generosity was his work too.

At the day of Jesus Christ. The finish line is named. Not the day you die, and not the day you finally get on top of the sin that has beaten you for thirty years. The day he appears, when he will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (3:21). The work has a completion date, and it is set by his diary, not yours.

The asymmetry of the grip. Here is the practical weight of it. The believer who lies awake asking whether he will still be a Christian in twenty years is asking a question about the strength of his own grip, and if that is where the answer lies, then the honest reply is: probably not. But that is not where the answer lies. The question Philippians 1:6 answers is a different one, whether God will let go, and to that the answer is not I hope so but I am sure of this. Paul is not expressing optimism about their character. He is expressing confidence about God’s. A drowning man held by a lifeguard is safe not because of how well he grips but because of how well he is gripped. “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:27–28).

Where Christians differ: the perseverance of the saints. Many Christians, in the Arminian tradition, hold that a true believer can turn away and be finally lost; they point to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6) and to Paul’s own call to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling (2:12). Verdict: Paul is confident that God will complete the work he began. Salvation rests on God’s faithfulness, not our grip. The warnings are real and must be heeded, but the very next verse in Philippians gives the reason the working out succeeds: it is God who works in you (2:13). True believers may stumble badly, but God will keep them to the end (John 6:39; 10:28–29; Romans 8:30). This is the perseverance of the saints, better called the preservation of the saints by God (Westminster 17.1–2). Those who fall away for good show that the work was never truly begun in them: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are passive. God works in us as we work out our salvation (2:12–13). That does not make effort pointless; it makes effort hopeful, which is a different thing entirely. And it does not mean that anyone who once prayed a prayer may live as he likes and be sure of heaven. The confidence of this verse is about a good work God has begun, and a work of God shows itself in a changed and changing life.

What about people who seemed to be real Christians and then walked away? This is one of the most painful questions in church life, and the honest answer has two parts. First, we cannot see hearts. Some who seemed strong were never born again, and their leaving reveals it (1 John 2:19; Matthew 13:20–21). Second, some who wander are true believers in a terrible season, and God will bring them back, as he brought back Peter after his denial and David after his fall. We often cannot tell which is which until the end. So do not write anyone off, and do not pretend all is well. Keep praying, keep loving, and keep calling them home. The final judgment belongs to God, and so does the power to restore.

I feel I am going backwards. Does that mean God has stopped working in me? No. Growth is not a straight line, and it is often invisible from inside. A child does not feel himself growing; others notice it. Seasons of struggle, dryness and failure are often the very places where God is digging deeper foundations. The fact that you are troubled by your coldness is itself a sign of life: dead men do not grieve over their deadness. Go back to the means God uses: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of other believers. And rest your weight on this verse. It does not say he will finish it if you feel it going well. It says he will finish it.

In a sentence. And Paul is confident of this: he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When you feel you are failing as a Christian, say this verse aloud, and notice who the subject of every verb is. Then do the next right thing, not to keep yourself saved, but because the one who is keeping you is at work in you. And look at one believer you have been worried about, and thank God that his work in them does not depend on your worry either.

For worship. He never starts what he does not finish. He finished creation and rested. He finished the work the Father gave him and cried out from the cross, it is finished. He will finish his work in every one of his people, and on the day of Jesus Christ not one of them will be missing, and not one will be left half-made. Our faithfulness flickers; his does not. The lifeguard has never yet lost a swimmer he took hold of, and the hand that holds us bears the marks of what it cost him to reach us.

verseByVerse.quote: It is right for me to feel this way about you all, because I hold you in my heart, for you are all partakers with me of grace, both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. For God is my witness, how I yearn for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is right for me to feel this way about you all, because I hold you in my heart, for you are all partakers with me of grace, both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. For God is my witness, how I yearn for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus.

It is right for me to feel this way about you all. Paul’s confidence and his joy are not wishful thinking or flattery; they are justified. The word for feel (phronein) is a favourite of this letter: it means to think, to have a settled mind and attitude, and it will come back in the great command of 2:5, have this mind among yourselves. Paul’s affection for them is not a passing emotion. It is the settled mind of a man who has thought about them and concluded that God is at work in them.

Because I hold you in my heart. They are deeply loved. The Greek can also be read the other way round, because you hold me in your heart, and both are true of this church, which had sent a man eight hundred miles to look after him. The ESV’s reading is the more natural one: Paul carries them with him into his cell.

For you are all partakers with me of grace. The word behind partakers (synkoinōnoi, fellow sharers) is from the same root as the koinōnia of verse 5. Paul is saying something stronger than you have supported me. He is saying that the grace given to him in a Roman prison has been given to them too, because they are in it with him. They sent money and a man (2:25); therefore the ministry that money bought is theirs. The soldier who heard the gospel while guarding Paul heard it partly because a congregation in Macedonia had paid for Paul to be there.

Both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. Defence and confirmation are both courtroom words: apologia, the speech for the defence, and bebaiōsis, the legal establishing of a claim. Paul may have been preparing his defence before Caesar. He is on trial, and he tells a church some eight hundred miles away that they are standing in the dock with him. And notice that he calls imprisonment grace. The chains are not where grace ran out; they are part of what grace gave him to share. The person who prays for and funds a work they will never see is not on the sidelines of it.

For God is my witness, how I yearn for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus. This is the most emotionally exposed sentence in the chapter. “Yearn” (epipotheō) is to long for, to ache to see. “Affection” translates splanchna, literally the inward organs, the gut. It is the Greek way of locating deep feeling not in the heart but lower down, where you actually feel it: the ache in the stomach when you think of someone you love and cannot reach. English has no polite word for this, which is why translators reach for affection and lose most of it. The same word is used in the Gospels of Jesus himself, moved with compassion when he saw the crowds like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36).

Whose affection? Notice whose gut it is. Not I yearn for you with great affection, but with the affection of Christ Jesus. Paul is not claiming merely to feel strongly. He is claiming that what he feels for the Philippians is Christ’s own feeling for them, running through him. He has become a channel: the love of Christ for this church reaching them by way of a man in chains who cannot stop thinking about them. That is why he calls God to witness. No one can verify an inward ache, so he swears to it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s love was mere emotion. It was Christ’s love, shown in action: in prayer, in letters, in sending Timothy and Epaphroditus, and in being willing to stay alive for their sake (v. 24). Nor is there anything cold about it. There is a way of caring about people that is entirely dutiful: correct, responsible and cold. Paul’s is not that. And there is a way of feeling strongly about people that is really about ourselves. Paul’s is not that either, because the affection is borrowed from Christ and therefore points away from Paul altogether.

What if I feel nothing for the people in my church? Do not pretend, and do not despair. Christ’s affection is not something you can produce by trying to feel it, but it grows where the conditions are right. Pray for them by name, with thanks (vv. 3–4), because it is hard to stay cold towards people you regularly bring to God. Serve them in practical ways, since feeling often follows action rather than preceding it. Spend time with them: Paul’s love was built over ten years of shared life and shared suffering. And ask Christ directly to love them through you. He is more willing to give his affection than you are to receive it.

In a sentence. It is right for Paul to feel this way about all of them, since he has them in his heart, and, whether he is in chains or defending and confirming the gospel, all of them share in God’s grace with him. God can testify how he longs for all of them with the affection of Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Think of the people in your church, and ask honestly: is there anything in me that moves? Then do one thing for one of them this week that costs you something: a visit, a meal, a letter, an hour. And if you support a missionary or a gospel worker, tell them in so many words that you count yourself in it with them, in their trials as well as their successes. It will mean more to them than you know.

For worship. The heart of Christ is not cool towards his people. He looks on them with compassion that moves him to the depths, he yearns over them, and he carries that love even into the prison cells of his servants and out through their letters. The love that reached the Philippians through Paul’s chains is the same love that took Christ to the cross: the love of the Good Shepherd who knows his sheep by name. Whatever affection we feel for one another is only a small stream from that great river, and the river does not run dry.

verseByVerse.quote: And it is my prayer that your love may abound more and more, with knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent, and so be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it is my prayer that your love may abound more and more, with knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent, and so be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

And it is my prayer that your love may abound more and more. Paul has given thanks; now he asks. And what he asks for repays a close look, because it is not what most of us pray for the people we love. He does not pray that their circumstances would ease, that the opposition would let up, or that the church would grow. He prays that their love would grow. Their love is already strong; he has just spent three verses thanking God for it. Paul prays for more. Love can always grow, and the verb (perisseuō) is a flooding word: love overflowing its banks.

With knowledge and all discernment. But an overflowing river without banks is not a blessing; it is a disaster, and Paul knows it. So he names the banks. Knowledge (epignōsis): the compound form suggests full or settled knowledge, knowing a thing through, and above all the knowledge of God. And discernment (aisthēsis): perception, the word for the trained senses, the ability to tell one thing from another by feel, the moral sensitivity that knows what a situation needs. Love that abounds with these is not less warm. It is warm, and it can see.

Two opposite failures. They are equal and opposite, and most of us are prone to one of them. There is love without discernment, which cannot say no to anything, is taken in by every plausible teacher, enables what it should confront, and calls its own softness kindness. And there is discernment without love, which is never taken in by anything, can spot an error at fifty paces, and has a cold and shrinking heart. The first is sentimentality; the second is not far from cruelty. Paul asks for neither. He asks for a love that has grown enough to know what it is doing.

So that you may approve what is excellent. What is the discernment for? The verb dokimazō means to test something and, having tested it, to approve it; it was used of assaying metal. And what is excellent (ta diapheronta) is not simply good versus bad. The phrase means the things that differ, the things that genuinely matter. The hardest decisions in a Christian life are almost never between good and evil. They are between good and best, between two legitimate claims on the same evening. Choosing well there requires exactly what Paul prays for: love with its senses trained.

And so be pure and blameless for the day of Christ. Then the goal: the same day named in verse 6, the deadline that governs everything. “Pure” (eilikrinēs) may come from judging a thing by holding it up to the sunlight; if so, it means what it appears to be when the light gets behind it, without hidden flaws or mixed motives. “Blameless” (aproskopos) means without stumbling, and can also mean not causing others to stumble. Both senses fit: a life that does not trip and does not trip others up.

Filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ. Then the source, and it rescues the whole prayer from being a to-do list. Not fruit they manufacture: fruit that comes through him, as sap comes through a branch that has no life of its own. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me (John 15:4–5). The fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23) grows on the branches of the Vine.

Is this fruit of righteousness the same as being justified? Not quite, but the two are joined. Here Paul means the righteous life that grows in a believer: love, honesty, purity, good works. In chapter 3 he speaks of the righteousness from God that depends on faith (3:9), the perfect righteousness of Christ counted to us when we believe. That righteousness is the root; this fruit is what grows from it. We are not accepted because of the fruit. We bear fruit because we have been accepted and joined to Christ. Both come through Jesus Christ, and both end in the praise of God.

To the glory and praise of God. The last line makes sure no one mistakes where the credit goes. Paul is not telling the Philippians to go away and become more discerning. He is asking God to do it in them, and when God does it, the glory is his. The goal of all Christian growth is not our self-improvement but God’s praise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean knowledge replaces love, or that the most theologically informed Christian is the most mature. It means knowledge guides love. Nor does it mean love must wait until it knows everything before it acts. Love grows in knowledge as it goes.

How does my love actually grow in knowledge and discernment? By being soaked in God’s word, which trains the senses to distinguish good from evil (Hebrews 5:14). Read Scripture not only for information but asking what it shows you about loving God and people. Watch mature Christians and learn from how they handle hard situations. Pray this very prayer for yourself. And practise: when you face a decision, ask not only whether it is allowed but what would be most loving and most for Christ’s glory. Discernment is like a muscle; it grows by use, and it grows slowly.

In a sentence. And this is Paul’s prayer: that their love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, so that they may be able to discern what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

On a Tuesday. Pray this prayer, phrase by phrase, for someone you love today, instead of praying that their week would go smoothly, and notice how different a thing you are asking for. Then take one decision in front of you this week where both options are good, and ask what the best one is: which one love, with its eyes open, would choose, and which one you will be glad of on the day of Christ.

For worship. God does not only forgive his people; he makes them fruitful. The life that grows in them is his life, flowing from the Vine into the branches, and every good thing it produces comes through Jesus Christ. He trains our blunt senses, enlarges our small love, and is preparing a people who will stand pure and blameless on the day of his Son. And when the harvest is finally gathered, no one will boast of his own fruit. It will all be to the glory and praise of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Chains, the Rivals, and the Choice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reports that his imprisonment has helped the gospel rather than hindered it. The imperial guard knows why he is in chains, and other believers have grown bolder. Some preach Christ out of rivalry, hoping to hurt him; others out of love. He rejoices either way, because Christ is being proclaimed. He expects, through their prayers and the Spirit’s help, that all this will turn out for his good, and his one hope is that Christ will be honoured in his body whether he lives or dies. Living means Christ; dying would be gain. Torn between departing to be with Christ and staying for their sake, he is convinced he will remain, for their progress and joy in the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence: The Chains Were Not a Setback

What Paul reports here is Romans 8:28 in biographical form. God’s providence is not merely reactive — not the salvaging of a situation that got away from him — but his active government of all things, including hostile human choices, toward his own redemptive ends. The Roman legal machinery believed it had detained Paul. Paul knew he had been stationed (v.16, keimai). Same cell, two accounts of the world.

The same doctrine governs his response to the rival preachers, and its limits need stating precisely. Paul is not indifferent to motive — he names theirs as envy and selfish ambition, and forbids that spirit in the Philippian church in the next chapter (2:3). Nor is he indifferent to content; the man who wrote Galatians 1:8 would anathematise a preacher of another gospel. His point is narrower and sturdier: where the message is true, its power lies in the message and not in the messenger, and God is not so fastidious as to let a soul perish rather than use a flawed instrument.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes as a prisoner whose usefulness looked finished, to a church that was funding a mission which appeared to have stalled. He gives them no general assurance that things work out. He gives them a report: here is what God has in fact done with the wreckage — a guard evangelised, a church emboldened, and a gospel travelling on roads nobody had planned.

Now: Two applications, and they pull in different directions. For the believer whose life has been derailed — the illness that ended the work, the split that closed the ministry — verse 12 is not a demand to feel that the loss was a gain. And for the believer who is afraid to die, verses 21–23 offer not a stoic’s courage but an accountant’s logic: whether death is gain depends entirely on what you have made your life. Fill in Paul’s blank — for to me to live is — and the word that arrives unbidden will tell you what you have built on.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel, so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard and to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel, so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard and to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ.

I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me. Now Paul turns to the thing they must have been agonising over. Their apostle is in chains. The man who brought them the gospel cannot travel, cannot plant churches, cannot preach in the open. From every ordinary angle the mission has stalled. “Brothers” includes the sisters of the church, Lydia among them: brothers and sisters in God’s family.

Has really served to advance the gospel. “Advance” is prokopē, progress, a word often explained from the picture of pioneers going ahead of an army, cutting a road through country that has none. That is Paul’s picture of his own imprisonment. Not a roadblock: roadworks. The chains are not what happened instead of the gospel’s progress; they are the instrument of it. What looked like defeat became advance.

So that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard. Paul is concrete about how. The ESV notes that “imperial guard” is literally the whole praetorium: the elite Praetorian Guard in Rome, the emperor’s own household troops, or the governor’s headquarters elsewhere. Roman custody of this kind meant Paul lived under guard, with a soldier assigned to him (Acts 28:16, 20), and the guard was relieved shift by shift. Consider what that arrangement actually delivered: a rotation of the most elite and politically connected soldiers in the empire, each one stationed for his shift beside the most compelling talker in the early church, with nowhere to go. The Roman state had accidentally built Paul a captive congregation and paid for the guards. By the end of the letter he can send greetings from believers in Caesar’s household (4:22).

And to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ. Notice what became known: not merely the message but the reason. The whole guard understood that this man was not in custody for sedition or fraud. He was there for a Galilean he claimed was alive. That clarity is itself an achievement. Plenty of Christians suffer in ways that leave everyone around them unclear about why.

Said carefully. This needs saying carefully, because God will use it can be a cruel thing to say too early. Paul is not offering a general optimism that bad things turn out fine. He is reporting, after the fact and from inside the situation, what God has in fact done. The man whose career has been ended by illness, whose ministry closed when the church split, whose plans died with a diagnosis, is not required to feel that his loss is a gain. He is invited to consider that the God who turned a prison into a pulpit is not out of options, and that the road being cut may not be the road he was walking. Paul could only write verse 12 from the far side of the disappointment. Most of us are asked to trust it from the near side.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering is good in itself, or that Christians should seek it out or pretend it does not hurt. Paul still wanted to be released and asked them to pray (v. 19). It means God uses suffering to advance his purposes, and that a believer’s circumstances are never outside his reach.

Does God cause my hard circumstances, or only use them? Scripture holds two things together. God is not the author of sin: the men who arrested Paul were responsible for what they did. Yet nothing happens outside God’s rule, and he governs even the wicked acts of men for his good purposes, as Joseph told his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The same is true supremely at the cross (Acts 2:23). So you do not need to blame God for evil, and you do not need to fear that evil has escaped him. Your hardship is not random, and it is not wasted. It is held in a Father’s hand.

Is it wrong to pray to get out of my situation? No. Paul himself expected and hoped to be released (vv. 19, 25), and asked for prayer. Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from him. Pray honestly for relief. But pray also, as Paul lived, that while you are there, Christ will be made known through you. The soldiers chained to Paul did not need his release first; they needed his faithfulness where he was.

In a sentence. Now Paul wants them to know, brothers and sisters, that what has happened to him has actually served to advance the gospel. As a result, it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that he is in chains for Christ.

On a Tuesday. Name the circumstance in your life you would most like to change: the job, the illness, the household, the limitation. Then ask who is chained to you in it: the colleague on your shift, the nurse, the neighbour, the family member who sees you every day. They are watching how a Christian bears what he did not choose. Make sure that, whatever else they conclude, they know why you live as you do.

For worship. The God who rules the empire also rules its prisons. He turned the chains of his servant into a pulpit and the emperor’s own guard into a congregation, and he did it with Rome’s money. Nothing can hold back the word of God: the preacher may be bound, but the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2:9). And it is the pattern of the gospel itself. The greatest defeat in history, the Son of God nailed to a cross, was the greatest advance, and from that day nothing that is done to his people has ever been able to stop his kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “imperial guard” is literally “the whole praetorium” — the Roman soldiers guarding him, or the governor’s headquarters.

verseByVerse.quote: And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.

And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment. The second advance is quieter than the first and, in the long run, larger. Paul’s imprisonment made other people brave. You would expect the opposite. When the leader is arrested, the sensible move is to lower your voice and wait for the weather to change. Instead, seeing Paul’s faithfulness in chains gave others courage. And Paul is careful about where the confidence is anchored: confident in the Lord. Not confident in Paul, and not confident that the authorities were bluffing. What his chains proved was not that the risk was small. It was that the gospel was worth the risk, and that a man could pay the price and still be full of joy. That is contagious in a way that argument is not.

Most, not all. Do not miss the honest word at the start: most of the brothers. Not all of them. Some in Rome went quiet, and Paul knows it and says so without naming or scolding them. It is a small mark of a truthful letter. The New Testament never reports a revival in which everybody rose to the occasion, and a Christian who has gone quiet under pressure should notice that Paul’s sentence leaves room for him without excusing him.

Are much more bold to speak the word without fear. “Much more bold” is tolmaō, to dare. And “without fear” (aphobōs) stands at the end of the sentence like a flag. These are not people who felt no fear; they are people who spoke anyway, which is the only kind of courage there has ever been. Notice also that what spread was not a mood but a practice: they were bolder to speak the word. Paul does not say the Roman Christians felt more positive about the mission, or that morale improved. They opened their mouths in places where it cost something to do so. Encouragement that never changes what anybody actually does is not what this verse is describing.

Faithfulness multiplies. There is a principle here that every Christian should know, because it changes how we read our own hard seasons. Faithfulness under cost multiplies. One person willing to absorb the loss, the job, the friendship, the standing in the family, quietly raises the ceiling for everyone watching. Nobody in Rome had planned this. Paul did not set out to run a boldness campaign; he set out to preach and got arrested. The emboldening was a by-product, invisible to him until it happened. Which means the believer who is currently paying a price in obscurity, and can see no result whatever, may be doing more for the people around him than he will learn about in this life. Courage is contagious; so, sadly, is cowardice.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fear disappeared entirely. It means faith overcame it. Nor does it mean that every Christian is called to be reckless or to court arrest. Boldness to speak the word is not the same as harshness, and it is joined in the New Testament to gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

I have gone quiet about my faith at work. What do I do? Begin with honesty before God: confess the fear without excusing it, and remember that Peter, who denied Christ three times, became the boldest preacher in Jerusalem. Then take one small step rather than a dramatic one: answer truthfully next time someone asks what you did at the weekend; mention that you will pray for a colleague who is struggling, and then do it. Ask God for boldness, as the first church did (Acts 4:29). And let your confidence rest where theirs did, in the Lord, not in your own nerve. Courage usually grows by use.

In a sentence. And because of Paul’s chains, most of the brothers and sisters have become confident in the Lord and dare all the more to proclaim the gospel without fear.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone whose faithfulness under cost has made you braver: a persecuted believer you have read about, a friend who kept his integrity at work and lost his promotion, a parent who held on through a long illness. Thank God for them. Then remember that someone is watching you in the same way. Your faithfulness in a hard place may be the thing that gives them courage. Be brave for their sake, and speak one word for Christ this week where it costs you something.

For worship. The Lord makes cowards bold. He did it with fishermen who had run away in Gethsemane, and with frightened Christians in Rome, and he still does it. He takes the suffering of one servant and turns it into courage in a hundred others, so that the enemy’s attempt to silence the gospel ends with more voices speaking it. The confidence he gives is not in us but in himself, and it rests on the one who was not ashamed to suffer for us outside the city gate.

verseByVerse.quote: Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will. The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel. The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will. The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel. The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment.

Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry. Now a genuinely ugly detail, and Paul does not soften it. Some of the preachers in Rome were jealous of Paul and saw his imprisonment as their chance to gain influence. They were preaching Christ in order to hurt him. Envy (phthonos) is resentment at another’s good; rivalry (eris) is strife, the spirit that must win.

But others from good will. The second half deserves its due too, because it is the kindest line in the paragraph. In a passage about envy it is easy to remember only the rivals. Paul had friends in Rome who preached because they loved him and loved Christ. Most churches contain both sorts, and a Christian who has been wounded by the first kind can end up unable to see the second.

The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel. The sentence not to miss is easy to skim past: “I am put here” is keimai, to be laid, set, appointed, stationed. It is what you say of a sentry given a post, or a stone set in a foundation. Paul does not regard himself as a man who was arrested. He regards himself as a man who was posted. The Roman legal system thinks it put him there. Paul knows better, and so do the friends who love him: they can see that the prison is an assignment, God’s appointment.

A sentry, not an unlucky prisoner. That word reorganises everything around it. If Paul is an unlucky prisoner, then the rival preachers are getting away with something and his life has been interrupted. If Paul is a posted sentry, then nothing has miscarried at all: he is exactly where his Commander stationed him, doing exactly what a sentry does, which is to hold ground he did not choose. Every reader who is somewhere he did not choose, a job, a marriage, a sickbed, a town, has to decide which of those two sentences describes his life. They are the same set of facts. They are not the same world.

The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely. “Selfish ambition” is eritheia, a word from the world of hired political canvassing: the spirit of working a crowd for your own advancement, party spirit, self-promotion. It will come back in 2:3, where Paul tells the Philippians to do nothing from it. He is not raising a distant Roman problem. He is showing them, in the wild, the exact disease he is about to warn them against in their own congregation. And their motives were wrong, but their message was right. Unlike the false teachers in Galatia, they preached the true Christ.

But thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment. The word for afflict means to raise up pressure, to make chafe, as a chain rubs a wound. They calculated that a surge of preaching under other names would grieve a man who could no longer preach himself, and perhaps that his rivals’ success would make him jealous. They were partly right about the psychology of most men and entirely wrong about Paul.

Who were these rival preachers? Paul does not name them, and we do not know. They were Christians in Rome who preached the true gospel, since Paul rejoices in their message (v. 18), but resented Paul’s prominence, perhaps because they had led the Roman churches before he arrived or because his imprisonment seemed to them a disgrace. What matters is that they were not false teachers. That makes the passage more searching, not less, because it means orthodox, gifted, busy Christian workers can be driven by envy, and not notice.

What it does not mean. It does not mean motives do not matter. God judges motives, and will bring to light the purposes of the heart (1 Corinthians 4:5). It means the true gospel can be preached even by flawed people, and that God is not hindered by the sins of his servants.

How do I know whether my own service is driven by rivalry? Ask a few uncomfortable questions. How do I feel when someone else’s ministry flourishes more than mine, in a church down the road or in my own congregation? Am I glad when good work is done that no one will connect with me? Do I find it hard to praise a fellow worker in his absence? Would I keep serving if nobody noticed? If the honest answers sting, do not despair. Confess it, ask God to purify your heart, and make a habit of praying by name for the success of those you feel rivalry towards. It is very hard to keep envying someone you pray for.

In a sentence. It is true that some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill. The latter do so out of love, knowing that Paul is put here for the defence of the gospel. The former preach Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing that they can stir up trouble for him while he is in chains.

On a Tuesday. Take the place you are in that you did not choose, and say the sentence over it: I am put here. Not stranded, not forgotten, not interrupted. Posted. Then ask what a faithful sentry does in such a post today. And if there is a fellow Christian whose success you resent, pray for his ministry by name, and if you can, say something good about him to someone else this week.

For worship. Christ is the Commander who posts his servants, and no prison, sickbed or unchosen town is outside his map. He sets them where they stand, as a builder sets a stone, and none of them is there by accident. He bore the envy of the religious leaders, who handed him over to Pilate out of envy (Mark 15:10), and he went to his post on the cross knowing exactly why he was put there. The rivalry of men could not derail his work, and it cannot derail the work of his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,

What then? It is a shrug you can hear: the sound of a man setting an injury down. So what? He has just described people trying to wound him. Now he weighs it, and finds it does not weigh much.

Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed. “Pretence” (prophasis) is a pretext, a show put on to cover the real motive. This needs guarding, because it can be misread in two directions. Paul is not saying motives do not matter. He has just called theirs envy and selfish ambition, and he will tell the Philippians to purge exactly that spirit from their own church (2:3). Nor is he saying that any message preached under Christ’s name is acceptable. The man who wrote Galatians 1:8–9 would call down a curse on a preacher whose content was false. The rivals in Rome were preaching the true gospel with rotten hearts. That is the case Paul is addressing, and only that one.

The power is in the message. What he is saying is that the power is in the message, not the messenger. A true gospel preached from a bad motive is still a true gospel, and the people who hear it can still be saved by it. God is not so fastidious that he will let a soul perish rather than use a flawed instrument, which is a mercy, since he has never yet had any other kind to use. The seed does not stop being seed because the sower is a scoundrel. We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).

And in that I rejoice. Notice what this costs Paul, and what it reveals. Their whole strategy depended on his caring more about his own standing than about Christ’s. It failed, and it failed for the reason he will state three verses later: to him, to live is Christ. Take a man whose life is Christ, and attack him by advancing Christ, and you have handed him a present. The rivals could not reach him because there was nothing of himself left in the place they were aiming at. It is a remarkable freedom from self.

Yes, and I will rejoice. Then the verse turns, and the turn is easy to lose because our eyes jump to the chapter’s famous lines. Present tense first, then future. He rejoices now, in a cell, over preachers who despise him, and he commits to going on rejoicing, before he knows the verdict of his trial. That second clause is a decision, not a feeling. Joy in this letter is repeatedly something Paul chooses and then commands (3:1; 4:4), which is only possible because its ground is outside him and cannot be got at by anyone in Rome.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul accepted false gospels. He condemns them fiercely (Galatians 1:8). Here the content is true; only the motives are wrong. And it does not mean we should be indifferent to the character of preachers and leaders. The New Testament requires that elders be above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2), and a church must deal with leaders whose lives deny their message. Paul is not lowering the standard for leaders; he is refusing to let his own wounded feelings decide whether he rejoices that Christ is known.

How can I rejoice when others get the credit or outshine me? By changing what you are rejoicing in. If your joy is in your own usefulness, every success of another is a small loss. If your joy is in Christ being known, every success of another is your gain too. John the Baptist showed the way when his disciples complained that everyone was going to Jesus: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30). Practically: thank God aloud for the fruitfulness of others, especially those who have hurt you. Refuse to talk down another’s ministry. And remember that on the last day, every faithful labour will be rewarded by the only judge whose opinion matters (1 Corinthians 3:8).

In a sentence. But what does it matter? The important thing is that in every way, whether from false motives or true, Christ is preached. And because of this Paul rejoices. Yes, and he will continue to rejoice,

On a Tuesday. When others get credit for gospel work you did, or for work you would have liked to do, say Paul’s two words to yourself: what then? Then ask whether Christ is being made known. If he is, rejoice, out loud if you can, and let go of your own reputation. Notice how much lighter you are without it.

For worship. Christ is so great that even envious men cannot preach him without spreading his glory. His gospel works through cracked vessels and crooked motives, because the power is his and not ours. And he gives his servants a joy that their enemies cannot reach, because it rests on him. The one who emptied himself and made himself of no reputation (2:7) shares that freedom with his people: the freedom of those who have nothing left to protect, because their life is hid with Christ in God.

verseByVerse.quote: for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my deliverance,
verseByVerse.commentary:
for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my deliverance,

For I know that through your prayers. This will turn out for my deliverance is not Paul’s own phrase. It is a quotation, word for word, from the Greek Old Testament at Job 13:16. And once you see it, the verse changes shape. Job says it at the point where his friends have finished explaining that his suffering proves his guilt, and he turns from them to God to argue his case directly: whatever happens, this will end in my vindication. Paul, in a Roman cell with his own accusers circling, picks up Job’s sentence and makes it his. He is placing himself in a long line: the righteous sufferer whose vindication comes not around the affliction but through it.

And the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. Paul names the two means, joined under a single article in the Greek as though they were one supply line: your prayers and the help of the Spirit. “Help” is epichorēgia, supply, provision, and the picture inside it repays a moment. The chorēgos was the wealthy citizen in a Greek city who undertook to fund a chorus for the festival: not a token gift but the whole cost, training, costumes, musicians, everything the production needed for as long as it needed it. That is the word Paul reaches for. The Spirit does not send occasional relief; he underwrites the entire performance. And he is the Spirit of Jesus Christ: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9), sent by the Son to supply his people.

One supply line. Do not miss how those two are yoked. The Philippians pray in Macedonia; the Spirit supplies in Rome; and Paul treats them as one movement, not two. That is a high view of ordinary intercession. The praying church is not doing something adjacent to what God is doing. When you pray for a Christian in a hard place, you are inside the supply line, and Paul is telling you plainly that he could feel it arriving.

This will turn out for my deliverance. That settles what deliverance means, and it matters, because the Greek word is sōtēria, the ordinary New Testament word for salvation. Does Paul mean I will get out of prison? Not chiefly. A few verses later he says he does not know whether he will live or die, which would be an odd thing to say if he had just predicted his release. Job was not promised his cattle back; he was promised a hearing. Paul means the larger thing: this will end in my standing before God unashamed, vindicated, whatever the Roman court decides. Verse 20 says so explicitly: whether by life or by death. The verdict of the Roman court is not the verdict he is waiting for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sure he would be released. He was sure God would bring good out of it, and that the outcome, life or death, would be his salvation and vindication. Nor does it mean his salvation depended on the Philippians’ prayers, as if God could not save him without them. God has chosen to work through the prayers of his people, and he gives them the privilege of taking part.

If God is sovereign, do my prayers actually change anything? Yes, because God has ordained not only the ends but the means, and prayer is one of his chosen means. Paul expected God to work through your prayers, not in spite of them or apart from them. God does not need our prayers to be informed, and he is not persuaded against his will. But he has bound himself to answer the prayers of his children, and he delights to give his gifts in a way that draws us into his work. You have not, because you ask not (James 4:2). Sovereignty is not a reason to stop praying. It is the reason prayer is not wasted: the one you are speaking to can actually do it.

In a sentence. For he knows that through their prayers and God’s provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ what has happened to him will turn out for his deliverance.

On a Tuesday. Choose one Christian in a hard place, someone persecuted for the faith, a missionary under strain, a friend in hospital, and pray for them every day this week by name. Ask not only for their relief but for what Paul wanted: that they would not be ashamed, and that Christ would be honoured in them. Tell them you are praying. You are part of the supply line.

For worship. The Spirit of Jesus Christ is a generous supplier. He funds the whole performance of a believer’s endurance, from the first step to the last, and he never runs short. The God of Job is the God of Paul, and the vindication he gave the one he gives to all who trust him. And above every praying church stands the Son, who always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Our prayers rise to the Father through him, and the supply comes down from him, and no believer in any prison of this world is ever cut off from it.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

As it is my eager expectation and hope. “Eager expectation” is one word, apokaradokia, and it is nearly a picture: the head stretched forward, craning, watching with outstretched neck for something to appear. Paul uses it of the whole creation waiting for the revealing of the sons of God (Romans 8:19). It is the posture of a man at a window straining down the road. Paul is not enduring; he is leaning out.

That I will not be at all ashamed. What he strains toward is stated negatively, then positively. Negatively: the fear is not execution. It is that under pressure he might crack, deny, hedge, go quiet, and so bring dishonour on the name; that he might be disgraced by failing Christ at his trial.

But that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body. Positively: “honoured” is megalynō, to magnify, to make great. Not like a microscope, which makes small things look bigger than they are, but like a telescope, which makes things that are unimaginably great but far away look as great as they really are. A life can do that for Christ: bring him near enough to be seen. And note “in my body”: not in his theology or his letters, but in this physical, chained, ageing body, which is the only place any of us ever honours Christ.

Whether by life or by death. Note the sweep: he is telling them that both outcomes of his trial are wins, before he knows which he will get. If released, he will serve Christ; if executed, he will die well for Christ. Either way, Christ is magnified.

For to me to live is Christ. Then the next line, which is nine Greek words and one of the summits of Scripture. Weigh what he did not write. Not Christ is important to me. Not Christ is the centre of my life, which still leaves a life with Christ installed in the middle of it. He writes that living is Christ. Take Christ out of the sentence and there is no predicate left: no residue of Paul that would carry on with other business. Knowing him, serving him, loving him, being loved by him: Christ is the content, purpose and goal of his life. Fill in the blank honestly for yourself and the verse becomes a diagnostic. For to me to live is ____, and whatever word arrives unbidden is the thing whose loss would end you.

And to die is gain. See how the second half follows from the first, because it does not work in reverse. If living is Christ, then dying cannot be loss; it can only be more of the one thing living was already about: being with him (v. 23). Death does not interrupt such a life; it delivers it. But put anything else in that blank, family, work, health, reputation, and death is exactly what it appears to be at every graveside: the end of the only thing you had. The second clause is not a brave sentiment bolted on. It is arithmetic. Whether death is gain depends entirely on what you filled the first blank with.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wished to die or despised this life. He saw both as good, because Christ is in both. Nor does to live is Christ mean that a Christian should lose interest in his family, his work or the good gifts of creation. Christ is not in competition with them. A life that is Christ loves its wife more, works more honestly and enjoys a meal more gratefully, because it receives everything from his hand and does everything for him.

I cannot honestly say that to live is Christ. What then? Most Christians cannot say it as fully as Paul, and the honesty is a good beginning. Paul did not arrive here overnight; he wrote it after some thirty years of walking with Christ and suffering for him. Do not try to work up a feeling. Instead, ask God to make it true, and give Christ more of your attention: in his word, where you see his glory; in prayer; in the Lord’s Supper. We become like what we behold (2 Corinthians 3:18). And look at what you have filled the blank with. Often the remedy is not to love the good gift less but to love the Giver more, so that the gift takes its proper place.

In a sentence. Paul eagerly expects and hopes that he will in no way be ashamed, but will have sufficient courage so that now as always Christ will be exalted in his body, whether by life or by death. For to him, to live is Christ and to die is gain.
