On a Tuesday. Fill in the blank honestly: for me to live is ____. Do it at the end of an ordinary day by looking at where your thoughts went when they were free, what you spent your money on, what made you anxious. Then pray that over the coming years the answer would become Christ. And ask, in one concrete place this week, how Christ could be made to look great in your body: in the way you speak to your family, handle a temptation, or bear pain.

For worship. Christ is worth living for and worth dying for, and he is the only one of whom both are true. Everything else we could put in the blank is lost at the grave. He alone is gained there. He is the life of his people now, and their reward in death, and their glory at the resurrection. He made himself small so that we could see how great he is, and he is magnified in weak and chained and dying bodies, because his power is made perfect in weakness. To live is Christ; to die is gain; and the gain is him.

verseByVerse.quote: If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.

If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. What follows is one of the strangest passages in Paul, because we are watching an apostle unable to decide which he would rather have: to go on living, or to be executed. Living means more gospel fruit: more churches strengthened, more people brought to Christ, more letters like this one.

Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. Paul does not mean he controls his fate, as if the decision were his. He means he cannot say which he prefers. He cannot decide because both are good.

I am hard pressed between the two. The word for hard pressed (synechomai) means squeezed from both sides, held in a narrow place with pressure on each hand, pulled both ways.

My desire is to depart and be with Christ. “Depart” is analyō, and its ordinary uses are all of them journeys ending: untying a ship from the quay, striking a tent, unyoking an animal after the day’s work, loosing a prisoner from his chains. Every one of those is a release, and every one implies somewhere to go. That is Paul’s word for dying. Not extinction: casting off. Years later, waiting for execution in his last imprisonment, he used the same word: the time of my departure has come (2 Timothy 4:6).

For that is far better. This verse is one of the clearest windows in the New Testament onto what happens when a believer dies, and plainness serves best here, because it is the question people actually ask at gravesides. Paul expects to be with Christ: immediately, consciously, and better. The words are stacked: literally much more better, awkward in Greek as in English, a man running out of comparatives. Being with Christ beats everything this life offers. Compare the promise from the cross, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and Paul’s words that we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8).

Where Christians differ: the intermediate state. Some say the dead sleep unconsciously until the resurrection. Verdict: Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, and that is far better. That would not be far better if it were unconscious sleep. If death meant oblivion until the resurrection, the choice he describes would be incoherent: he could not weigh a nothing against continued fruitful labour and call it far better. Believers who die go immediately into Christ’s conscious presence, where they await the resurrection of the body (2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43; Westminster 32.1). Nor is there any purgatory in between. Paul expects to go straight to Christ, and the blood of Christ has already cleansed those who are his from all sin.

Far better, not yet best. Hold two things together, though, and the New Testament always does. To be with Christ at death is far better than this life. It is not yet the best; the best is the resurrection of the body when he appears, which Paul comes to at 3:20–21. The Christian dead are not waiting in a corridor, but they are waiting for something.

But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account. Here the passage becomes searching. Having said that departing is far better, Paul concludes that he will stay, because love for others keeps him willing. The tie-breaker is not his preference. It is their need. He wants the better thing; he chooses the useful one. That is what a life given away looks like when it is put under pressure and made to decide. Most of us are not choosing between heaven and ministry. But every ordinary week presents the same shape in miniature, the rest you have earned against the person who needs you tonight, and Paul shows us which way a man leans when Christ has become his life.

Is it wrong for a Christian to long to die? Paul longed to be with Christ, and so may every believer, especially in suffering. But notice what he did with the longing. He did not act on it; he left the timing to God and gave himself to the people who needed him (vv. 24–25). Wanting heaven is faith; taking one’s own life is not, because our times are in God’s hand (Psalm 31:15). So this passage does not make suicide acceptable; Paul leaves the timing to God. Anyone whose longing for death has become a plan should tell someone today, a friend, a pastor or a doctor, and hear what Paul concluded: to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account. You are needed here.

If death is gain, is it wrong to grieve when a Christian dies? No. Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus (John 11:35), knowing he was about to raise him. Paul himself speaks of the sorrow he would have had if Epaphroditus had died (2:27). Death is still an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and parting hurts. What changes is the kind of grief: we grieve, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The one who has died in Christ has gained; we have lost, for a while. So weep, and let others weep with you, and hold on to the truth that the one you miss is with Christ, which is far better, and that you will see them again.

Do believers who have died know what is happening on earth? Scripture does not say that they watch over us, and we should not build on guesses. What it does say is enough: they are with Christ, conscious and at rest, and far better off (Revelation 14:13). We are not to pray to them or try to contact them (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Our communion with them is through the one Lord we share. Every time you draw near to Christ, you are near to the one in whose presence they now are.

In a sentence. If he is to go on living in the body, this will mean fruitful labour for him. Yet what shall he choose? He does not know! He is torn between the two: he desires to depart and be with Christ, which is better by far; but it is more necessary for them that he remain in the body.

On a Tuesday. If being with Christ is far better, you need not fear death, and you can say so at a graveside without pretending it does not hurt. And while you live, labour fruitfully for others. This week, when your preference and someone else’s need pull in different directions, let Paul’s tie-breaker decide: what is more necessary on their account?

For worship. For the believer, death is a ship untied from the quay and a tent struck at the end of a march, because Christ has gone through death ahead of us and made it a door. He has prayed that those the Father gave him may be with him where he is, to see his glory (John 17:24), and that prayer is answered every time a Christian dies. To be with him is far better than anything this world can give, and better still is coming: the morning when he raises his people in bodies like his own. He holds the keys of death, and he uses them to bring his people home.

verseByVerse.quote: Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith, so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith, so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again.

Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all. Paul has reasoned his way to a settled expectation: since his continuing is what the churches need, he expects to be given it. He is not claiming a revelation about the trial’s outcome; he has just said he cannot tell which he would choose, and in 2:17 he is still reckoning with the possibility of being poured out as a drink offering. This is the confidence of a man who has worked out what would be most useful and trusts that God is at least as interested in usefulness as he is. Paul expected to be released, and he probably was: the letters to Timothy and Titus suggest he travelled again before a second imprisonment and his death (1 Timothy 1:3; Titus 1:5; 2 Timothy 4:6).

For your progress and joy in the faith. And notice what he expects to remain for. “Progress” is prokopē again, the pioneer word from verse 12. In verse 12 it was the gospel that was advancing through Paul’s chains. Here it is the Philippians who are to advance. The same road-making is going on in the mission and in the congregation, and Paul wants to stay alive to see the second kind. That is a striking measure of a pastor’s ambition. Not their comfort, not their numbers, not even their soundness on its own: their movement forward, and their gladness in it.

Joy in the faith. This deserves a pause, in a letter written from a prison by a man who mentions joy more often than in any other letter he wrote. Paul does not treat gladness as an optional temperament for the sunnier sort of Christian. He treats it as something a congregation can make progress in, and something worth staying alive to produce. Faith and joy grow together: the better you know what you believe, the more there is to rejoice in.

He did not make them feel like the obstacle. There is a pastoral instinct here worth naming. Paul has just spent several verses saying that he would rather die and be with Christ. A lesser man, having said that, would have left the church feeling like the obstacle, the reason he is stuck here. Paul does the opposite: he tells them that staying for them is a thing he is glad to be convinced of, and that their growth is worth postponing heaven for. He never lets his longing for glory become a rebuke to the people who still need him.

So that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again. Verse 26 gives the goal a final turn, and the turn is entirely characteristic. Paul imagines walking through the gate at Philippi, the church seeing him alive, and the room overflowing, and he is careful to say where the overflow is to be directed. Not at him. Through him, to Christ. He is willing to be the occasion of their boasting so long as he is not its object. A man who has just told them that living is Christ cannot afford to become the point of his own homecoming.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul had a guarantee from God. He had a strong conviction, reached by spiritual reasoning, and he held it humbly. Nor does it mean Christians should claim to know the outcome of every uncertain situation. We may hope, and reason from God’s character and purposes, but the outcome remains in his hands.

How can I know what God will do in my situation? Usually you cannot know the details in advance, and Scripture does not promise that you will. What you can know is what Paul knew: God’s purposes for his people, that he works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), that he will complete his work in you (v. 6), and that Christ will be honoured whether by life or by death. Reason from those truths, make your plans humbly, say if the Lord wills (James 4:15), and leave the rest with him. Paul’s confidence was really confidence in God’s goodness, and that is open to every believer.

In a sentence. Convinced of this, he knows that he will remain, and he will continue with all of them for their progress and joy in the faith, so that through his being with them again their boasting in Christ Jesus will abound on account of him.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are living for in the lives of others: their progress and joy in the faith, or only their comfort and approval? Then do one thing this week aimed at someone else’s growth: read Scripture with a younger believer, encourage someone who is struggling, write to someone who helped you. And when people praise you, quietly pass the glory on to Christ.

For worship. Thank God for those whose lives have helped your progress and joy in the faith, and above all thank him for the Shepherd who gives them. Christ does not leave his flock untended; he keeps his servants alive for the sake of his people, and takes them home when their work is done. Every pastor’s visit, every friend’s encouragement, every word that moved you forward, came from his hand. And when we glory, we glory in him, the one in whom all our joy begins and ends.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul calls them to live as citizens whose conduct matches the gospel, standing together in one spirit and contending side by side for the faith, unafraid of their opponents. Their courage will be a sign of the opponents’ ruin and of their own salvation from God. Suffering for Christ, like believing in him, is something God has graciously given them, and they are now in the same struggle they once saw Paul endure.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as a Grace-Gift

That suffering for Christ is granted — echaristhe, from charis, grace — is one of the most counter-intuitive claims in the New Testament. Not that God permits it, or merely redeems it after the fact, but that he bestows it, as he bestows faith, on those who belong to his Son. The apostles understood this when they left the Sanhedrin rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name (Acts 5:41).

Reformed theology has never treated suffering for the gospel as an aberration in the Christian life but as a feature of it in this present age: through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom (Acts 14:22). Union with a crucified and risen Lord means fellowship in both his death and his resurrection (3:10); the one cannot be taken and the other refused. A gospel that promises exemption from all hardship has misread the gift it is offering.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi was a garrison colony where loyalty to the emperor was ordinary civic decency, and confessing another Lord was a visible social defection. The opposition these believers faced was not random hostility; it was the predictable friction of two citizenships in one city. Paul answers it by telling them which capital they actually belong to — a point he will make explicit at 3:20.

Now: Verse 28 forbids the bolt, not the fear; a believer who is frightened and stays put has obeyed it. And it is composure under opposition for the gospel, not opposition as such, that counts as evidence — and even that is credited to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel,

Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ. Everything so far has been Paul’s situation. Now, with “only”, he turns the whole letter toward theirs, and gives the single command that the rest of the letter unpacks. “Let your manner of life be worthy” is a fair translation, but it hides the word Paul actually used. The verb is politeuesthe, from polis, city: it means to live as a citizen, to conduct yourself as a member of a commonwealth. Paul had a dozen ordinary words available for live or walk, and he uses them constantly elsewhere. He does not use one here.

A colony of heaven. And of all the cities he could have written this to, Philippi is the one where it would land hardest. Philippi was a Roman colonia, a settlement of discharged legionaries planted in Macedonia and granted special Italian rights, so that its citizens held Roman citizenship on Macedonian soil. They used Roman law, Latin was spoken in the forum, and the city answered to Rome some eight hundred miles away. The city’s whole identity was that it belonged somewhere else, and its business was to conduct itself so that the distant capital was accurately represented on this frontier. Every reader of this letter knew exactly what a colony was for. So Paul says: be citizens, worthy of the gospel. There is a capital, and it is not Rome; there is a Lord, and he is not Caesar. You are the outpost. He will make the point explicit at 3:20, “But our citizenship is in heaven”, but he plants it here in a single verb, and it is the frame for everything that follows.

Worthy is not moralism. This is also why worthy does not mean earning. A colonist does not earn his citizenship by good behaviour; he already has it, and behaves in a way that matches it. Grace first, then a manner of life that fits the grace. Worthy (axiōs) is a word of weighing: a life that balances the scales against the gospel it claims, so that people looking at it are not misled about what the gospel is.

So that whether I come and see you or am absent. Whatever happens to Paul, release or death, he wants to hear the same thing. The test of a church is what it is like when the apostle is not in the room. The test of a Christian is much the same. Conduct worthy of the gospel is not a performance staged for visiting authority; it is what the colony is like on an ordinary Tuesday, with the capital a long way off.

I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit. Then the content, and it is corporate through and through. “Standing firm” (stēkō) is what a battle line does when it holds, soldiers keeping their ground. “In one spirit” may mean with one shared spirit among them, or in the one Holy Spirit who unites them; the second is quite possible, since Paul speaks of participation in the Spirit at 2:1, and the two belong together, because the one Spirit makes them one.

With one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel. “With one mind” is literally with one soul. “Striving side by side” is synathleō, competing together as a team, from the word behind our athlete. Both pictures require other people. You cannot hold a line alone; a man alone is not a line. And they strive for the faith of the gospel: the truth of the gospel, believed and defended. This is the answer, planted early, to the fracture Paul will name in 4:2.

What it does not mean. It does not mean uniformity of personality, opinion on every matter, or taste. It means unity of purpose and of the gospel. A team needs different players; it does not need players who are trying to beat each other.

What does unity look like when Christians in the same church disagree? First, distinguish. On the gospel itself there must be one mind; Paul strives for the faith of the gospel and will not compromise it. On many other matters believers may differ in conscience (Romans 14:1–5). Then, keep the main thing in view: you are side by side against a common opponent, not face to face against each other. Speak to the person, not about them (Matthew 18:15). Assume the best motives you honestly can. Be quick to apologise for your share. And keep turning up, serving and praying together, because the line holds when people stand next to each other, not when they agree about everything.

In a sentence. Whatever happens, conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ. Then, whether Paul comes and sees you or only hears about you in his absence, he will know that you stand firm in the one Spirit, striving together as one for the faith of the gospel

On a Tuesday. You are a citizen of heaven, stationed in your street, your office, your family. Ask what someone watching your life this week would conclude about the capital you belong to. Then ask who is standing next to you in the line at church, and whether there is anyone you have stopped standing beside. Go and stand beside them again: a conversation, an apology, an invitation, a shared task.

For worship. Christ the King has a commonwealth, and its capital is not on any map of this world. He has given us its citizenship as a free gift, bought at the price of his own blood, and planted his colonies in every city of the earth. He holds his people together in one Spirit, as one body, and he is coming from his capital to bring them home. Every faithful congregation, holding the line on an ordinary week, is a small embassy of the city that will last when Rome and every other empire is dust.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “manner of life” means living as a citizen — fitting for a Roman colony proud of its status.

verseByVerse.quote: and not frightened in anything by your opponents. This is a clear sign to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and not frightened in anything by your opponents. This is a clear sign to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God.

And not frightened in anything by your opponents. The word is ptyromenoi, and it is used of horses: the sudden shying of an animal that has caught a movement in the hedge. It is not the word for considered fear. It is the word for the bolt, the panic that runs through a line and breaks it. Paul has just described a church standing shoulder to shoulder; this is the one thing that would undo the formation, and he names it with the exact word for how formations come undone. The Philippians faced opposition, perhaps from pagan neighbours and the Roman authorities of a city fiercely loyal to Caesar, where Paul and Silas had been charged with advocating customs unlawful for Romans (Acts 16:21).

Fear refused the reins. It is also worth saying what Paul does not command. He does not tell them to feel no fear. Ptyromenoi describes the bolting, not the pulse rate; the instruction is about what the fear is allowed to do to the line, not about whether it is felt. A believer who is afraid and stays put has obeyed this verse completely. Courage in Scripture is almost never the absence of fear; it is fear that has been refused the reins.

This is a clear sign to them of their destruction. Then he says something startling about what the opposition means. The word for “clear sign” (endeixis) is a legal term for evidence produced in court. The steadiness of a frightened little church under pressure is submitted as evidence, and it reads two ways at once. To the persecutors it is the first indication that they are fighting a losing battle against God, because people do not stand like that over nothing.

But of your salvation, and that from God. To the church it is the confirmation that they are genuinely God’s. Courage under persecution is evidence of God’s work. And the last words carry the weight: and that from God. The whole arrangement, the opposition, the courage, the sign it constitutes, is his doing, not theirs. Which is the only reason a small congregation in a garrison town could read its own steadiness as evidence of anything. If the courage were self-generated it would prove nothing except that they were brave that week. Because it is God-given, it is admissible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never feel fear; it means faith overcomes it. And it does not mean that being disliked proves you are right. Plenty of people are opposed because they are obnoxious, and this verse is no shelter for them; let none of you suffer as a wrongdoer, Peter says (1 Peter 4:15). Paul is speaking of a specific case: opposition incurred for the gospel, met without panic. It is the composure, not the conflict, that is the evidence.

Who are my opponents, if I am not being persecuted? For many Christians in the West, opposition is quieter than in Philippi, but it is real: mockery at work or school, family members who resent your faith, pressure to keep silent about what Scripture teaches, the threat of losing a job or a friendship. Elsewhere in the world, believers face prison and death, and you should pray for them. Remember too that the real enemy is not people; we do not wrestle against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12). Those who oppose you are people to be won, not crushed, and your steady, gentle courage may be the evidence God uses to bring them to himself, as he did with a jailer in Philippi.

What if I have already panicked and run? Then you stand where Peter stood after the rooster crowed. He bolted, and Jesus restored him, asked him three times whether he loved him, and sent him back to feed the sheep (John 21:15–19). Within weeks he was standing before the same council that had condemned his Lord, and they were astonished at his boldness. Confess your failure to God, and if others were affected, to them. Then go back to your place in the line. Your courage was never meant to come from you anyway; it is from God.

In a sentence. Without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you. This is a sign to them that they will be destroyed, but that you will be saved, and that by God.

On a Tuesday. Think of the situation where you are most tempted to bolt: the conversation you avoid, the question you deflect, the stand you are afraid to take. Ask God for a steady heart there, not a fearless one. Then, when the moment comes, do not run: stay where you are, say what is true gently, and leave the outcome to him. And pray by name for a persecuted church somewhere in the world this week.

For worship. The Lord is the strength of his trembling people. He takes a frightened congregation in a garrison town and makes it stand like a wall, and their steadiness becomes a witness to his power. He stood before Pilate and did not flinch, though he knew what was coming, and he has overcome the world. The opponents of his people are already on the losing side, and every believer who holds his ground in weakness is a sign, written by God himself, that the victory of the cross will be complete.

verseByVerse.quote: For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake, engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake, engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have.

For it has been granted to you. The little word that carries this verse is echaristhē, from charis, grace: it has been graciously given to you, given as a gift. And Paul sets two things side by side under that one word: to believe in Christ, and to suffer for his sake. Both are gifts.

That for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him. Even faith itself is not the one thing we contribute to our salvation but a gift God grants (Ephesians 2:8; Acts 13:48). The Spirit awakens what was dead and draws what was unwilling. In Philippi itself the first convert believed because the Lord opened her heart (Acts 16:14).

Where Christians differ: is faith a gift? Some say faith is our own contribution, the one thing we bring to God. Verdict: Paul says believing in Christ was granted, given by grace. Faith is our act, but it is God’s gift, produced by the Spirit in regeneration (Ephesians 2:8–9; John 6:44, 65). So even faith gives no ground for boasting. This is effectual calling: God gives the faith he requires (Westminster 14.1). It does not mean God forces people to believe. He changes the heart so that they gladly believe.

But also suffer for his sake. Paul is not writing here to settle a debate about the will; he is writing to steady a frightened, suffering church (v. 28), and it is the second gift he wants them to feel. For here is the startling thing: suffering for Christ is not a sign that grace has run out, but a grace in its own right. Not merely that God permits it, or can use it, but that he bestows it: a privilege handed to those who truly belong to Christ, a share in his sufferings. The apostles grasped it when they left the council “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name” (Acts 5:41). So the Philippians were not to read their hardship as God’s abandonment, nor as the mere cost of living in a hostile Roman colony, but as real fellowship with their Lord. “But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed” (1 Peter 4:13).

Engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have. Verse 30 makes the fellowship concrete, and its force depends on a memory. They had watched it happen. These were the people who saw Paul and Silas dragged into the marketplace, stripped, beaten with rods, and thrown into the inner prison, and who heard of them praying and singing hymns to God at midnight (Acts 16:19–25). Paul is not asking them to imagine an apostle’s sufferings from a distance. He is reminding them of a night some of them could still see. The word for “conflict” is agōn, the contest in the arena; it is the same arena as the striving side by side of verse 27. One arena, one contest, and Paul and this church are in it together.

The fellowship of the cross. And that reframes everything. To be joined to a crucified and risen Lord is to share in both his death and his resurrection (3:10); you cannot take the one and refuse the other. A faith that expects to be spared all hardship has misread the very gift it was given. So when suffering comes for his sake, it is neither wasted nor a punishment; it is the fellowship of the cross, and one day it opens into the fellowship of the glory (Romans 8:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering is to be sought out. Paul never went looking for a beating; he left Philippi when the magistrates asked him to. Nor does it mean that every hardship a Christian faces is suffering for Christ. Some suffering we bring on ourselves by folly or sin, and that is to be repented of, not celebrated.

Is my illness or bereavement suffering for Christ? Strictly, suffering for his sake is what comes on you because you belong to him and confess him: mockery, loss, opposition, persecution. Illness, grief and the ordinary troubles of a fallen world are not that in the same sense. But they are not outside his care either. For those who love God, all things work together for good (Romans 8:28), and when you bear them trusting him, for his glory, he is with you in them, and they too are shaping you into the likeness of his Son. In every kind of suffering a believer is never alone, and never without purpose.

How can suffering be a gift when it hurts so much? Because the gift is not the pain itself but what God gives through it and with it: closer fellowship with Christ, who suffered first; proof that your faith is real; a share in his work; and a weight of glory that the suffering cannot compare with (2 Corinthians 4:17; Romans 8:18). Gifts are not always pleasant to receive. A surgeon’s operation hurts, and you thank him afterwards. You do not have to pretend to feel grateful in the moment. But you may ask God to help you see the hand that gives it, and to trust that he gives nothing to his children that is not, in the end, for their good.

In a sentence. For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him, since you are going through the same struggle you saw Paul had, and now hear that he still has.

On a Tuesday. Thank God by name for the gift of your faith: you did not produce it, and you could not have. And if you are suffering for Christ, however small the cost, see it as a privilege, not a punishment, and tell another believer, so that you can stand in the arena together. If you know a Christian who is suffering for the faith, write to them this week and remind them they are not alone.

For worship. Every good thing in the Christian life is a gift of grace, even the faith with which we receive grace, and even the sufferings that join us to the Saviour. He gives us to believe in him, and then he gives us the honour of sharing his road. He went first into the arena, and bore the full weight of the cross alone, so that no suffering of his people would ever be a sign of his anger. Those who share his sufferings will share his glory, and the night of beating and singing in Philippi is the pattern of the whole Christian life: chains at midnight, hymns in the dark, and a door that God himself opens.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed at Philippi.

2.title: The Mind of Christ: Humility, the Incarnation, and the Cross
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a church under pressure from outside. Chapter 2 turns to the pressure inside: rivalry, conceit and grumbling, the kind of thing that later surfaces in two named women who cannot agree (4:2). Paul’s answer is not a management technique but a person. He sets before them the mind of Christ, in what may be the most important paragraph on the incarnation in the Bible (2:6–11): the one who was in the form of God did not use his equality with God for his own advantage, but emptied himself by taking the form of a slave, obeyed to the point of a slave’s death on a cross, and was therefore exalted by God to the name above every name, so that every knee will bow to him as the Lord of Isaiah 45.

Then come the consequences. Work out your salvation, because God is working in you. Stop grumbling, as Israel grumbled in the wilderness, and shine like stars in a twisted generation. Paul himself may be poured out as a drink offering, and is glad. The chapter closes with two portraits of the same mind in ordinary men: Timothy, who genuinely cares for others when everyone else looks after themselves, and Epaphroditus, the church’s courier, who nearly died bringing their gift and was more upset that they had heard he was ill than that he was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Appealing to all they have received in Christ, Paul asks them to complete his joy by being united in love and purpose, acting not from rivalry or vanity but humbly putting others first and caring for their interests. The attitude he wants is the one that belongs to them in Christ, and he describes it in a great passage about Christ himself. Though truly God, Christ did not use his equality with God for his own advantage. He emptied himself by taking the nature of a slave and becoming human, and then humbled himself further, obeying all the way to death on a cross. So God has raised him to the highest place and given him the supreme name, so that all creation will bow to him and confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the Father’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kenosis: What the Son Laid Aside, and What He Did Not

Verse 7 is the classic text for the incarnation, and its most important feature is grammatical: “he emptied himself” has no object. Paul does not say what the Son emptied himself of. He explains the emptying by what follows — “by taking the form of a servant.” The kenosis is therefore not subtraction but addition. He did not become less than God; he took to himself what he had never possessed, a full human nature.

What was laid aside was the independent exercise of divine prerogatives — the free use of what remained fully his. The glory was veiled rather than surrendered, and broke out once on the mountain to prove it had been there all along (Mark 9:2–3). This is Chalcedonian orthodoxy, which the Reformed tradition has always confessed: two natures in one person, without confusion and without division. He was not less than God in the manger, and not less than man on the cross.

Verses 10–11 raise a second question that must be answered honestly. Every knee bowing does not mean everyone is saved; the same letter speaks of opponents whose end is destruction (1:28; 3:19). Isaiah 45 itself distinguishes those who come gladly from those who come to him ashamed. Universal acknowledgement is certain; universal salvation is not taught here. The question the passage puts to the reader is not whether he will bow, but when — and in which posture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi had a status problem. Two women in the congregation could not agree (4:2), and the vocabulary Paul reaches for — eritheia, selfish ambition, the same word he used of the rival preachers in 1:17 — suggests the quarrel was less about doctrine than about position. Into that he drops the deepest thing he knows: the one with the highest claim in the universe declined to press it.

Now: The useful question in verse 6 is not “do I have a right here?” In most church conflicts you probably do. It is what you intend to do with the right you have. And verse 3 asks for a decision rather than a feeling: to count others more significant is a verb of judgement, a reckoning, not an emotion you must manufacture. Think of the person you find hardest in your congregation. Humility is not pretending you find them easy; it is deciding, before the next conversation, that what they need from it matters more than what you want from it.

verseByVerse.quote: So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind.

Meaning first. Philippians 2 contains one of the greatest passages in the Bible about Christ, and Paul uses it for an intensely practical purpose: unity and humility in the church. First, he appeals to them to be of one mind, doing nothing out of selfish ambition, but in humility counting others more significant (vv. 1–4). Then he gives the supreme example: Christ Jesus, who was in the form of God, did not cling to his equality with God, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, became man, and humbled himself to death on a cross. Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (vv. 5–11). Next, Paul calls them to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, because God is at work in them; to do everything without grumbling, shining like stars in a twisted world (vv. 12–18). Finally, he commends two men who embody Christ’s mind: Timothy, who genuinely cares for them, and Epaphroditus, who nearly died serving Christ (vv. 19–30). The chapter moves from the throne of God to a sickbed in Rome, and insists that they belong together.

So if there is any encouragement in Christ. Four “if” clauses, and not one of them is in doubt. In Greek they are framed as real conditions, and the context shows Paul takes them as true: closer to since there is than to if there happens to be. Paul is not wondering whether the Philippians have these resources. He is naming what they already possess and then presenting the bill. “Encouragement” (paraklēsis) is the word for being called alongside, the strengthening that comes from union with Christ, from someone standing with you.

Any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy. “Comfort” (paramythion) is the gentler word, consolation, what you say quietly to someone who is grieving: the comfort of Christ’s love. “Participation” is koinōnia again, the partnership word from chapter 1, now applied to the Holy Spirit himself: shared life in the one Spirit whom all of them have. “Affection” is splanchna once more, the gut word Paul used of his own longing in 1:8, and “sympathy” (oiktirmoi) is compassion, mercy that feels. Four realities, and they are not abstractions. They are the actual furniture of an ordinary Christian’s life.

No excuse for division. Here is the force of the argument, which is easy to miss because we read the list as a warm-up. Paul is saying: you have all of this. You have been strengthened by Christ, comforted in love, made partners in the Spirit, and moved in your own inward parts by mercy. A church that had none of these things might be forgiven for fragmenting. A church that has all four and still cannot get along has not run out of resources; it has declined to spend them.

Complete my joy by being of the same mind. Then the request, and it is startlingly personal. Paul, who has told them in chapter 1 that he rejoices in prison, that he rejoices over rivals, that he will go on rejoicing whatever the verdict, says his joy is not yet full. One thing is missing. Not his release. Not his acquittal. Their unity. He would rather have a united church in Macedonia than an open cell door in Rome, and he says so without embarrassment. “Same mind” is to auto phronēte, think the same thing, and phroneō, thinking, mindset, is a key word in Philippians, appearing about ten times. This is a letter about how Christians think, because how they think decides how they treat one another.

Having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind. What he asks for is spelled out four ways: the same mind, the same love, full accord, one mind. The repetition is not padding; it is a man leaning on a point, because there were tensions in the church (4:2). “Full accord” translates sympsychoi, soul-joined, breathing together. It is possible to disagree with someone about a good deal and still be soul-joined to them; it is equally possible to agree with someone about everything and be nothing of the kind. Paul is after the first, not mere agreement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean agreeing on every opinion. Paul never asks a church to think identically about everything. It means one shared mindset: the mind of Christ (v. 5), the same love, the same direction, the same Lord.

What if the other person will not be reconciled? You are responsible for your part, not theirs. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). So do what is yours to do: confess your own share of the fault without adding but, ask forgiveness, offer it freely, and speak to them directly rather than about them. If they refuse, keep your heart free from bitterness, go on praying for them, treat them with courtesy, and leave the door open. Sometimes a wise third person can help (Matthew 18:16). Unity is a gift of the Spirit you are to keep, not a result you can force; but you can make sure the wall is not being built from your side.

In a sentence. Therefore if you have any encouragement from being united with Christ, if any comfort from his love, if any common sharing in the Spirit, if any tenderness and compassion, then make Paul’s joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being one in spirit and of one mind.

On a Tuesday. Is there a broken or cooled relationship in your church? Before you think about what the other person did, run through Paul’s four ifs and ask whether you have really received them: encouragement in Christ, comfort from his love, the fellowship of the Spirit, his mercy towards you. Then spend one of them on that person this week: a word of encouragement, a kindness, an act of mercy. Work for unity, for Christ’s sake.

For worship. The Father, the Son and the Spirit have lived for ever in perfect oneness, without rivalry or envy, in a love that has never once been strained, and they have drawn sinners into that fellowship. Christ strengthens, his love comforts, the Spirit joins, and mercy moves us from within. Everything a church needs for unity has already been poured out on it from the life of God himself. The oneness he asks of us is only the overflow of the oneness he is, and the oneness he died to create.

verseByVerse.quote: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.

Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit. Now the two roots of division, named exactly. “Selfish ambition” is eritheia, the same word Paul used of the rival preachers in 1:17, the spirit of the hired canvasser working a crowd for his own advancement. “Conceit” is kenodoxia, and the two halves of it repay separating: kenos, empty, and doxa, glory. Empty glory: vainglory, in the old English word. It is the pursuit of a reputation with nothing behind it, wanting to be thought something more than wanting to be something. These are the two great enemies of unity.

How they talk. These two are the engine of nearly every church quarrel that has ever happened, and they very rarely announce themselves. Nobody in Philippi was saying I am pursuing empty glory. They were saying they had concerns about the direction of things, that certain people were not being listened to, that a principle was at stake. That is how eritheia always talks. It never uses its own name.

But in humility. Against them Paul sets tapeinophrosynē, humility, literally lowly-mindedness. In classical Greek the root was mostly an insult, used of the servile and the mean-spirited, a slave’s trait; no self-respecting Greek aspired to it. Christianity took a word for a defect and made it a virtue, because it had seen something that Greece had not: God on a cross.

Count others more significant than yourselves. The verb (hēgeomai) means to reckon, to regard, to judge a thing to be so, and it is the same verb used of Christ in verse 6, who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped”. Paul is asking them to do the sum the way Christ did it. And notice that this is an act of judgement, not a feeling. He is not telling them to feel inferior, which would be both impossible on command and in many cases untrue. He is telling them to assign other people’s interests a higher place in their reckoning than their own. Humility is not thinking less of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less. You can do that on a Tuesday morning whatever you happen to feel.

Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others. “Look” (skopeō) is to watch, to aim at, to keep your eye on. And verse 4 supplies the guard that keeps this from becoming morbid. That little word “only” is doing careful work. Paul is not prohibiting care for yourself, and he is not describing the person who has no legitimate needs of his own. Your interests are real and you may attend to them. They are simply not the only ones in the room. A great deal of unhealthy Christian self-denial has been built by reading this verse with the word only quietly deleted.

What it does not mean. It does not mean false modesty or denying your gifts; Paul himself knew what he had been given and used it. It does not mean pretending every other Christian is wiser or godlier than you. It means putting others first: giving their good, in your planning and choosing, the priority you would naturally give your own.

Does this mean I must let people walk all over me? No. Counting others more significant is a choice to serve, freely made, not a duty to be exploited. Jesus served his disciples and washed their feet, and he also rebuked them, refused the crowd that wanted to make him king, and walked away from those who tried to throw him off a cliff. Looking to another’s interests sometimes means saying no, because indulging someone’s sin is not seeking their good. And this verse never requires anyone to remain under abuse. An abuser’s real interest is repentance, not continued power over you; the vulnerable must be protected, and wrongdoing brought into the light and, where it is a crime, reported. Humility serves; it does not enable evil.

A test. Think of the person in your church you find most difficult. Humility here is not pretending you find them easy, and it is not concluding they are a better Christian than you. It is deciding, before the next conversation, that what they need out of it matters more than what you want out of it. That is the ledger entry. Everything else is sentiment.

In a sentence. Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves, not looking to your own interests but each of you to the interests of the others.

On a Tuesday. Before your next meeting, family conversation or church gathering, decide in advance one way you will look to someone else’s interests in it: the person you will listen to rather than answer, the preference you will let go, the credit you will give away. Then notice afterwards whether you missed anything. Most of us find we lost far less than we feared, and gained a good deal.

For worship. The God who owes nothing to anyone has always looked to the interests of others. The Son came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). He reckoned our need more significant than his own comfort, and did the sum all the way to the cross. Humility was a slave’s word until the Lord of glory wore it, and now it is the family likeness of the children of God, because it is the likeness of their elder Brother.

verseByVerse.quote: Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus,

Have this mind among yourselves. One short verse, and it is the hinge of the letter. “Mind” is phroneō again: an attitude, a way of thinking, and here it is plural and corporate: think this way, together, as a community. This is not primarily an instruction about an individual’s inner attitude, though it certainly includes that. It is about the atmosphere between people: what it feels like to be in that room, whose interests get raised in that meeting. Paul is describing the culture of a congregation, and he is about to ground it in the deepest thing he knows.

Which is yours in Christ Jesus. The verse contains a translation question that changes how the great hymn is heard, so it needs stating plainly. Older versions read: let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus; that is, imitate him, here is your example. The ESV reads: which is yours in Christ Jesus; that is, this is the mind that belongs to you because you are united to him. The Greek is compressed, the second half has no verb, and translators must supply one. Both readings are true. The mind of Christ is our model and our possession.

Why the difference matters. Take the verse as pure example and the hymn becomes a mountain to climb: be as humble as God was, which is a command guaranteed to crush anyone who takes it seriously. Take it as union and something else happens. The mind of Christ is not only an ideal held out in front of you; it is a possession already given to you because you are in him. Paul is saying: this is now the atmosphere of the place where you live; behave like it. And that is Paul’s pattern everywhere. He never begins with the demand. He begins with what is true of you in Christ and then tells you to live there. The command always rests on the gift, and reversing them turns the gospel into mere religion within a single sentence.

The Christ hymn. Verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung in worship before Paul wrote, or composed by Paul himself. It has a poetic structure: Christ’s descent (vv. 6–8) and his exaltation (vv. 9–11). It is among the earliest and highest statements of Christ’s deity, written within about thirty years of the crucifixion. And notice why Paul reaches for it. The hymn that follows is not first a proof-text about the two natures of Christ, though it is that and the church has rightly fought over it. It is first an argument about how to behave in a church meeting. Paul reaches for the incarnation to settle a squabble, which tells you both how seriously he took the squabble and how practical he expected his highest doctrine to be.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can copy Christ’s atoning work. Nobody else empties himself from the form of God, and nobody else’s death redeems the world. We copy his attitude, and we can do even that only because his atoning work has joined us to him.

Can I really have the mind of Christ? How? Yes, if you are in Christ, because the Spirit who lived in him now lives in you, and we have the mind of Christ (1 Corinthians 2:16). It grows in three ways. First, by looking at him: in the Gospels, in this hymn, in the Lord’s Supper. We are changed into the likeness of what we behold (2 Corinthians 3:18). Second, by asking for it, since this is a work God delights to do (2:13). Third, by practising it in small decisions: choosing the lower seat, the hidden service, the other person’s good. You will fail often. But it is already yours to grow into, not a foreign mind to be manufactured.

In a sentence. In your relationships with one another, have the same mindset as Christ Jesus:

On a Tuesday. Before a decision today, large or small, ask not only what would be right but what would be like him: what would the humble mind of Christ do here, for this person? And remember that the question is not a ladder you must climb alone. It is the mind of the one you belong to, and he is in you.

For worship. The highest truth about God, that the Son of God came down, is given to us not only to be admired from afar but to be lived in the kitchen and the church meeting. Christ does not merely show us his mind and leave us to copy it. He shares it, by uniting us to himself. The humility of God has become the atmosphere of his people’s home, and the one who descended from the throne lives in us still, making us like himself.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn.

verseByVerse.quote: who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,
verseByVerse.commentary:
who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,

Who, though he was in the form of God. The word is morphē, and it does not mean shape or outward appearance in the way the English form can suggest. It means the outward expression of what something genuinely is: the visible reality of an inner nature. To be in the form of God is to be God, showing. Christ possessed the nature of God, with all its glory. He was, and is, God.

Was. And note the tense. “Was” (hyparchōn) means existing, being: his continual state before the incarnation, already, before the sentence gets anywhere near Bethlehem. Paul is not describing a man who was promoted. He is describing someone who was there first. And the same word will return in verse 7, where he takes the form of a servant. Whatever happened at the incarnation, it was not the exchange of one appearance for another. He who really was God really became a slave.

Did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped. Then the hinge of the whole hymn. “Equality with God” (isa theō): he was equal with God. The noun behind grasped is harpagmos, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and has given scholars a great deal of trouble. The root means to seize or snatch; it is the root behind the Harpies, the snatchers of Greek legend. Two readings are possible. Either he lacked equality with God and refused to snatch at it, or he possessed it and refused to exploit it, to hold on to it for his own advantage. The first cannot be right, because the line before has just said he was in the form of God. So it is the second: he held it by right, and would not use it for himself.

The second Adam. That distinction is the moral centre of the passage. The temptation Christ refused was not the temptation to become something he was not. It was the temptation to use what he genuinely was for his own advantage. Adam, who was not God, grasped at being like God (Genesis 3:5). Christ, who was God, did not grasp. And it was precisely the temptation Satan brought to him in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11): you are the Son of God, so use it, feed yourself, prove it, take the kingdoms now without the cross. He would not. He had every right and opened his hands.

Aimed at the quarrel. And that is why this verse is aimed straight at the Philippian quarrel. The question in a church fight is almost never whether I have a right here. Usually you do. The question is what you do with the right you have. Christ’s answer, holding the highest rights in the universe, was to decline to press them for himself. Anyone who has ever been genuinely wronged in a congregation knows how much that costs, and how little like weakness it is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was not equal with God and tried to become so. He was equal, and did not use it for himself. Nor does form of God mean that he only looked like God or was a lesser divine being. The word means the real nature showing.

If Jesus is God, how can he be distinct from the Father? This is the mystery of the Trinity, and Scripture teaches both sides plainly. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), and the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each fully God, three persons sharing the one divine nature, distinct but never divided. The Son is not a part of God or a lesser god; he is equal with the Father in power and glory (Westminster 2.3). In this hymn you can see both truths: he was in the form of God, and yet he obeyed the Father and was exalted by the Father. We cannot fully understand how God is three and one, but we can worship, because this is how he has shown himself.

In a sentence. Who, being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage;

On a Tuesday. Name a right you hold in some relationship: to be listened to, to have your way on a decision, to be thanked, to have the last word. It may be a real right. Ask what it would look like this week to open your hand over it for someone else’s good, as Christ did with infinitely more.

For worship. Before there was a world, the Son shared the glory of the Father, equal in majesty, power and honour. He did not need us, and he did not need to come. He held the highest place by right, and he would not clutch it. Where Adam grasped and fell, he opened his hands and stooped. Worship Jesus as God, equal with the Father, who would not cling to his rights for our sake. There is no other God like this.

verseByVerse.quote: but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.

But emptied himself. The verb is ekenōsen, from kenoō, to empty, make of no account, pour out; from it theology gets the word kenosis, and it needs handling with care, because it has been made to say things Paul did not say. Look at the sentence: there is no object. Paul does not write he emptied himself of his divinity, or of his glory, or of anything else. He writes that he emptied himself, and then immediately explains how: by taking the form of a servant. The emptying is not subtraction. It is addition. He did not become less God; he took to himself what he had never had before: a human nature, a body, a mother, a birth. He emptied himself not by subtracting his deity but by adding humanity, and by setting aside the privileges and glory he had a right to.

Veiled, not surrendered. What he laid aside was not deity but its independent exercise for his own benefit: the free use of what was his. The glory was veiled, not surrendered; it broke out once on a mountain (Matthew 17:2) to show it had been there all along. The Son who holds the universe together grew tired (John 4:6), needed sleep (Mark 4:38), asked questions, and said he did not know the day or the hour (Mark 13:32). Not because his divine knowledge had been destroyed, but because he had taken a genuine human life and would live it genuinely, depending on the Father and the Spirit.

By taking the form of a servant. The same word, form (morphē), as verse 6. He truly became a servant, as truly as he was God. Doulos, slave: and there is the word from 1:1, where Paul introduced himself. The apostle called himself the slave of Christ; here is Christ becoming a slave. Paul’s self-description was not modesty; it was imitation, and now we can see of what. The highest became the lowest. Pause on how strange this would have sounded in Philippi. The Greek world had stories of gods appearing in human shape, but they were disguises, put on and taken off, and no god in them ever became a slave. The Roman world had a ladder of status that every citizen understood and spent his life climbing. Paul announces a God who came down the ladder, all the way, on purpose.

Being born in the likeness of men. “Likeness” (homoiōma) guards a real truth on both sides. He was truly human: not a phantom, not God in a costume, like us in every way except sin (Hebrews 2:17; 4:15). But likeness leaves room for the difference: he was human as we are, sin excepted. And the word born carries its own quiet astonishment. The one who was in the form of God arrived the way every one of us arrives, helpless, at somebody else’s mercy, unable to lift his own head. Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Where Christians differ: what did Christ empty himself of? Kenotic theories teach that the Son gave up some divine attributes, such as omniscience or omnipotence, when he became man. Verdict: the Son did not cease to be God or lose any divine attribute; God cannot stop being God. He emptied himself by taking human nature and the role of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine rights for his own benefit. He remained fully God while becoming fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion or change (Chalcedonian Definition; Westminster 8.2). During his earthly life, he chose to depend on the Spirit and the Father. He was not less than God in the manger, and he was not less than man on the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was only part God or only part man, or a mixture of the two. He is fully both, one person for ever.

If Jesus was God, how could he not know the day of his return? Because he had two natures, divine and human, in one person. As God, the Son knows all things. As man, he had a true human mind that grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and knew what the Father gave him to know for his mission. When he said he did not know the day (Mark 13:32), he was speaking truly of his human knowledge. This is not a contradiction but the wonder of the incarnation: the eternal Son really did live a human life from the inside, with its limits, without ever ceasing to be what he always was. It means he understands our limits too.

In a sentence. Rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness.

On a Tuesday. Look for one task this week that only a servant would do: the job nobody notices, the service nobody will thank you for, the person nobody else wants to help. Do it quietly, and remember who did it first, and for whom.

For worship. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The Creator was laid in a manger he had made; the Lord of angels took the form of a slave; the one who fills heaven and earth was carried in his mother’s arms. He did not lay aside his glory because he had too much of it, but because we had none. Marvel at the humility of God the Son becoming a servant, and bow before him, because nothing in all of history is lower or higher than this.

verseByVerse.quote: And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

And being found in human form. The descent is not finished. Verse 7 brought him from God to man; verse 8 takes him from man to a criminal’s execution, in steps, each lower than the last. “Form” here is a different word, schēma, outward appearance, bearing. He looked like any other man. There was no halo in Nazareth.

He humbled himself. “Humbled” (tapeinoō) is to make low, from the same root as the humility of verse 3. The first humbling was becoming man at all; this is a second step down, taken from inside the human life. Having become one of us, he went on going down. And the verb is active and reflexive: he humbled himself. Nothing was done to him that he did not accept. That matters when you come to the arrest and the trial, where he looks entirely passive. He is not a man overtaken by events. He is a man descending on purpose: no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

By becoming obedient to the point of death. Obedient to whom? To the Father. He obeyed perfectly, all the way, even to death (Hebrews 5:8). Stop there, because obedience implies a will that can be submitted, and here is the eternal Son submitting his human will to his Father’s in a garden at night: not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). “To the point of death” is how far the obedience ran before it stopped, which is to say it never stopped. And his obedience is our righteousness. By the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). Every day of that obedient life was lived on behalf of people who had not obeyed.

Even death on a cross. Then Paul adds words his readers would have felt in their stomachs. We have made the cross jewellery, and it takes an effort to recover what it was. Crucifixion was designed not merely to kill but to degrade: public, naked, slow, deliberately obscene. It was the most shameful form of Roman execution, reserved for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals. Roman citizens, like many in Philippi, could not normally be crucified. Cicero said the very word cross should be kept far from the eyes, ears and thoughts of a Roman citizen. And Philippi was a Roman colony full of citizens who knew exactly what that meant.

The floor of the universe. So follow the line all the way down. From the form of God, to the form of a slave, to death, to the one death the empire kept for slaves. He began at the highest point there is and did not stop descending until he reached the lowest point available in the world he had made. And there is one more depth the Romans could not see: to hang on a tree was to die under the curse of God’s own law (Deuteronomy 21:23). Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). That is the floor of the universe, and he touched it.

Why did he have to die, and on a cross? Because our sin deserved the curse, and he came to bear it in our place. God is holy and just; sin cannot simply be overlooked. At the cross the Father laid on his Son the penalty we owed, so that it could be lifted from us: for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The manner of his death matters: the cursed death of the tree showed that he was carrying the curse of the law, and the shameful death of a slave showed how low love would go. This is penal substitution, and it is the heart of the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the cross was only an example of humility. It was the atoning sacrifice for sin, once for all. But it is also the supreme example, and Paul uses it that way here. Do not lose why he is telling them this. He is settling an argument in a small church about who gets deferred to. His argument is that the Lord of glory went from the throne to the gallows, and that this is now the mind they live inside. Set any grievance you are currently holding beside that descent and see whether it survives the comparison.

In a sentence. And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross!

On a Tuesday. Take the grievance you are holding most tightly, the slight, the unfairness, the person who has not apologised, and set it in your mind beside the cross. Do not pretend it did not happen. Simply ask whether, in the light of how far he went down for you, you can let it go a little further down too. Then pray for the person by name.

For worship. Look at the cross and see how low Christ went for you. He obeyed where we rebelled; he was cursed where we deserved to be; he was shamed so that we could be welcomed; he died the death of a slave so that slaves of sin could become sons of God. The one who was in the form of God hung naked on a Roman tree outside the city wall, and it was not defeat. It was obedience, all the way down, and love that would not stop until there was nowhere lower to go.
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful form of Roman execution.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

Therefore God has highly exalted him. “Therefore.” The hymn turns on that word, and the whole direction of travel reverses. Everything from verse 6 has been descent; from here it is all ascent. And the therefore says the second follows from the first. This is the pattern of the entire gospel, and Jesus stated it as a law: he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11). The way down is the way up. “Highly exalted” (hyperypsoō) is super-exalted, lifted above and beyond: resurrection, ascension, enthronement at God’s right hand (Acts 2:33; Ephesians 1:20–21).

Who acts. Note carefully who acts. Through the descent, Christ was the subject of every verb: he did not count, he emptied, he humbled. Now he is the object: God has highly exalted him, God has bestowed on him the name. The Son did not lift himself. He went down as far as there is to go and left the raising to his Father, which is exactly what he had told his disciples to do, and exactly what the people quarrelling in Philippi were failing to do. If you are busy exalting yourself, you have taken over the Father’s job.

And bestowed on him the name that is above every name. Which name? Not Jesus in itself; that was a common name in first-century Palestine, and he had borne it from birth. Verse 11 tells us: the confession that is coming is “Jesus Christ is Lord.” Kyrios, Lord, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses to render the divine name, Yahweh, the name too holy to pronounce. What is given to the risen Christ is God’s own name. The name above every name.

So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow. And then Paul does the most audacious thing in the letter. The words echo Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD says, “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.” Read the context of that chapter and you will find the most uncompromising monotheism in the Old Testament: I am the LORD, and there is no other (Isaiah 45:5, 18), from the God who says elsewhere, my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8). Paul takes the homage that God there reserves exclusively to himself, and says it is given to Jesus. There is no higher statement about Christ anywhere in the New Testament, and it was written within thirty years of the crucifixion.

In heaven and on earth and under the earth. The phrase sweeps the whole of created reality. In heaven: angels. On earth: humans. Under the earth: the dead, and perhaps demons. All creation, every rational creature, will bow.

And every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. This is the earliest Christian creed: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3). In Philippi, a Roman colony, the loyal phrase was that Caesar is lord; to say Jesus is Lord was to say who really holds the throne.

To the glory of God the Father. The last line keeps the whole thing in proportion. The Son’s exaltation is not a rival to the Father’s honour but the means of it: whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him (John 5:23). There is no competition inside the Trinity, no jockeying for position, which is precisely the disease Paul is treating in the Philippian church. He has shown them a God in whom there is no eritheia at all, and asked them to live inside that.

Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved? Some read this as meaning every person will eventually confess Christ willingly and be saved. Verdict: every knee will bow and every tongue confess, but not all willingly or savingly. Some will confess in joyful worship; others will be compelled to acknowledge his lordship at the judgement (Romans 14:10–11; Revelation 20:11–15). Isaiah 45:24 adds that all who were incensed against him will come to him and be ashamed. The letter itself forbids the universalist reading: Paul has just spoken of the destruction of the opponents (1:28) and will speak of those whose end is destruction (3:19). This is the universal acknowledgement of Christ’s lordship, not universal salvation. Hell is real and eternal (Matthew 25:46). The question this passage puts to a reader is not whether you will acknowledge him, but when, and in which posture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became God at his exaltation. He was always in the form of God (v. 6). He was exalted as the God-man, the Mediator: the one who had always shared the Father’s glory now received, in his human nature too, the honour due to his finished work.

Did Jesus earn his exaltation? In a sense, yes, as the Mediator, and that is good news for us. The Son did not need to earn his divine glory; he always had it (John 17:5). But as the obedient man who finished the work the Father gave him, he was rewarded with exaltation, and he was exalted not for himself alone but as the head of his people. Where he has gone, we will follow. The reward of his obedience is given to all who are united to him: because he lives, we will live also.

What does it mean to confess Jesus as Lord now? It means saying freely now what everyone will say one day. Confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, and you will be saved (Romans 10:9). It is more than words. It means owning him as your rightful King: trusting him to save you, obeying him when it costs, letting his word overrule your preferences, and naming him openly before others. To bow now is joy and life. To bow then, without having bowed now, is shame. The knee that bends today will never be ashamed.

In a sentence. Therefore God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

On a Tuesday. Bow your knee to Jesus today, willingly and joyfully: one day everyone will. Name one area of your life where you have not yet let him be Lord, your money, your tongue, your screen, your plans, and confess his lordship there, in prayer and then in action. And when you are tempted to push yourself forward, remember who does the exalting, and leave it to him.

For worship. The crucified one is enthroned. The hands that were nailed now hold the sceptre of the universe, and the name that was mocked over the cross is the name before which angels fall. He went down to the lowest place, and the Father has lifted him to the highest. Every knee will bow to him, in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and the whole creation will confess what his people already sing: Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.note: The words echo a passage where the LORD says every knee will bow to him alone; Paul applies them to Jesus.
