verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — Working Out What God Works In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them, now that he is absent, to keep working out their salvation with reverent seriousness, because God himself is at work in them, giving both the desire and the power to do his will. They are to stop grumbling and arguing, so that, like stars in a dark sky, they shine with blameless lives in a twisted world as they hold on to the message of life. Then Paul will know on the last day that his work among them was not wasted. Even if his life is poured out like a drink offering on their faith, he is glad, and they should share his gladness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereignty and Responsibility in Sanctification

Verses 12–13 are the New Testament’s most exact statement of how holiness actually works, and the decisive word is the little conjunction between them. Paul does not write “work out your salvation, but remember God is working too,” as though effort and grace divided the task between them. He writes work, for God is at work. Divine agency is the ground of human effort, not its rival. The two do not compete for the same square inch; they rise and fall together.

And the working-in reaches further than the ability to obey: God works “both to will and to work.” He is beneath the desire itself. A Christian who finds in himself a genuine wish to please God is looking at evidence of grace, not of good character. This is why “fear and trembling” is the fitting posture — not the dread that God might drop him, which 1:6 has already excluded, but the seriousness of a man who has realised whose workshop he is standing in. Note also that every pronoun here is plural: Paul is telling a congregation with a quarrel in it to work this out together.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had a good record of obedience, but it had been built with an apostle available. Paul’s concern is what happens now that he is in chains and may never return — and the first sin he names is the wilderness sin of murmuring.

Now: Grumbling is the respectable Christian’s sin, and almost no one repents of it. Verse 13 is the word for the believer who feels the gap between who he is and who he longs to be: the longing itself is God’s doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed. “Therefore” ties this to the hymn: because Christ obeyed all the way down, and because God raised him, therefore work. They have been obedient. And Paul calls them beloved before he asks anything of them.

So now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence. Paul frames it with a compliment and a challenge. They have a good record, but their record was built with an apostle in the room, or at least on the road. The real test is now, with him in a cell and unable to come. Their obedience is not to Paul but to God. Obedience that requires supervision is not yet obedience; it is compliance.

Work out your own salvation. Three things need saying, because few verses have been more misread. First, work out is not work for. The verb katergazesthe means to carry a thing through to its finish, to bring out what is there, as one works out a seam of ore that is already in the ground. Nobody works for a salvation Paul has already told them God began and will complete (1:6). They are working out what has been worked in.

Together. Second, the pronoun is plural throughout. English hides this; your own salvation sounds like a private project. Paul is addressing a congregation with a quarrel in it, and the whole context from verse 1 has been corporate. In context, working out includes working out their life together as a community, in unity. Read individually, the verse becomes an anxious solo performance. Read as Paul wrote it, it is a body doing this work in one another’s company.

With fear and trembling. Third, fear and trembling is not terror of hell. Paul uses the same phrase of his own weakness in Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3) and of a slave’s service to his master (Ephesians 6:5), so it cannot mean dread of damnation. It is reverent awe before God, and humble dependence: the seriousness of someone who knows what he is handling. The trembling is not the fear that God might drop you; it is the awe of discovering that God is at work in you, and that you had better not be careless in his workshop.

For it is God who works in you. Then verse 13, which supplies the reason and turns the whole thing on its head. Notice the logic. Paul does not say work hard, but remember God is also working, as though the two were in competition, each taking a share. He says work, because God is working. God’s activity is the ground of ours, not its rival. The verb is energeō, to energise, to be at work, from which we get energy.

Both to will and to work for his good pleasure. And see how deep it goes. Not merely the power to obey once you have decided: the wanting too. God gives both the desire and the ability. He gets under the desire itself. Which means that the Christian who notices in himself a genuine desire to please God is looking at evidence of God at work, not at his own good character. The wanting was a gift before the doing was. And he does it for his good pleasure: because it pleases him to. You are not a project he took on reluctantly.

Where Christians differ: God’s work and ours. Some say sanctification is all God’s work and we are passive; others that it is all our effort. Verdict: both are fully true. God works in us; therefore we work out. Our working does not compete with his; it is the result of his. This is not cooperation as equal partners, but our real activity flowing from his prior and deeper work (Westminster 16.3). We pray as if everything depends on God, because it does, and work because God is working.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our effort. It is God’s work from start to finish. But it is lived out through our effort: real choices, real discipline, real fighting against sin.

How do I know whether I am working out my salvation or just trying hard in my own strength? Look at where the effort is aimed and what it leans on. Effort in your own strength is anxious, proud when it succeeds and despairing when it fails, and it rarely prays. Working out what God has worked in begins in prayer, uses the means he gives (his word, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church), keeps going after failure because it rests on his promise and not on its record, and gives him the thanks when it succeeds. The test is not how hard you try but whom you are trusting while you try.

I feel the gap between who I am and who I long to be. Is God still working? Yes. If you feel the gap between the person you are and the person you long to be, that gap is not proof that God has left you to it. The longing itself is his. He is not standing at the end of the road waiting to see whether you make it; he is in you, this morning, producing both the appetite and the ability. Take the next small step of obedience in front of you, and thank him for the desire to take it.

In a sentence. Therefore, dear friends, as you have always obeyed, not only in Paul’s presence but now much more in his absence, continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you to will and to act in order to fulfil his good purpose.

On a Tuesday. Pick the area of your life where obedience is hardest at the moment. Pray first, asking God to work in you to will and to do. Then take one concrete step today, not waiting until you feel strong. And ask how your church, not only you, needs to work out its salvation together: is there a relationship, a ministry, a habit of speech in your congregation that needs your share of the work?

For worship. God does not save his people and then leave them to manage. He works in them, under their desires, giving them a new will and the strength to act, and he does it because it gives him pleasure. Every good desire we have ever had was his gift before it was our choice. He began the work, he works it in, and he will finish it. And so we work, not trembling lest he let go, but trembling with wonder that the living God has made our hearts his workshop.

verseByVerse.quote: Do all things without grumbling or disputing,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do all things without grumbling or disputing,

Do all things without grumbling. Seven words in English, and it is one of the most searching commands in the New Testament, precisely because it addresses a sin almost nobody repents of. “Grumbling” is gongysmos, and the word sounds like what it means: a low muttering. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses over and over for Israel in the wilderness: murmuring about the water, the food, the leadership, the destination (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27; 1 Corinthians 10:10). And remember what that murmuring cost. It was not a minor flaw in an otherwise faithful generation. It was the thing that kept them out of the land and turned a journey of weeks into forty years of funerals. God took it as an insult aimed past Moses at himself, because that is what it was.

Or disputing. “Disputing” (dialogismos) is the other half: the arguing, the questioning, the endless relitigating of decisions, quarrelsome arguments that divide. Grumbling is what happens in the car on the way home; disputing is what happens in the meeting. Between them they can hollow out a church while every doctrine on the noticeboard stays orthodox.

All things. Note the scope. Paul allows no category of exception: not the genuinely annoying, not the badly organised, not the decision that really was wrong. And notice where it stands. It comes immediately after the highest teaching about Christ in the New Testament and immediately after God is at work in you. The application of the Christ hymn, the thing Paul reaches for first after the throne and the cross and the name above every name, is: stop muttering.

The respectable sin. That is deliberate, and it is a mercy. Most of us would find it easier to be told to do something heroic. Grumbling is the sin of the respectable Christian: it never gets anyone disciplined, it feels like honesty, it can even be framed as discernment. But trace it to its root and it is a complaint about the way God is running things, delivered to a third party because it cannot be said out loud to him. Which is exactly what it was in the wilderness. And there is a reason it comes precisely here, after God works in you. Grumbling is the natural response of someone who believes he is on his own with a set of circumstances he did not choose. If God is genuinely at work in the situation and in you, the muttering loses its footing. Paul does not tell them to cheer up; he tells them who is in the room.

What it does not mean. It does not mean never expressing concerns or lament. The Psalms are full of honest complaint brought to God, and Paul himself was frank about his troubles. It means rejecting a complaining spirit: the muttering that goes sideways to others instead of upwards to God, and that assumes the worst about him and about people.

Is all complaining sin? No. There is a difference between lament and grumbling. Lament takes the pain to God, honestly, even angrily, and ends in trust: how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1), and then, I have trusted in your steadfast love (13:5). Grumbling takes the pain to everyone except God and ends in bitterness. Lament is faith in distress; grumbling is unbelief in conversation. So weep, ask, and pour out your heart to him. What you must refuse is the muttering that hardens into a settled grievance against God or his people.

How do I raise a real concern without grumbling? Take it to God first and pray about it until your heart is not hot. Then take it to the person who can actually do something about it, not to everyone else (Matthew 18:15). Speak plainly and kindly, assuming good motives where you honestly can. Suggest a remedy if you have one, and offer to help. Then accept the outcome graciously, even if you still disagree, unless a matter of conscience or sin is at stake. A concern raised this way builds a church. The same concern muttered in the car park tears it down.

In a sentence. Do everything without grumbling or arguing,

On a Tuesday. Run a test for one week: when something goes wrong, notice whether your first instinct is to take it to God or to tell someone about it. The wilderness generation always chose the second. So, usually, do we. Each time you catch yourself muttering, stop and turn it into a prayer, and then into a thanksgiving for one thing God has given in the same situation.

For worship. The Lord who led Israel through the wilderness fed them every morning with bread from heaven, gave them water from the rock, and bore with their murmuring for forty years. His patience outlasted their grumbling. And his Son walked a harder road than the wilderness and opened his mouth only to bless, to pray and to forgive; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, he did not complain. The one who gives us every good thing, and is at work in us, deserves a people whose mouths are full of thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.

That you may be blameless and innocent. Now the purpose, and it is a good deal larger than a quieter church. “Blameless” (amemptos) means no just cause for blame. “Innocent” (akeraios) means unmixed, pure, like wine not watered down or metal without alloy.

Children of God without blemish. “Without blemish” (amōmos) is drawn from the sacrificial system: it is what an animal had to be to be offered at all. Paul is looking at a congregation and using the language of what goes on the altar. And notice the name he gives them before the description: children of God. It is not a title they must earn by being blameless. It is who they are, and blamelessness is the family likeness.

In the midst of a crooked and twisted generation. The phrase is a quotation from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:5), and Paul has done something sharp with it. In Deuteronomy the crooked and twisted generation is Israel: God’s own people in the wilderness, murmuring. Paul lifts the phrase and applies it to the surrounding unbelieving world, having just warned the church against the very sin that earned Israel the label. The line between the crooked generation and the children without blemish is not drawn by ancestry. It is drawn by grumbling. And note the preposition: in the midst. Believers live in the middle of it, not withdrawn from it.

Among whom you shine as lights in the world. “Lights” is phōstēres, and it is not the word for a lamp. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 1:14–16 for the sun, moon and stars, the luminaries God hung in the sky. It echoes Daniel 12:3, where those who are wise shine like the brightness of the sky and like the stars for ever. So the picture is not a candle in a room. It is a small church in a garrison town set into the dark like a star, visible for the same reason stars are visible: because it is dark. The darkness does not defeat the light; it is what makes it possible to see. You are the light of the world, Jesus said (Matthew 5:14–16).

A star does not lecture. And a star does not shine at people. It simply is what it is, and anyone who looks up can see it. Paul’s picture of Christian witness here is not primarily a message delivered but a community visible, which is why the command that produces it was about grumbling. A church that does not mutter is already preaching something to a city that does.

Holding fast to the word of life. The verb epechontes can mean either holding fast or holding out: gripping something tightly, or extending it to someone. Both fit, and the ambiguity is a happy one. The church clings to the gospel for its own life and holds it out to a world that has none. You cannot do the second for long without the first. And it is the word of life: the gospel gives life, because it is the word about the one who is the life.

So that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain. Then the verse ends somewhere unexpected. The metaphors are athletic and agricultural: the runner and the labourer. And here is Paul, who has just written the most self-effacing passage in Scripture, admitting frankly that on the last day he wants something to show for his life. There is nothing unhealthy in it. He does not say he wants to be admired; he says he wants his running not to have been for nothing. Their faithfulness will prove his work was not wasted. This is what a pastor’s ambition looks like when it has been converted: the people are the prize.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians are sinless; Paul will say in the next chapter that he has not already obtained it (3:12). It means their lives should be visibly different, and that when they fail, they confess and are cleansed, which is itself part of the difference.

Should Christians withdraw from a corrupt world? No. Stars shine in the night sky, not in a bunker. Jesus prayed not that his Father would take his people out of the world, but that he would keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). So stay in your workplace, your street, your school, your family. Be careful about what shapes you: guard your heart and choose your closest influences wisely. But do not mistake isolation for holiness. A light hidden under a basket has not been kept pure; it has simply stopped being a light.

How do I shine without being self-righteous? Remember that the light is borrowed. You shine as the moon does, by reflecting the sun, and you were part of the crooked generation yourself until God called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. So be honest about your own failures; humility is part of the shine. Be kind, generous, truthful and cheerful, especially in hard circumstances. Do not grumble about the culture as though you were better than it. And when people ask, be ready to point them to the source of the light rather than to yourself.

In a sentence. So that you may become blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a warped and crooked generation. Then you will shine among them like stars in the sky as you hold firmly to the word of life. And then Paul will be able to boast on the day of Christ that he did not run or labour in vain.

On a Tuesday. Think of the darkest place you will be this week: the office culture, the group chat, the family gathering. That is where you are meant to shine. Decide one thing you will refuse to do there (join the grumbling, the gossip, the cynicism) and one thing you will do (an honest word, a kindness, a word about Christ if the door opens). Then thank God for the person whose faithfulness helped bring you to the light.

For worship. God who said let light shine out of darkness has made his light shine in the hearts of his people, and set them like stars in the night of this world. He makes crooked people straight, makes blemished people his unblemished children, and sends them out holding the word of life. Christ is the light of the world, and in his light his people shine. On the day of Christ, when every work is tested, no gospel labour done in his name will be found to have been in vain.

parallels.desc: those who are wise shall shine

verseByVerse.quote: Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all. Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all. Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me.

Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering. The image is precise, and Paul’s readers would have caught it at once, whether they thought of the temple in Jerusalem or the altars of Philippi. The drink offering was wine poured out with a sacrifice (Numbers 28:7): the last act, the smallest quantity, the thing that completed an offering someone else had brought. Paul pictures his possible death as his life poured out. He will use the image once more, years later, when the possibility has become a certainty: “For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come” (2 Timothy 4:6).

Upon the sacrificial offering of your faith. Now watch how Paul distributes the roles, because it is startling. He is not the sacrifice. Their faith is the sacrifice, their faith and service offered to God (Romans 12:1), the main event on the altar. His own violent death, if it comes, is merely the cup of wine poured over the top of theirs. The apostle casts himself as the small addition to the offering of an obscure congregation in Macedonia. Consider what a man has to believe about his own importance to write that sentence while awaiting a capital trial. And notice that it makes his execution an act of worship rather than a political accident. Rome thinks it is disposing of a troublemaker. Paul sees a priest at an altar. He is not being killed; he is being poured.

I am glad and rejoice with you all. Even facing death, he rejoices. Four verbs of joy in two verses, on the subject of his own execution. This is not stoicism, which grits its teeth and feels nothing, and it is not denial. It is the settled gladness of a man who worked the question out in chapter 1, to die is gain, to depart and be with Christ is far better, and has nothing left to be afraid of.

Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me. The command is the harder half. He does not merely tell them not to grieve; he tells them to rejoice with him. Joy is the keynote of the letter. That is a genuine demand, and anyone who has sat with a dying Christian who was more at peace than the family around the bed knows exactly how demanding it is. Paul is asking them to look at his death from his side of it. Grief is not forbidden; he himself speaks of sorrow upon sorrow ten verses later. But he refuses to let the church treat his death as a defeat, because it is not one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s death atones for anything. Christ’s sacrifice is the only atoning sacrifice, offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). What believers offer is an offering of thanks, not of atonement: their faith, their service, their bodies, and if God wills, their lives.

Was Paul in fact martyred? Not at this point, it seems. He expected release (1:25; 2:24), and the letters to Timothy and Titus suggest he was freed and travelled again. Early Christian tradition says he was later imprisoned a second time and executed in Rome under Nero, in the mid-60s AD, by beheading, as a Roman citizen. 2 Timothy, written near the end, shows the drink offering finally being poured, and Paul still at peace: the time of my departure has come.

How can I rejoice when a Christian I love is dying? You do not have to choose between grief and joy; in a believer they can run together. Weep, because death is an enemy and parting hurts. And rejoice, because for them it is gain, and their life has been an offering God accepted. Tell them what their faith has meant to you. Pray with them, read them the promises, sing if they want to sing. Many Christians have found that the joy came not by forcing it but by looking at death from the dying believer’s side, as Paul asks, and seeing Christ waiting there.

In a sentence. But even if Paul is being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service coming from your faith, he is glad and rejoices with all of you. So you too should be glad and rejoice with him.

On a Tuesday. Ask what in your ordinary life could be an offering to God: the work you will do today, the care you give a child or a parent, the money in your account, the hours of a hard week. Offer it to him in so many words this morning. And if you are facing loss, ask God for the kind of joy that does not deny the sorrow but rises under it.

For worship. Christ poured out his life once for all, the true sacrifice that takes away sin, and now the lives of his people become offerings of thanks on his altar. He accepts the faith of obscure congregations and the blood of his martyrs, and makes them fragrant. And he gives his servants such joy in him that they can speak of their own deaths as a cup poured out in worship. No life given to him is wasted, and no death in him is a defeat.
verseByVerse.note: A drink offering was wine poured out with a sacrifice, completing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–30 — Two Men Who Show You the Mind of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul hopes to send Timothy soon to bring back news of them. No one else shares his concern for them so genuinely; others are taken up with their own affairs, but Timothy has proved himself, serving with Paul in the gospel like a son with his father. Paul himself hopes to come later. Meanwhile he is sending back Epaphroditus, the man they sent to look after him, who fell ill and nearly died, but whom God spared, sparing Paul grief upon grief. Epaphroditus is homesick and upset that they heard he was ill, so Paul sends him gladly and asks them to welcome and honour him, because he risked his life for Christ’s work to do for Paul what they could not.
verseByVerse.theology:
Virtue Has to Be Seen in a Face

Reformed ethics has never treated Christian character as an abstraction. It is a way of living that exists only in particular people, and Paul’s method here follows his Lord’s: after the doctrine, a person. Timothy embodies 2:4 — looking to the interests of others — and Epaphroditus embodies 2:7–8, pouring himself out to the point of nearly dying. Neither is presented as an exceptional case. They are what the gospel ordinarily produces in people it has actually got hold of.

Two pastoral truths sit inside this section and should not be missed. First, Paul could not heal Epaphroditus. The apostle through whom God worked extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12) here watched a friend nearly die and credited the recovery to mercy alone. Healing is a gift God gives as he chooses, never a technique the church operates. Second, Paul admits to sorrow, and to sorrow that could have been piled upon sorrow. The man who wrote “rejoice always” was carrying grief while he wrote it. Joy in this letter runs underneath sadness; it does not replace it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Epaphroditus had been sent from Philippi to stay and serve, and was returning early, ill and with the job unfinished. Every congregation contains people ready to draw conclusions about that. Paul heads them off before the man reaches the gate — he is not coming back a failure, he is coming back a soldier who gambled his life and lost his health doing it. The phrase “to complete what was lacking in your service to me” is not a rebuke of Philippian stinginess; what was lacking was simply the one thing some eight hundred miles prevented them from sending, their own presence.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be cheered by news of you. For I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be cheered by news of you. For I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare.

I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon. After the highest teaching about Christ in the New Testament, travel arrangements. That is not an anticlimax; it is the point. Paul has spent eleven verses on the mind of Christ and seven more on how a church should live it, and now he introduces two men in whom it can actually be seen. The Philippians did not need another idea. They needed a face. And even the itinerary is held inside Christ: Paul’s plans are in the Lord. He does not make plans and then ask God to bless them; he holds his intentions in a hand that may close on them, and he will say so again in verse 23: as soon as I see how it will go with me.

So that I too may be cheered by news of you. A small clause that is easy to walk past. The verb is eupsycheō, which appears nowhere else in the New Testament: literally to be good in soul, to have one’s spirit lifted. Paul is not sending Timothy chiefly to inspect them or to correct them. Timothy would bring back news, and hearing it will do Paul good. Here is the man who rejoices in prison, who is glad about his own possible execution, and he admits that he needs cheering up and that news from this church is what would do it. Contentment in Paul is never self-sufficiency. He needed people.

For I have no one like him. The Greek is a single word, isopsychos, of equal soul, like-minded: nobody else of one soul with me. Timothy shares Paul’s heart. And what makes him unique is not his ability.

Who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare. “Genuinely” (gnēsiōs) means sincerely, and the root means true-born, legitimate: not the counterfeit article. Plenty of people can produce concern for a congregation when the situation calls for it. Timothy’s was the real thing, and Paul, who had watched him for perhaps a dozen years, could tell the difference. Timothy embodies the humble mind of verse 4: looking to others’ interests. That is verse 4 walking about in a body. Paul does not say so, because he does not need to. He has given them the pattern and then a man, and left them to make the connection.

The gift Paul could least spare. And there is a quiet rebuke in the arrangement, if the Philippians cared to notice it. Paul is sending them his most valuable colleague, the one man of his own soul, at the moment he is least able to spare him. A church arguing about who ranks where is about to receive, as a gift, the person its founder could least afford to give away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean no one else cared about the Philippians. It means Timothy was unique in his like-mindedness with Paul, and the one best suited to this errand.

If Christ is enough, why did Paul need cheering up? Because Christ is enough in a way that includes his people, not excludes them. God made us to need one another, and he often sends his comfort through them: God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus (2 Corinthians 7:6). Needing friends is not a failure of faith; it is how the body of Christ is designed. Paul’s joy in Christ was real, and so was his joy in good news from people he loved. If you are lonely and low, it is not unspiritual to say so, and it is not unspiritual to ask for company.

In a sentence. Paul hopes in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that he also may be cheered when he receives news about you. He has no one else like Timothy, who will show genuine concern for your welfare.

On a Tuesday. Be someone who genuinely cares for others’ welfare, like Timothy: not concern produced for the occasion, but the real thing, shown when there is nothing in it for you. Think of a Christian leader or friend who is carrying a heavy load, and send them good news this week: what God is doing in your life, or in theirs, or a word of thanks. You may be the cheer they need.

For worship. Christ is the Shepherd who cares for his sheep genuinely, not as a hired hand who runs when the wolf comes. He gives his people men and women who share his heart, and sends them where they are needed most, even when it costs. Every true pastor, every friend whose care is the real thing, is a gift from his hand and a small picture of his own care. He never seeks his own interests at our expense. He gave us the one he could least spare: his own life.

verseByVerse.quote: For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven worth, how as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me, and I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven worth, how as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me, and I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also.

For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. It is one of the bleakest sentences Paul ever wrote, and commentators have worked hard to soften it. A sad comment on others around Paul. He cannot mean literally every Christian in Rome: he has just said in 1:14 that most of the brothers were emboldened, and Epaphroditus was faithful. He most likely means the pool of people who might have been sent: of everyone available for this errand, only Timothy could be trusted to go and genuinely care. Even softened, it is a hard verse, and it should be allowed to stay hard. The greatest missionary in the church’s history looked around for someone who would put a distant congregation ahead of his own convenience, and found one man.

Their own interests. Notice the exact form of the failure. Paul does not say they sought sin; he says they sought their own interests, the same phrase from verse 4. These were not scandalous people. They were ordinary Christians with their own things to be getting on with, and that was enough to disqualify them. Self-interest is the opposite of the mind of Christ, and it does not need to be dramatic to be deadly.

But you know Timothy’s proven worth. Verse 22 gives the evidence, and it is the warmest line in the chapter. “Proven worth” is dokimē: tested character, the quality of metal that has been through the assayer’s fire and come out genuine. It is not a word for promise or potential. It is a word for what has been tested. The Philippians had watched this happen; Timothy had been with Paul in their city from the beginning (Acts 16:1–3; 17:14).

How as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. And then Paul’s grammar slips, beautifully. He begins the comparison as a son with a father, like an apprentice son learning his father’s trade, and then cannot finish it that way, because it would require him to say he served me, and Timothy is not his servant. So he changes course mid-sentence: he served with me in the gospel. Not under Paul: alongside him. “Served” is douleuō, slaved: both of them slaves of the same Master. It is a small stumble in the Greek, and it tells you more about how Paul regarded this younger man than a paragraph of praise would.

I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me. Verses 23–24 close the plan and quietly reveal Paul’s state of mind. The trial is still undecided, and he wants Timothy to be able to carry definite news after the outcome is known.

And I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also. He expects release. Not because he has had a revelation, but because he reasoned it out in 1:24–25: they need him, so he expects to be given to them. The confidence is real, and it is carefully hedged, I trust in the Lord, by a man who has just said he might be poured out as a drink offering (2:17). He holds both without strain, which is what hope looks like when it has stopped needing certainty.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian around Paul was selfish. Some were faithful, like Epaphroditus and Luke. It is a warning, not a census.

How do I know if I am seeking my own interests rather than Christ’s? Look at the ordinary choices, because that is where these Christians failed. When a need arises that would cost you time or comfort, what is your first reaction? Do you serve only where you will be seen or thanked? Are your plans for the year shaped by what will advance Christ’s kingdom, or only by what suits you, with Christ fitted in around the edges? Seeking his interests does not mean neglecting your family or work; those are part of his interests. It means asking, before you decide, what would serve him and his people, and being willing for the answer to cost you.

How do I find a Timothy, or become one? Spiritual fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, are formed by shared life, not just shared classes. If you are older in the faith, look for a younger believer and invite them alongside you: to pray with you, to serve with you, to see how you handle real situations. If you are younger, ask a mature Christian whether you can spend time with them and learn. Paul took Timothy on his journeys (Acts 16:3). Proven worth is built over years of faithfulness in small things, watched by someone who loves you enough to tell you the truth.

In a sentence. For everyone looks out for their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know that Timothy has proved himself, because as a son with his father he has served with Paul in the work of the gospel. Paul hopes, therefore, to send him as soon as he sees how things go with him. And he is confident in the Lord that he himself will come soon.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself whose interests filled your diary last week. Then do one thing this week purely for the interests of Jesus Christ: a task in your church that nobody wants, a visit, a gift, an hour of prayer for missions. And thank God, by name, for a spiritual father or mother who served alongside you and helped you grow.

For worship. Thank God for spiritual fathers and sons, mentors and apprentices in the faith, because they are his gift. And thank him supremely for the Son who never once sought his own interests above his Father’s, who said, my food is to do the will of him who sent me (John 4:34). The Father tested him, and he was found genuine in every fire. And that obedient Son is not ashamed to call us brothers, and works alongside us in the gospel by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need, for he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Indeed he was ill, near to death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need, for he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Indeed he was ill, near to death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.

I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus. Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul (4:18). Now Paul sends him home, probably carrying this letter. He had been sent to stay and serve; he is coming home early, ill and empty-handed, and everyone in Philippi will have a view about that. So Paul, before the man arrives, builds him a reputation. He is not returning a failure. He is returning a soldier.

My brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier. Epaphroditus gets five titles in one sentence, and they climb. Three titles of honour first: brother, family; fellow worker, the same task; fellow soldier, the same danger. That last one is not decorative, since Paul is in custody and the man nearly died getting to him.

And your messenger and minister to my need. Then the two that belong to the Philippians. “Messenger” is apostolos, sent one: not an apostle of Christ like Paul, but their envoy. “Minister” is leitourgos, priestly servant, a word for public and sacred service, from the same root as the sacrificial offering of verse 17. His service was worship. Their gift, carried by this man, was an act of worship to God.

For he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Read that again, because it is remarkable. He was near death, and the thing that troubled him was not his own condition but the knowledge that the news had reached home and they would be worried. He was upset that they were worried about him. The word for distressed (adēmoneō) is a strong one: deeply troubled, the word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). This was not mild concern. Here is the mind of Christ at the level of a sickbed: a dangerously ill man whose distress was for the people who were distressed about him.

Indeed he was ill, near to death. Paul refuses to dress it up. Seriously ill. No suggestion that faith would have prevented it, no hint that the illness was a failure of somebody’s prayers.

But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow. His recovery was God’s mercy, credited entirely to mercy, not to Epaphroditus’s constitution or his usefulness. Paul does not say he healed him miraculously, though he had the gift. And Paul extends the mercy to himself: the man who wrote to die is gain admits here that he was already carrying sorrow, the prison, the rivals, the uncertainty, and that losing this friend would have piled more on top. Paul admits he would have grieved deeply. Grief is not unbelief. Paul’s joy was never the absence of grief; it ran underneath it. Any Christian who has been told that sadness is a failure of faith should sit with this verse for a while.

Why did Paul not simply heal him? Because even the apostles could not heal at will; the signs were God’s to give, not theirs to command. An apostle who healed people elsewhere (Acts 19:11–12) here watched his friend nearly die and could not stop it, and he also left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). The miraculous gifts were signs given through the apostles to confirm the gospel in its foundation (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and we hold, charitably towards brothers who see it otherwise, that such sign gifts have ceased, while God still heals in answer to prayer as he wills. So Christians today should pray for the sick in faith, use the means God gives, including medicine, and leave the outcome to his mercy, as Paul did here.

What it does not mean. It does not mean healing is automatic for those with faith. Paul could not heal at will; God showed mercy as he chose. And it does not mean that when a believer is not healed, God has been unmerciful or someone’s faith was weak. Sometimes God’s mercy is recovery; sometimes it is taking his child home, which is far better (1:23).

Is it unspiritual to be deeply distressed, or even depressed? No. Epaphroditus was deeply troubled; Paul expected sorrow upon sorrow; Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane and said his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Mark 14:33–34). Strong emotion, even overwhelming distress, is not in itself sin or a lack of faith. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmists did. Let other believers help you carry it. And if low mood persists or deepens, seek help from your doctor as well as your pastor: the body and the mind are both God’s creation, and using medical help is no more unspiritual than Paul’s concern for Epaphroditus’s recovery.

In a sentence. But Paul thinks it is necessary to send back to you Epaphroditus, his brother, co-worker and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger, whom you sent to take care of his needs. For he longs for all of you and is distressed because you heard he was ill. Indeed he was ill, and almost died. But God had mercy on him, and not on him only but also on Paul, to spare him sorrow upon sorrow.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for healing when it comes, and do not be ashamed to grieve when it does not. If someone in your church is ill, pray for them by name and visit, call or write this week. And if you are the one who is ill, let people care for you; that, too, is part of the fellowship of the body.

For worship. God is rich in mercy. He gives back friends from the edge of death, spares his servants sorrow upon sorrow, and counts the errands of obscure believers as priestly service. And the Lord who was distressed in Gethsemane knows the weight of every believer’s trouble from the inside. He bore the sorrow upon sorrow that our sin deserved, so that no grief of his people would be without hope, and so that one day he could wipe every tear from their eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again, and that I may be less anxious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again, and that I may be less anxious.

I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again. One verse of travel arrangement, and it is among the most human sentences in the letter. The word for eager carries urgency: Paul is hurrying. He is not waiting for a convenient moment or for his own affairs to settle, which is very likely why this letter was written when it was: it went in the hand of a man who needed to go home. Paul gives up the help of a dear friend so that the Philippians can rejoice: looking to others’ interests. He is picturing the moment Epaphroditus walks through the gate alive, in front of a church whose last news of him was that he was dying.

And that I may be less anxious. Literally, less sorrowful, freer from grief or care. Paul will be relieved knowing they are reassured. Both reasons he gives are about the relief of feeling, and neither is about the mission. He is honest about his feelings.

Chapter 4 in working clothes. Which gives away a good deal about the man who two chapters later writes do not be anxious about anything (4:6). He is not describing a summit he has reached and now recommends from above it. He is a man with entirely real cares, a friend’s health, a frightened congregation, a capital trial with no date on it, who is doing what he can to reduce them. That is not a contradiction of chapter 4; it is chapter 4 in working clothes. Freedom from anxiety in Paul is never the absence of things worth worrying about. It is what a man does with them.

Protecting a servant’s reputation. Notice, too, the care he takes over how Epaphroditus will be received. He does not simply announce the return; he explains it twice, in verse 26 and again here, so that nobody in Philippi can assemble a story about a man who gave up and came home. Protecting a servant’s reputation before he arrives is an unglamorous kind of love, and it is the kind most churches need and few practise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul disobeyed his own command to be anxious for nothing (4:6). He felt concern and brought it to God, and he took sensible action to relieve it. Concern that prays and acts is love; anxiety that frets and broods is what chapter 4 forbids.

How can Paul be anxious and yet tell me not to be? Because there are two different things under the same English word. Concern is the right weight of love for people and situations God has given you: Paul speaks elsewhere of his daily anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). Sinful anxiety is fretting that takes the burden away from God and carries it alone, imagining the worst and trusting nothing. Paul’s way was to feel the concern fully, pray about it, do the practical thing within his power, and leave the rest with God. That is exactly what 4:6–7 commands. You will still feel concern; the question is where you take it.

In a sentence. Therefore Paul is all the more eager to send him, so that when you see him again you may be glad and he may have less anxiety.

On a Tuesday. Is there a reunion you could make possible: a visit to a lonely relative, a call to a friend you have lost touch with, a lift for someone who cannot get to church? Give someone the joy of seeing a face they love. And take your own present concern, name it to God, do the one practical thing you can, and leave the rest with him.

For worship. Thank God for reunions with those you love, and for the God who makes them. He sets the lonely in families, brings his scattered children together, and is preparing the greatest reunion of all, when he gathers his people from every place to see his face. Christ himself longs for that day, and has gone to prepare a place, so that where he is, we may be also. Every glad homecoming in this world is a small foretaste of that one.

verseByVerse.quote: So receive him in the Lord with all joy, and honor such men, for he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to complete what was lacking in your service to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So receive him in the Lord with all joy, and honor such men, for he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to complete what was lacking in your service to me.

So receive him in the Lord with all joy. Paul is still managing the homecoming. He wants no cool reception at the gate, no disappointment that he came home early, no unspoken question about why. Welcome him with all joy, and do it in the Lord: as a brother in Christ, not as an employee who failed to complete his contract.

And honor such men. Then a wider instruction: hold people like this in honour; make it your policy. People who risk themselves for Christ deserve honour. And that is a pointed thing to say to a church with a status problem. Paul has spent the chapter dismantling the pursuit of empty glory, and he does not finish by abolishing honour altogether. He redirects it. There is a right way to esteem people; the question is what you esteem them for. Honour is to go to the man who nearly died on an errand and has nothing to show for it, not to the impressive, the gifted or the visibly successful.

For he nearly died for the work of Christ. His illness came through his service. It was the work of Christ that brought him to the edge of death, and Paul wants that work to be the thing his church sees.

Risking his life. The word behind risking is paraboleuomai, a gambler’s term: gambling, staking, throwing your money onto the table. He staked his life. It is rare enough that the early church took it up as a name. In later centuries a brotherhood of Christians called the parabolani, the gamblers, cared for the sick, including in times of plague, carrying the dying through cities others had fled; their name is usually traced to this word. That is how the church understood it: not recklessness, but a deliberate bet that a life is worth staking on Christ’s work.

To complete what was lacking in your service to me. The final clause needs care, because in English it can sound like a rebuke. It is not one. The Philippians had given generously; what was lacking was simply the one thing they could not send: themselves. They could not be there in person, and eight hundred miles is eight hundred miles. Epaphroditus went in their place and served on their behalf, filling the gap with his own body. He was not making up for their stinginess. He was their hands, arriving where they could not.

The chapter ends on the ground. And so the chapter ends where it began, but on the ground. It opened with the Son of God emptying himself and taking the form of a slave; it closes with an unremarkable Christian from a provincial church gambling his life to carry a gift to a prisoner. Nobody has written a hymn about Epaphroditus. Paul puts him in the same chapter as the Son of God, and means the comparison. The mind of Christ is not reserved for the great; it is mostly worked out by people whose names would otherwise never have been recorded.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Philippians had failed. They could not be present; he represented them. Nor does honouring such people mean building a celebrity culture around those who suffer. The honour Paul commands is a warm welcome, respect and gratitude, not a platform.

How should we honour people like this without creating celebrities? Honour them in the way Paul does here: welcome them warmly, speak well of them, tell their story truthfully so that people praise God for them, care for their needs, and listen to them. Honour the quiet servants especially: the carer, the volunteer, the missionary back from a hard place, the believer who lost a job for the faith. Honour should point beyond them to Christ, whose work they did. The danger is not honouring people but honouring the wrong things in them: gifts and visibility instead of faithfulness and sacrifice.

What does risking for Christ look like for an ordinary Christian? For some it is literal: believers in hostile countries, missionaries in dangerous places, doctors and nurses who serve where disease is rife. For most of us it is smaller but real: risking a friendship by speaking about Christ, risking a career by refusing to lie, risking comfort by caring for someone who is difficult or ill, risking money by giving generously. Epaphroditus did not seek danger; he took on a task for Christ and did not let the danger stop him. Ask not how to be heroic, but what task Christ has given you that you have been avoiding because it might cost you.

In a sentence. So then, welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honour people like him, because he almost died for the work of Christ. He risked his life to make up for the help you yourselves could not give Paul.

On a Tuesday. Honour someone this week who risks much for Christ: write to a missionary, thank a quiet servant in your church in front of others, or pray by name for believers serving in danger. And ask what Christ is asking you to stake for his work this year.

For worship. Christ staked everything. He did not gamble, because he knew exactly what it would cost, and he paid it in full: his life laid down for the work his Father gave him. He went in our place where we could not go, and supplied, with his own body, all that was lacking in our service to God. And now he honours his servants, welcomes them home with joy, and remembers every risk taken in his name. One day he will say, well done, to people nobody else ever thought to praise, and the hymn that the angels sing about the Son will make room for the names of men like Epaphroditus.

3.title: Knowing Christ: The Surpassing Worth and the Pressing Forward
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a warning and a testimony. Travelling teachers, Jewish Christians, were telling Gentile believers that faith in Christ was not enough: to belong fully to God’s people they must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul had fought this battle in Galatia and Antioch (Galatians 2; Acts 15), and he expects it to reach Philippi. His answer is his own life story. If anyone could have earned God’s approval by pedigree and performance, it was Saul of Tarsus: circumcised on the eighth day, a Benjamite, a Pharisee, zealous to the point of persecuting the church, blameless in the law. All of it he now counts as loss, even as dung, compared with knowing Christ and being found in him with a righteousness that comes from God through faith.

Then he guards against the opposite error. Having this righteousness does not mean you have arrived. Paul has not reached perfection; he presses on like a runner, forgetting what lies behind, because Christ has already taken hold of him. He warns of people who live as enemies of the cross, ruled by their appetites, and reminds the Philippians, proud citizens of a Roman colony, that their real citizenship is in heaven. From there they await a Saviour who will transform their weak, ageing bodies to be like his glorious body.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Everything I Had, and What It Was Worth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to rejoice in the Lord, and then warns them sharply against teachers who insist that Gentile believers be circumcised. The true people of God, he says, are those who worship by the Spirit, boast in Christ and put no confidence in human credentials. Paul himself had every credential: born into Israel and circumcised on the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a strict Pharisee, zealous enough to persecute the church, outwardly faultless in keeping the law. All of it he now writes off as loss, even refuse, for the surpassing value of knowing Christ, to be found in him with a righteousness that is not his own but comes from God through faith. He wants to know Christ, the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, and so to reach the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification: A Righteousness From Outside

Verse 9 is among the clearest statements of justification in the New Testament, and its decisive word is own. Paul does not say his law-righteousness was insufficient, or that he needed more of it; he has just called himself blameless. He says he does not want it — it is the wrong kind of thing. A righteousness of one’s own can produce only two outcomes, and both are fatal: if you believe you have achieved it, it makes a Pharisee, and Paul has shown you what that produced in him; if you know you have not, it crushes you.

Against it stands a righteousness that comes through faith and from God — faith being the channel and not the achievement, the beggar’s open hand rather than the coin. This is what the Reformers meant by imputation: Christ’s record credited to those who are in him. Luther called it an alien righteousness, alien not because it is strange but because it comes from outside — which is exactly its comfort. A standing that rests on his record is the same on your worst day as on your best, and will be the same on the day you are found in him.

Verse 11 should not be read as doubt. The man who has written that to die is gain and that departing is far better is not privately unsure whether he will be raised. “By any means possible” is openness about the route, not uncertainty about the destination.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers offered the Philippians a supplement — faith plus circumcision, grace plus performance. Paul’s answer is autobiographical and devastating: I held the complete set, more of it than any of you, and beside Christ it went out with the kitchen refuse. Note that this is not a man who found his old life worthless and therefore turned to Christ. It runs the other way. Everything on that list was real gain; he met something beside which it could not hold its value. Carry a lamp outdoors at noon and you would set it down and forget it, and nothing has happened to the lamp.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.

Meaning first. Philippians 3 is Paul’s great testimony of what it means to know Christ, set against the danger of trusting in religious achievement. First, he warns against Judaizing teachers who insisted on circumcision, calling them dogs and mutilators. True believers are the real circumcision: they worship by the Spirit, boast in Christ, and put no confidence in the flesh (vv. 1–3). Then Paul lists his own impressive religious credentials: circumcised, Israelite, Benjaminite, Hebrew, Pharisee, zealous, blameless under the law. But all of it he now counts as loss, even rubbish, compared with the surpassing worth of knowing Christ, being found in him with a righteousness not his own but from God through faith, and sharing his sufferings and resurrection (vv. 4–11). Yet he has not arrived. Like a runner, he forgets what lies behind and strains forward to the prize of the upward call of God in Christ (vv. 12–16). Finally, he warns against those who live as enemies of the cross, devoted to their appetites, and reminds believers that their citizenship is in heaven, from which they await the Saviour who will transform their lowly bodies to be like his glorious body (vv. 17–21). It is a chapter about a man who lost everything and found that he had gained the only thing worth having.

Finally, my brothers. “Finally” is a word that has misled generations of readers, and preachers have made jokes about it. It does not mean Paul is winding up: he has two chapters to go, and the sharpest passage in the letter is about to begin. The Greek phrase (to loipon) means something more like as for the rest, or furthermore. It is a hinge, not a conclusion, and Paul often uses it mid-letter (1 Thessalonians 4:1). Some scholars think chapter 3 was originally a separate letter, but there is no manuscript evidence for this, and the change of tone is explained by the danger Paul is about to name.

Rejoice in the Lord. Notice first that it is a command. Paul is not observing that joy is pleasant or wishing it on them; he is commanding it, as he will again in 4:4. And that ought to stop us, because you cannot order someone to feel something. Tell a grieving man to be happy and you have only added a burden to his grief. The answer is in the words that follow the verb. The command is not be cheerful; it is rejoice in the Lord, and that names an object, not a mood. Paul is not telling them to generate a feeling out of nothing. He is telling them to look at someone, on the reasonable assumption that joy will follow the looking. What can be commanded is where you direct your attention.

The place you stand. And see what the object is not. Not his circumstances, which amount to a cell and a pending capital charge. Not the health of the church, which has a quarrel in it he will have to name. Not the absence of enemies, since he is about to warn them against enemies. Christian joy is not the conclusion you reach after surveying your situation; it is the place you stand while you survey it. Which is why a man in prison can command it of a church without absurdity. And it is the keynote of the letter for a reason: joy in Christ is the protection against the false teachers he is about to warn of. Those who rejoice in Christ do not need anything else added to him.

To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you. What same things? He may mean the call to rejoice, which he does keep repeating. He may mean the warning that follows, which he says in verse 18 he has often told them before. Either way, the principle stands, and it cuts against a real instinct in teachers and preachers: the fear of being boring. Paul gives two reasons, and they are beautifully matched. It costs him nothing, no trouble to me, and it protects them: the word is asphales, the term for something secure, unlikely to slip; a firm foothold. Repetition is not the teacher’s failure of imagination. It is the handrail on the stair. Peter said the same: I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them (2 Peter 1:12–13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must always feel happy. Paul himself knew sorrow upon sorrow (2:27). It means they always have reason to rejoice, in the Lord, because he does not change when their circumstances do.

How do I rejoice in the Lord when I feel nothing, or feel low? Begin with the object, not the feeling. Rejoicing in the Lord starts as a decision to turn your attention to him: to read about him, to remember what he has done, to sing or say back to him what is true. Feelings often follow slowly, and sometimes they lag a long way behind. The psalmists show the way: why are you cast down, O my soul? Hope in God (Psalm 42:5). They talked to their own souls. Joy in Scripture can sit alongside tears, illness and grief; it is a settled gladness in God rather than a constant mood. And if low mood is deep and lasting, it is no failure of faith to seek medical help as well. God uses both.

Why do I need to hear the same truths over and over? Because we forget, and because the truths that matter most are deep enough never to be exhausted. Say that to anyone who has ever sat through a sermon on a text they already knew and felt vaguely cheated. The things a Christian most needs to hear are almost never new. They are the same handful of truths, driven in again, because we leak. Paul knew that about the Philippians and he knows it about us, and he refuses to be too sophisticated to say a thing twice.

In a sentence. Further, Paul’s brothers and sisters, rejoice in the Lord! It is no trouble for him to write the same things to you again, and it is a safeguard for you.

On a Tuesday. When your mind turns to your problems today, turn it deliberately, for one minute, to the Lord: name one thing that is true of him and one thing he has done for you, and thank him. And next Sunday, when the sermon covers ground you already know, listen as someone being kept safe, not as someone being bored.

For worship. The Lord himself is the joy of his people, and he does not change. Circumstances rise and fall, churches quarrel, prisons close their doors, but the one we rejoice in is the same yesterday and today and for ever. He is enough to make a prisoner glad, and enough to keep his people safe. And he does not tire of telling us the same good news again and again, because he does not tire of us.

verseByVerse.quote: Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh—

Look out for the dogs. The tone changes without warning. Three times in one verse: blepete, look out, beware, keep your eye on. And three names for the same people, each one calculated to sting. In the ancient world dogs were not pets; they were the scavengers that worked the rubbish heaps outside the town, unclean and half-wild. And dog was a Jewish insult for a Gentile: the outsider, ceremonially unclean, outside the covenant. Paul picks the word up and turns it round. The people insisting that Gentiles must be circumcised to belong, the Judaizers, are themselves the dogs: they are the ones outside, scavenging at the edge of a covenant they have not understood.

Look out for the evildoers. Literally the evil workers. They prided themselves on works of the law; Paul calls their works evil, because works offered as a ground of acceptance with God are not obedience but rivalry with Christ.

Look out for those who mutilate the flesh. Here is a pun that does not survive into English. Circumcision is peritomē, a cutting around. Paul calls what they practise katatomē, a cutting down, a hacking; and the verb behind it is used in the Greek Old Testament for the pagan gashing that the law forbade (Leviticus 21:5; 1 Kings 18:28). His point is not that circumcision was never anything. It is that a sign severed from the thing it signified is no longer a sign. Take away the covenant reality, and insist on the knife as a condition of salvation, and what remains is not a sacrament. It is surgery.

For we are the circumcision. Then the counter-claim, and it is breathtaking. Not we are the spiritual equivalent of it: we are it. A congregation of Macedonian Gentiles, most of them uncircumcised, is told they are the covenant people, and the men pressing the knife are not. Believers in Christ, Jew and Gentile, are the true circumcision: circumcised in heart by the Spirit (Romans 2:28–29; Colossians 2:11). This is what the prophets had said all along: circumcise the foreskin of your heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4), and the LORD your God will circumcise your heart (Deuteronomy 30:6).

Who worship by the Spirit of God. Paul defines the true circumcision by three marks, which together make a fair test of any church or any soul. First, they worship by the Spirit of God. “Worship” (latreuō) is to serve in worship, the word for the temple service. True worship is by the Spirit himself, not by machinery, ritual or technique (John 4:23–24).

And glory in Christ Jesus. Second, the boast has moved outside the self altogether. “Glory” (kauchaomai) is to boast, to exult. Their only boast is Christ: far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Galatians 6:14).

And put no confidence in the flesh. Third, and this is the one to sit with, because flesh here is broader than circumcision. It means human status, achievement and religious performance: everything about you that could be offered as a reason God should accept you. Your family, your record, your discipline, your usefulness, the fact that you have never done anything really disgraceful. The question is not whether you have such things; Paul is about to list an impressive set of his own. The question is whether any weight is resting on them, and the honest way to find out is to notice what happens inside you when one of them is taken away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was anti-Jewish. He was a Jew and loved his people, and could wish himself cut off for their sake (Romans 9:1–5). He opposed those who made circumcision a requirement for salvation, because that turned the gospel of grace into a gospel of Christ plus something.

Is such harsh language ever right for Christians today? Rarely, and only in Paul’s kind of case. Jesus called the Pharisees “You serpents, you brood of vipers” (Matthew 23:33), and Paul uses strong words of those who corrupt the gospel (Galatians 5:12). But both reserve them for false teachers who lead others astray from the way of salvation, not for honest doubters, opponents in ordinary disputes or weaker believers. The rule for ordinary correction is that the Lord’s servant must be kind to everyone, correcting his opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25). Sharpness has its place when the gospel itself is under attack, and even then it must not become contempt or the pleasure of a fight.

Where Christians differ: does we are the circumcision mean the church has replaced Israel? Some read it that way; others hold that Israel as a people still has a distinct future in God’s purposes. Paul means that all who worship by the Spirit and trust in Christ, Jew and Gentile alike, are the true people of God, the reality to which circumcision pointed. He does not say here that the Jewish people have no further place in God’s purposes; elsewhere he insists that they are still beloved for the sake of their forefathers (Romans 11:28), and Christians hold different views about how that future will unfold. What is clear is that there is one people of God in Christ, and Jewish people are welcome in it, and need Christ to enter it, on the same terms as everyone else.

Who are the Judaizers today? Anyone who says: Christ, plus something, is needed for you to be right with God. Today it is rarely circumcision. It may be a ritual, a church membership, a set of rules about food, dress or days, a particular spiritual experience, a level of commitment, or a list of good works. Any of these can be good in their place. The danger comes when one of them is made a condition of acceptance with God, or a badge of being a real Christian. Then Christ is no longer enough, and the gospel has been changed. Watch for it in your own heart, too, where it is quieter and more dangerous.

In a sentence. Watch out for those dogs, those evildoers, those mutilators of the flesh. For it is we who are the circumcision, we who serve God by his Spirit, who boast in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh,

On a Tuesday. Finish this sentence honestly: God accepts me because Christ died for me, and because I… If anything comes after the and, that is where your confidence in the flesh is hiding. Bring it to God, set it down, and thank him that Christ is enough.

For worship. God does what no human hand can do: he circumcises the heart. By his Spirit he cuts away the old hardness and makes Gentile pagans and proud Pharisees alike into one holy people who worship him in Spirit and truth. He gives us nothing to boast in but his Son, and that is the best boast in the world. Glory in Christ Jesus, for in him the covenant is kept, the sign is fulfilled, and the outsiders are brought home.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a Jewish insult for Gentiles; Paul turns it on those insisting on circumcision. “Mutilate” plays on the word for circumcision. A pun: “those who mutilate the flesh” (katatomē) versus “the circumcision” (peritomē) in v. 3.

verseByVerse.quote: though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.

Though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. Paul now does something risky. Having said the Christian puts no confidence in the flesh, he immediately says that if anyone could trust in religious credentials, he could. He will not let anyone dismiss him as a man rejecting what he never had.

If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more. He outranks the Judaizers on their own terms. If this is a competition, he says, I can win it, and then he lists his hand. Seven credentials follow, and the list falls cleanly into two halves: four inherited, three achieved.

Circumcised on the eighth day. The first four are things done to him before he could have any say. Circumcised exactly on the day the law required (Leviticus 12:3; Genesis 17:12): not a convert circumcised as an adult, not an Ishmaelite circumcised at thirteen, but born into the covenant.

Of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin. A member of the covenant people by birth. And Benjamin is a real boast. Benjamin gave Israel her first king, Saul, whose name Paul carried as his Hebrew name. Benjamin alone stayed with Judah when the kingdom tore in two, and Jerusalem itself lay in Benjamin’s territory (Joshua 18:28). A prestigious tribe.

A Hebrew of Hebrews. This may mean he kept the Hebrew language and customs, though raised in the Greek city of Tarsus: a pure-bred Hebrew from Hebrew parents, from a family that had kept the language and the ways when it would have been easier to let them go.

As to the law, a Pharisee. Then three things he achieved himself. The Pharisees were the strictest party, devoted to keeping the law and its traditions (Acts 23:6; 26:5): not the sneering caricature, but the most rigorous and respected school in Judaism, men who had given their lives to obeying God in the detail.

As to zeal, a persecutor of the church. And note that he offers this as a credential. His zeal for God’s law drove him to persecute those he thought were betraying it (Acts 8:3; Galatians 1:13–14). In the tradition of Phinehas and the Maccabees, zeal that acted was the proof of a serious man. Paul is telling them, without flinching, that on the old accounting his worst act was his best qualification.

As to righteousness under the law, blameless. This one stops the modern reader, because we expect the man of Romans 7 to say the opposite. But he is not claiming sinlessness. Measured by outward law-keeping, as people saw it, no one could fault him: the record any neighbour in Tarsus or Jerusalem could inspect. Which is precisely the horror of his position, and he intends us to feel it: this man kept the rules impeccably and was, at the same time, the chief enemy of the Son of God. Blamelessness had not made him good. It had made him dangerous.

The argument. The Judaizers are offering the Philippians a package. Paul says: I had the complete set, birth, pedigree, sect, zeal and an unblemished record, more of it than any of you. So when I tell you what it is worth, understand that I am not making a virtue of what I lacked.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul thought he was sinless. He called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15), and in Romans 7 he says it was the commandment against coveting, the one sin no neighbour can see, that showed him what he was. It means his outward record was impressive.

Is it wrong to be thankful for my Christian upbringing, my church or my heritage? Not at all. Paul elsewhere lists Israel’s privileges with gratitude (Romans 9:4–5), and Timothy’s faith was first in his grandmother and mother (2 Timothy 1:5). A godly home, good teaching and a faithful church are great gifts. The danger is only in trusting them. Thank God for them as means he used to bring you to Christ, and then make sure your confidence rests on Christ himself and not on the gifts. A Christian heritage cannot save you, and the lack of one cannot keep you out.

In a sentence. Though Paul himself has reasons for such confidence. If someone else thinks they have reasons to put confidence in the flesh, he has more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; in regard to the law, a Pharisee; as for zeal, persecuting the church; as for righteousness based on the law, faultless.

On a Tuesday. Write your own list of the things you are tempted to trust in for God’s approval: upbringing, church involvement, Bible knowledge, good behaviour, the sins you have never committed. Be honest; nobody else needs to see it. Then read on, and watch what Paul does with his.

For worship. Christ’s grace reached the man with the best record and the worst heart: a blameless Pharisee breathing threats against the church. It stopped him on the road, showed him that all his righteousness was a wall between him and God, and made him the apostle of free grace. If grace could undo Saul of Tarsus, it can undo anyone. No record is too good to need it, and none too bad to receive it.
verseByVerse.note: Benjamin was the tribe of King Saul, Paul’s namesake. “Hebrew of Hebrews” may mean he was raised speaking Hebrew or Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ
verseByVerse.commentary:
