But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ

But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Now the ledger, and Paul keeps it in the vocabulary of the counting-house. “Gain” (kerdos) is profit. He has already used the verb count (hēgeomai) twice in chapter 2: Christ did not count equality with God something to exploit; you are to count others more significant. Here he applies the same reckoning to his own accumulated assets, and moves every one of them across the page. And the tense is perfect: a decision made and still standing, from the day of his conversion. He moved everything from the profit column to the loss column.

Indeed, I count everything as loss. Watch the escalation, because it happens in three stages. First the past tense, the moment on the Damascus road when the books were rewritten. Now the present tense, and the category has widened from his religious credentials to everything. That first verdict was not a young convert’s enthusiasm; some thirty years later he is still saying it, and saying it wider.

Because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. But do not misread the arithmetic. This is not a man who decided his old life was worthless and therefore turned to Christ. It runs the other way. Everything on that list was genuinely valuable: the covenant, the law, the zeal, all of it real gain. What happened was that he met something beside which they could not hold their value. “Surpassing worth” (hyperechon) is that which excels, outranks, rises above. Bring a lamp into a room at night and it is a genuine treasure; carry it outside at noon and you would put it down and forget it. Nothing has happened to the lamp. And knowing Christ means not just facts about him but personal relationship.

My Lord. Notice the two words that make the sentence personal. Paul is not describing a doctrine. In all his letters this singular, personal phrase about Christ appears almost nowhere else. Whatever else the Damascus road did, it left this man with a person he could call his own.

For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things. And it was not only an accountant’s reckoning. Paul really lost: status, career, friends, perhaps family, comfort and safety. The man who had been a rising star of the Pharisees became a hunted itinerant who was beaten, stoned, shipwrecked and imprisoned (2 Corinthians 11:23–27).

And count them as rubbish. Then the language turns violent. Skybala is not a polite word, and rubbish is a translator’s kindness. It meant kitchen refuse, scraps thrown to the dogs, and, in its coarser use, dung. Paul has just called his opponents dogs; now he says his own pedigree belongs on the rubbish heap where they scavenge. The man is not being decorous. He is trying to make a church feel the difference in value, and he chooses the strongest word available. Compared with Christ, the most impressive religious record is garbage.

In order that I may gain Christ. The trade: everything lost, Christ gained. It is the best exchange ever made, the man who found treasure hidden in a field and in his joy sold all that he had and bought that field (Matthew 13:44–46). And notice the word joy in that parable. The man is not grimly sacrificing. He is getting a bargain.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s heritage was evil. The law was holy, and the privileges of Israel were God’s gifts. But as a ground of confidence before God, they were worthless compared with Christ.

Does counting everything as loss mean I should despise my family, my work or the good things of life? No. Paul counts them as loss in comparison with Christ and as a ground of standing before God, not as worthless in themselves. Elsewhere he says that everything created by God is good, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4), and he commands husbands to love their wives and parents to care for their children. The point is ranking, not rejecting. When Christ is first, every other good thing finds its proper place and is enjoyed more, not less, because it is no longer asked to carry the weight of a god. What must go is whatever competes with him.

How do I come to value Christ like this? Not by trying to despise other things, but by seeing more of him. The lamp is put down because the sun has risen. So spend time looking at Christ in the Gospels and the letters; ask God to open your eyes to his worth (Ephesians 1:17–18); sing about him; listen to believers who love him. And notice what happens when you lose something precious and still find him there: that is often when people discover his worth most deeply.

In a sentence. But whatever were gains to him he now considers loss for the sake of Christ. What is more, he considers everything a loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord, for whose sake he has lost all things. He considers them garbage, that he may gain Christ

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable. Paul is not asking whether you would say Christ is worth more than your career, your family name, your reputation for soundness. Everyone in church says that. He is asking what actually happened the last time one of them was threatened, and whether the loss felt like the loss of a lamp at noon, or like the end of the world. Tell Christ today what he is worth to you, and mean it.

For worship. Christ is worth more than everything. Worth more than pedigree and achievement, worth more than reputation and safety, worth more than the whole world (Mark 8:36). He is the treasure in the field and the pearl of great price, and the one who gains him has lost nothing that matters. And the wonder is that he counted us worth gaining: he, who had everything, gave up all things to make us his own. He is my Lord, and every believer may say it with Paul, and there is no gain like him.

verseByVerse.quote: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith—
verseByVerse.commentary:
and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith—

And be found in him. This verse is the doctrinal centre of the letter and one of the clearest statements of justification in the New Testament. Every phrase is load-bearing. Found by whom, and when? On the day of Christ, the day this letter keeps returning to (1:6, 10; 2:16). Paul is imagining the final inspection, the day of judgement, and his entire strategy for it is to be discovered inside someone else: united to Christ, sheltered in him. Not standing beside Christ with his own record in his hand. In him.

Not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law. Two kinds of righteousness. The first is my own: produced by my law-keeping, my effort, my record. This is the righteousness Paul once trusted, and now rejects as rubbish. The crucial word is own. Paul is not saying his law-righteousness was a little short of what he needed. He has just told us he was outwardly blameless. He is saying he does not want it. It is the wrong kind of thing altogether: not a small coin but a forged one, and the trouble with a forged coin is not that it is small.

Pride or despair. Why the wrong kind? Because a righteousness of your own can only ever produce one of two results, and both are fatal. If you think you have achieved it, it makes you a Pharisee, and Paul has just shown you what that produced in him. If you know you have not, it crushes you. There is no third outcome. The whole system can generate pride or despair and nothing else.

But that which comes through faith in Christ. The other righteousness is received through faith in Christ. The ESV note mentions a possible rendering, through the faithfulness of Christ. Faith in Christ is the better reading here, as in Galatians 2:16: the verse itself goes on to say this righteousness depends on faith, which can only be our believing. Christ’s faithful obedience is the righteousness; our faith is how we receive it. Either way the righteousness comes from Christ and is received by faith.

The righteousness from God that depends on faith. Note the two prepositions doing the work. It is from God (ek theou), not from me: his own righteousness, given. And it comes through faith: faith is the channel, not the achievement. It is God’s gift, credited to believers (Romans 3:21–22; 2 Corinthians 5:21). This is what the Reformers meant by imputation: a righteousness that is not produced in me but credited to me, Christ’s record entered in my account because I am in him. Luther called it an alien righteousness: alien not because it is strange but because it comes from outside, and that is precisely its comfort.

The empty hand. And faith itself contributes nothing to the transaction; it is simply the empty hand. A beggar’s open palm is not what buys the bread. Which is why assurance is possible at all. If my standing rested on a righteousness of my own, every bad week would move the ground under me. Because it rests on his, my standing on my worst day is exactly what it was on my best, and it will be the same on the day I am found in him.

Where Christians differ: whose righteousness? Some interpreters, including some New Perspective scholars, say the righteousness of my own that comes from the law means only Jewish identity, the privileges of belonging to Israel, and that the righteousness from God means God’s own covenant faithfulness, or covenant membership, rather than a righteous status credited to the believer. Verdict: this verse is one of the clearest in Scripture on imputed righteousness. Paul’s list in vv. 5–6 does include his Jewish credentials, but it also includes his zeal and his blamelessness under the law, and he sets all of it against a righteousness that is God’s gift. He contrasts a righteousness of my own, from the law, with a righteousness from God, through faith. It is a status given by God, not produced by us, received by faith. This is justification by the imputed righteousness of Christ (Romans 4:5–6; Westminster 11.1). Covenant membership follows, but the heart is a righteous standing before the Judge.

What it does not mean. It does not mean righteous living does not matter. Those clothed with Christ’s righteousness are being made righteous in life, and the very next verse speaks of being conformed to Christ. But their acceptance rests on Christ’s righteousness, not their own.

If I am clothed in Christ’s righteousness, why does my sin still matter? Because you belong to the one whose righteousness you wear. Sin no longer threatens your standing, since Christ has borne its penalty, but it grieves your Father, harms you and others, and contradicts who you now are. God disciplines his children not to pay for their sin but to make them share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). And a person who truly rests in Christ’s righteousness will want to be like him; a faith that is content to go on in sin has not understood what it was given (Romans 6:1–2). Confess your sins honestly, knowing that confession does not earn your acceptance but enjoys it.

In a sentence. And be found in him, not having a righteousness of his own that comes from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness that comes from God on the basis of faith.

On a Tuesday. When you feel unworthy before God, and you will, remember: you stand not in your own righteousness, but in Christ’s, given to you. Say it to yourself in so many words after you have sinned, before you have done anything to make up for it. Then go and confess the sin, not to restore your standing, but because your standing is secure.

For worship. The Judge has provided the righteousness he requires. What we could never produce, he gives; what we could never earn, he credits; and the one who is found in Christ is found clothed in the spotless obedience of the Son of God. My hope is built on nothing less than Jesus’ blood and righteousness. On the last day, when every record is opened, those in him will be found exactly where Paul longed to be, and their standing will be as secure as his.

verseByVerse.quote: that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death,
verseByVerse.commentary:
that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death,

That I may know him. Everything in the passage has been building to this, and the smallness of the object is the point. Not that I may know about him; not even that I may know his benefits. Him. The verb (ginōskō) means personal, experiential knowledge, deeper and deeper. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses when Adam knew his wife, and when God says of Israel, you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). It is knowledge by acquaintance and covenant, the knowing that happens between persons. And here is the striking thing: the man writing has known Christ for some thirty years, has seen the risen Lord, has been caught up to the third heaven, and he writes as though he were still at the beginning. Nobody in the New Testament knew Christ better, and nobody wanted to know him more.

And the power of his resurrection. The power that raised Christ is at work in believers now: new life, victory over sin, strength in weakness (Ephesians 1:19–20; Romans 6:4). And notice the order, which is not the order of Christ’s own life. In his life the suffering came first and the resurrection after; Paul reverses it. That is because he is describing the Christian’s experience rather than Christ’s history: you meet the risen Lord first, and it is his resurrection power that then makes it possible to walk into suffering at all. Nobody shares Christ’s sufferings on his own steam.

And may share his sufferings. “Share” is koinōnia, fellowship, the partnership word of chapter 1. Fellowship with Christ includes fellowship in suffering for his sake (Romans 8:17; 1 Peter 4:13). Not that our sufferings atone, but that we share his path. And Paul yokes two things most of us would prefer to separate: the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings are held under one article in the Greek, as a single object. Not two experiences to be chosen between. One thing with two faces.

Becoming like him in his death. “Becoming like” is one word, symmorphizomenos, conformed to, and there is morphē again, the word from 2:6–7, the form of God and the form of a servant. The hymn is not left behind in chapter 2; it is being pressed into Paul. He is being shaped into the same form his Lord took: the form of the one who poured himself out. It means dying to self daily, as Christ died (2 Corinthians 4:10–11), and perhaps also being willing to die as a martyr. It is the present tense, continuous: a thing being done to him while he writes, in a cell, awaiting a verdict. Name that plainly, because this verse is often quoted with the second half left off. Christians ask for resurrection power constantly and rarely for fellowship in his sufferings. Paul asks for one thing containing both, and he does not regard the suffering as the price of the power. He regards it as part of the prize, because it is the way you come to know a person, and the person he wants to know went to a cross.

Why would anyone long for this? Most of us do not, and Paul was not asking for pain for its own sake. Five things explain his longing.

1. The goal is Christ, not the pain. The sentence begins: that I may know him. Everything after it unpacks what knowing him involves. A wife who spends nights at her husband’s hospital bed does not long for hospitals; she longs to be with him, and that is where he is. Love wants to share the beloved’s life, the hard parts too (Ruth 1:16). Paul had counted everything else as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (vv. 7–8), and he would not leave out the part of Christ’s life that was the cross.

2. In this life the power and the suffering come together. Paul names resurrection power and shared sufferings in one breath, because he had found that Christ’s power is known most deeply in weakness. My power is made perfect in weakness, the Lord told him (2 Corinthians 12:9). He carried the death of Jesus in his body so that the life of Jesus might be shown in it (2 Corinthians 4:7–11). When everyone deserted him at his trial, the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). The times he suffered for Christ were the times he knew Christ nearest.

3. Suffering for Christ marks you as his. Jesus said the world would treat his followers as it treated him (John 15:18–20). So to be opposed for Christ is a sign of belonging to him. The apostles left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41). Paul tells these same Philippians that suffering for Christ has been granted to them, a gift, alongside faith (1:29).

4. The road leads to glory. Christ went through the cross to the resurrection, and his people follow the same road: becoming like him in his death, so as to attain the resurrection (v. 11). We suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). Paul weighed it and called it light, momentary affliction beside an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17; Romans 8:18).

5. Paul was in prison as he wrote. This is not a wish from a comfortable armchair. He was in chains (1:7, 13), facing possible death (1:20–23). He is not asking for a suffering he has not tasted. He is saying: I would rather have Christ with chains than comfort without him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean seeking suffering, enjoying pain, or inflicting it on yourself. Paul begged three times for his thorn to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:8), and Jesus himself prayed that the cup might pass (Matthew 26:39). It means accepting suffering, when it comes in Christ’s service, as part of knowing him. Nor does it mean that you are a poor Christian if you do not feel this longing. Start where Paul starts: ask to know Christ. The willingness to share his path grows as love for him grows.

What “dying to self” actually means. The phrase is not in the Bible, but it sums up what the Bible says in several ways: deny yourself and take up your cross daily (Luke 9:23); I have been crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:20); put to death what is earthly in you (Colossians 3:5); unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone (John 12:24). Put together, it has three parts.

1. Something that has already happened. If you trust Christ, your old self, the you that was ruled by sin, was crucified with him (Romans 6:6). It is not something you achieve, but a fact you believe and then live out: consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus (Romans 6:11). Sin is no longer your master, even when it still shouts.

2. Something you do every day. The self that wants to be on the throne still fights, so each day you say no to it: my will above God’s, my comfort above another’s good, my reputation above the truth. In ordinary life it looks like this. You bite back the cutting reply. You admit you were wrong, without excuses. You give up your Saturday to help someone move house. You let your spouse’s preference win on something that matters more to them than to you. You turn down the deal that would mean bending the truth. You put to death the particular sins Paul names: sexual immorality, greed, anger, slander, lying (Colossians 3:5–9).

3. Always for the sake of life. Dying to self is never the end point. The grain dies to bear much fruit (John 12:24). You put off the old self in order to put on the new (Ephesians 4:22–24). If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live (Romans 8:13). What dies is selfishness and sin; what lives is the real you, made new and becoming like Christ.

What dying to self does not mean.

Not erasing your personality. God made you, with your temperament, gifts, likes and desires. Paul stayed recognisably Paul: blunt, warm, learned. Your self is redeemed, not abolished.

Not self-hatred. The verse that says I have been crucified with Christ goes on: who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). You die to self as someone deeply loved, not as someone worthless.

Not being a doormat. It does not mean you may never say no, never have needs, or must let others use or abuse you. Jesus withdrew from the crowds to pray (Luke 5:16) and took his disciples away to rest (Mark 6:31). Dying to self is death to sin and selfishness, not to wisdom, boundaries or protecting the vulnerable (see the notes on Matthew 5:5 and 5:38–40).

Not neglecting or punishing your body. No one hates his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it (Ephesians 5:29). Harsh treatment of the body has no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:20–23). Rest, food, sleep and medical care are not selfishness.

Not something you manage in your own strength. It is by the Spirit that you put to death the deeds of the body (Romans 8:13). Trying to kill the self by willpower alone usually ends in pride when it works, and despair when it does not.

Not the loss of joy. Jesus endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). Whoever loses his life for Christ’s sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). The aim is not a smaller life, but a fuller one.

How do I actually get to know Christ better? The same way you come to know any person: by spending time with him and listening to him. Read the Gospels slowly, asking not only what Jesus did but what it shows you about him. Pray, and not only with requests: tell him what you are thinking and what you love about him. Come to the Lord’s Table, where he gives himself to be received by faith. Obey him, because he shows himself to those who keep his word (John 14:21). Spend time with Christians who know him well. And when hard times come in following him, do not waste them: ask to meet him there, because that is where Paul knew him nearest.

In a sentence. Paul wants to know Christ so fully that he welcomes both his resurrection power and a share in his sufferings, because the road with Christ through death leads to resurrection.

On a Tuesday. Pray Paul’s prayer this morning: Lord, let me know you, the power of your resurrection, and the fellowship of your sufferings. Then choose one ordinary way to die to self today from the list above: the cutting reply you will not make, the apology you will give without excuses, the preference you will let go. Do it not to prove anything, but because you belong to the one who died for you and lives in you.

For worship. Christ is worth knowing more than anything else can be known. He is the risen Lord whose power raises the dead, and the suffering Saviour who walks with his people through every dark place, and he is both at once. He went into death so that his people would never meet death without him, and he rose so that the road through death would end in resurrection. The one who loved me and gave himself for me is the one I am being shaped to resemble, and the fellowship of his sufferings is the doorway to the fellowship of his glory.

verseByVerse.quote: that by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.

That by any means possible. The sentence sounds uncertain: literally, if somehow. And it has troubled readers who have just been told in 1:6 that God finishes what he starts. Is Paul hedging about whether he will be raised? He is not, and the letter itself settles it. This is the man who has said that to die is gain, that departing is far better, that he will be with Christ. In the very next verse he will say Christ has already made him his own. Nobody who writes those sentences is privately unsure whether he is saved.

Open about the route. What the phrase expresses is not doubt about the outcome but humility about the way. By any means possible means: whatever it takes, whatever road it goes by, however God chooses to bring me there, through suffering and death if need be. Paul does not know whether he reaches the resurrection through a Roman sword or through years more of labour and an old man’s bed. He is not attached to the road. He is attached to the destination, and he is saying he will accept any terms.

Certain, but not casual. There is also a note of reverent seriousness in it that we should not sand away. A Christian can be certain of the end and still refuse to be casual about the journey. The New Testament holds both without embarrassment: God will keep you, and you must press on. The same Paul who wrote that he who began a good work will bring it to completion also wrote, “But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27). The certainty never produces a shrug.

I may attain the resurrection from the dead. “Attain” (katantaō) is to arrive at, to reach the destination. The final goal is the bodily resurrection of the righteous at Christ’s return (v. 21; 1 Corinthians 15:23). Literally it is the out-resurrection from among the dead, the rising of those who belong to Christ out from the realm of death. Not merely the general raising of all the dead, which requires no striving from anyone, since the wicked are raised too (John 5:28–29), but the resurrection that is glory: the thing he will describe in verse 21, this humiliated body remade like Christ’s. That is what he is running for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul doubted his salvation. He was sure (1:21–23). It means he pursued the goal humbly, aware that the way would be costly.

Does the out-resurrection mean believers are raised at a different time from everyone else? Some read it that way, as a first resurrection of believers separated from a later one. But the phrase describes the character of the resurrection, not a separate timetable. Scripture teaches one return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, both the righteous and the unrighteous (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), and then the judgement. For believers it is a resurrection to glory, out from among the dead and into life with Christ; for others it is a resurrection to judgement. So Paul is longing for the glorious side of that one great day, not for an earlier event.

What if I am unsure whether I will make it? Paul’s sentence is a useful corrective. Christians sometimes fear that any uncertainty in them proves their faith is counterfeit. A man utterly sure of his destination can still write a cautious-sounding line about the road, because the caution is not about God’s faithfulness but about his own ignorance of what the next year holds. Not knowing what is coming is not the same as doubting who is waiting. Your assurance rests on Christ’s promise and work, not on your ability to foresee the road (John 10:28). Keep looking to him, keep pressing on, and trust him to bring you there.

In a sentence. And so, somehow, attaining to the resurrection from the dead.

On a Tuesday. Keep your eyes on the resurrection. Every step of faithfulness today leads toward it, even the dull ones. When you face something hard this week, tell God: whatever road you choose to take me by, I want to arrive with you. And then take the next step.

For worship. The risen Christ is the firstfruits of a great harvest. Because he lives, his people will live; because his tomb is empty, theirs will be too. Whatever road he leads them by, through prisons or sickbeds or long, ordinary years, it ends in the resurrection of the body and the glory of his presence. He has walked that road ahead of us, and he holds the keys of death and Hades. No one he has made his own will fail to arrive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Not Arrived, and Still Running
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul insists he has not yet arrived or reached perfection. He presses on to take hold of the goal because Christ has already taken hold of him. Leaving the past behind, he strains forward like a runner towards the finish and the prize of God’s upward call in Christ. Mature believers should think the same way, and where they differ, God will make things clear; meanwhile they should keep living by what they have already reached.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sanctification Is Progress, Not Arrival

The Reformed tradition has always held that sanctification in this life is real but incomplete — the Westminster Confession speaks of it as imperfect in this life, with remnants of corruption abiding in every part. Verse 12 is the apostle’s own testimony to exactly that, and it is aimed at anyone claiming a settled plateau where striving is over.

The engine of the passage is the second half of verse 12: I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. The same verb both times — to seize, to lay hold of. Paul chases Christ because Christ has already caught him on the Damascus road, while he was travelling the other way with warrants in his bag. Get that order wrong and the Christian life is unbearable: running in order to be apprehended is exhausting and never finished. Running because you were apprehended is another thing altogether, and it is why Paul can admit he has not arrived without the admission destroying him.

Verse 15 then supplies the paradox that defines maturity: the teleioi are precisely those who know they are not yet teleios. Anyone who believes he has finished has thereby proved he has not begun to think properly.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some in the early church claimed a completed spiritual state, and Paul’s disclaimer is a direct correction of it. But note how he handles the difference in verse 15 — he does not repeat the argument louder or threaten. He hands them to God and expects God to do the persuading. That is patience, not indifference: he plainly thinks he is right and expects them to come round.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect. Having written some of the loftiest sentences in Scripture, Paul immediately puts a guard on them. It is one of the most important disclaimers in the New Testament. “Perfect” (teleioō) means complete, mature, brought to the goal: Paul has not reached full conformity to Christ. There were people in the first century, as there have been in every century since, who taught that a Christian could arrive, reach a settled plateau where the striving was over, and perhaps some in Philippi claimed it. Paul, of all people entitled to claim it, refuses.

But I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Then the sentence that turns the whole passage. “Press on” (diōkō) is to pursue, to chase, and it is the word used of his persecuting the church in verse 6: the same energy, now redirected. And “make it my own” (katalambanō) is to seize, to lay hold of, to catch, and it is used both times. Paul is chasing Christ because Christ has already caught him. That is the entire logic of Christian effort in one line. He is not running to be apprehended; he was apprehended on the Damascus road, seized by a light and a voice while he was travelling in the opposite direction with warrants in his bag. Every step since has been the response of a man already taken. Grace comes first; effort follows.

The order matters. Get that order wrong and the Christian life becomes unbearable. Running to be caught is exhausting and never finished. Running because you were caught is something else entirely, and it is why Paul can admit he has not arrived without the admission destroying him.

Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do. Emphatic honesty, and then single-minded focus. Consider who is saying it: a man with a dozen churches on his conscience, a trial pending, letters to write, collections to organise. And he says his life has one thing in it. Not a balanced portfolio of priorities. One.

Forgetting what lies behind. Biblical forgetting is not amnesia; Paul remembers his past perfectly well and has just spent three verses listing it. It means refusing to let it govern, whether to boast or to despair. And it cuts both ways, which is the pastoral gold here. The runner must forget his failures and sins: Paul had a genuinely terrible past, blood on his hands, and could have spent his life doing penance in his own head. And he must forget his successes and his sufferings, which is harder and less often preached. A man glancing back at either one is a man losing the race.

And straining forward to what lies ahead. “Straining forward” (epekteinomai) is a vivid double compound: stretching out toward. The picture is a runner in the stadium, the whole body stretched out toward the tape, the way a sprinter’s chest reaches the line ahead of his legs.

I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus. “Goal” (skopos) is the mark, the target the eye is fixed on. “Prize” (brabeion) is the victor’s award (1 Corinthians 9:24), the wreath handed down at the games, and the games were a fixture of life in a city like Philippi. The upward call is God’s call to come up, as winners at the games were called up to receive their prize. And the herald’s summons calling the victor up is the same summons that will call Paul up at the end. The prize is Christ himself, and eternal glory. The prize is not a thing God gives. It is God calling him home.

Where Christians differ: Christian perfection. Some traditions teach that believers can attain sinless perfection or entire sanctification in this life. Verdict: the apostle Paul, late in his ministry, says he is not yet perfect and is still pressing on. Believers grow in holiness, but perfection comes only at glorification (1 John 1:8; 3:2; Westminster 13.2). The Christian life is a race to the end, not a plateau.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is uncertain or earned by running. Christ made Paul his own first. The race is the life of the saved, not the way to become saved.

How do I forget what lies behind when my past is terrible, or when I was badly hurt? Forgetting does not mean pretending it did not happen, and it does not mean that wrongs done to you must never be named or brought to justice. It means that the past no longer gets to steer. If your past is your sin, it has been nailed to the cross; confess anything unconfessed, make what amends you can, and then refuse to keep paying for what Christ has paid for. If your past is what others did to you, bring it to God, get help to heal, seek justice where that is right, and ask him for the grace to forgive. Healing may take a long time. But your future is defined by the upward call of God, not by what happened behind you.

What if I feel I am barely running at all? The race is long, and runners have bad stretches. Paul’s own word for himself is that he has not arrived. What matters is the direction you are facing and that you keep getting up. Look again at the reason for the race: Christ has made you his own. Run because you are held, not to get held. Lean on other runners; the Christian race is never a solo event (Hebrews 12:1–2). And fix your eyes on Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, who ran ahead of you and is waiting at the line.

In a sentence. Not that Paul has already obtained all this, or has already arrived at his goal, but he presses on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of him. Brothers and sisters, he does not consider himself yet to have taken hold of it. But one thing he does: forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, he presses on toward the goal to win the prize for which God has called him heavenward in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. What past failure or success do you need to forget today? Name it, hand it to God, and stop looking over your shoulder at it. Then ask what one thing your life is about, and whether this week’s diary shows it. Lean forward toward Christ.

For worship. Christ laid hold of us before we ever reached for him. He seized persecutors on the road and rebels in their pride, and he does not let go of those he has caught. He calls them upward, and the call will not fall silent until they are home. The prize at the end of the race is not a wreath that withers but the Lord himself, and the God who called us is the God who will crown us. Every runner who finishes will lay the crown at his feet.
verseByVerse.note: The picture is of a runner straining toward the finishing line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let those of us who are mature think this way, and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you. Only let us hold true to what we have attained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let those of us who are mature think this way, and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you. Only let us hold true to what we have attained.

Let those of us who are mature think this way. The word is teleioi, and it is the same root as perfect in verse 12, where Paul denied being it. He is doing something deliberate and slightly wry. Three verses ago: I am not perfect. Now: let those of us who are mature think this way. The apparent contradiction is the lesson. Maturity is not having arrived; maturity is knowing you have not. The mark of a grown-up Christian is precisely the refusal to claim completion, and anyone who thinks he has finished has thereby proved he has not started thinking properly.

And if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you. This is one of the most gracious sentences Paul ever wrote about disagreement. Consider the restraint. This is an apostle, writing with authority, who has just spent twelve verses on the most important doctrine there is, and who two paragraphs earlier called his opponents dogs. He is perfectly capable of pressing. And on this matter he does not. He does not repeat the argument louder, threaten, or demand immediate agreement. He hands them over to God and expects God to do the work. Paul trusts God to correct believers on secondary matters as they grow: patience with those still learning.

Knowing which question is in front of you. The distinction he is making is one every church needs and few manage. On the gospel itself, whether righteousness comes by law or by faith, Paul gives no ground whatever; there the language is dogs and mutilators. On the outworking of the pressing-on life, where sincere Christians see differently, he is patient and confident that the Spirit who teaches will keep teaching. Knowing which question is in front of you is most of pastoral wisdom. Treat every disagreement as a first-order matter and you will shred a congregation; treat none of them as first-order and you will lose the gospel.

Patience, not indifference. Notice also what he does not say. He does not say the disagreement does not matter, or that both views are equally good. He plainly thinks he is right and expects them to come round: God will reveal that also to you. This is patience, not indifference. Paul is confident enough in the truth to let God do the persuading, which is a very different thing from being unsure whether there is anything to persuade anyone of.

Only let us hold true to what we have attained. Then the floor. “Hold true” (stoicheō) is a marching word: keep in line, walk in step with. Whatever remains unresolved, live up to the truth you already know. It is a wonderfully practical instruction for anyone stuck on a question they cannot settle. You do not have to solve everything before you obey anything. Live up to what you know, and trust God for the rest.

What it does not mean. It does not mean truth is relative. It means God leads his people into truth over time, and they should obey what they already know.

How do I tell a gospel issue from a secondary one? Ask whether the question touches how a sinner is made right with God, who Christ is, or the authority of Scripture. Those are first-order: the deity and humanity of Christ, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, justification by grace through faith, the Trinity. On these, there can be no compromise. Many other matters, such as the details of church practice, views of the end times, or questions of conscience about food and days, matter and are worth discussing, but sincere believers differ on them and remain brothers. Hold your convictions firmly there too, but hold your brothers more firmly.

What should I do when I think a fellow believer is wrong on such a matter? Pray for them before you talk to them. Speak humbly, from Scripture, and listen as well as argue; you may be the one who needs correcting. Then do what Paul does: leave the persuading to God, and keep walking in step together. Do not make it a test of fellowship, do not campaign, and do not gossip. And look to your own obedience first: are you living up to what you already know?

In a sentence. All of us, then, who are mature should take such a view of things. And if on some point you think differently, that too God will make clear to you. Only let us live up to what we have already attained.

On a Tuesday. Pick one thing you already know God wants of you, and that you have been putting off until you have sorted out other questions. Do it this week. And think of a believer you disagree with on a secondary matter, and pray for them by name, with thanks.

For worship. God is a patient teacher. He does not abandon slow learners, and he leads his people into truth step by step, by his Spirit and his word. He is gentle with those who are still growing and faithful to finish what he started. He reveals what we need when we need it, and the one who has taught us thus far will teach us all the way home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Two Ways to Walk, and Where You Are From
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul invites them to follow his example and that of others who live the same way, because many, he says with tears, live as enemies of the cross: ruled by appetite, proud of what should shame them, their minds fixed on earthly things, and heading for ruin. Believers, by contrast, are citizens of heaven, waiting for a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, from there. By the power with which he rules all things, he will transform their weak and humble bodies to be like his glorious body.
verseByVerse.theology:
Citizenship, and a Body That Will Be Raised

The noun in verse 20 is politeuma, sister to the verb Paul used at 1:27 when he told them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel. He planted it there; here is the flower. And the picture is not evacuation. A Roman colonia — which is exactly what Philippi was, settled with discharged legionaries and granted the standing of Italian soil — was not a party of homesick expatriates waiting for a boat. It was Rome made visible on the frontier. Heavenly citizenship does not license withdrawal from the city; it tells you what you are doing there. Note too that Soter and Kyrios were both Caesar’s titles, said in a town full of men who had sworn him an oath.

Verse 21 completes the pattern of the chapter 2 hymn and turns it on us. There Christ took the form of a slave; here the body of our humiliation — the noun is the one behind “he humbled himself” in 2:8 — is conformed to his body of glory. Against the Greek assumption that salvation means the soul escaping the body, Paul insists the body is not the problem and will not be discarded but changed: the same body made glorious, as Christ’s risen body was recognisably his own and still bore the wounds (John 20:27). And the guarantee runs from greater to lesser — the power that will subject all things to him is the power that will be applied to your body.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Join in imitating me” was said to people with no New Testament and no Christian upbringing, for whom the gospel had to be seen before it could be copied — and it was said by a man who had just admitted he had not arrived.

Now: Verse 21 is a word for the one who is ill, or ageing, or watching a body they love fail. What you live in now is the body of humiliation. It is not the last word about you.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us. For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us. For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things.

Brothers, join in imitating me. And the modern reader flinches. Is that not arrogance? “Join in imitating” (symmimētai) means fellow imitators, together. It would be arrogance, but for three things. First, Paul never means it without the qualifier he makes explicit elsewhere: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). He is not the destination; he is a signpost, and a signpost points away from itself. Second, remember what these Christians did not have: no New Testament, no shelf of books, no Christian upbringing, many of them barely a decade out of paganism. The gospel had to be seen before it could be copied. It reached them in a man they had watched with their own eyes, flogged in their own city, and singing hymns at midnight in the cell (Acts 16:22–25). Third, look who is saying it. Five verses earlier this same man wrote that he had not obtained it and was not yet perfect. The one who says imitate me is the one who has just said he has not arrived, and that is exactly what makes him safe to follow.

And keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us. “Keep your eyes on” is skopeō, to watch, to mark, the same root as the goal of verse 14. Look for good models. And notice how quickly he widens it: not Paul only. Any life bent that way will do. Somewhere in your own congregation there is a quiet old saint worth watching more closely than you have.

For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears. Then the contrast, and Paul’s composure breaks. He weeps over them. That is the tone to hold on to. He is not sneering at these people or enjoying the denunciation. He is weeping while he writes, which is the only posture from which anyone should ever describe another person’s ruin.

Walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Who are they? Paul does not say, and the description fits more than one group. Not necessarily open opponents, but those who professed faith while living for themselves, rejecting the cross-shaped life; perhaps libertines who abused grace as licence. What he gives is not a doctrinal profile but a way of walking, which is the point. These are enemies of the cross practically, not theoretically. The cross is the pattern of chapter 2: self-emptying, obedience, the interests of others. A life organised around self-indulgence contradicts that pattern whatever it professes on a Sunday.

Their end is destruction. Four marks are given, and they descend. The terminus is named first, because Paul wants the trajectory visible before the symptoms. “Destruction” (apōleia) is ruin, perdition: eternal loss, the same word as 1:28.

Their god is their belly. Appetite in the place of worship: food, sex, comfort, pleasure (Romans 16:18). Whatever in you says I want has been enthroned, and it is a god that must be fed daily and never says thank you.

And they glory in their shame. The boast has been inverted. They boast about what should shame them: the very things that should have caused them to hide are the things they advertise.

With minds set on earthly things. And the root of all of it. “Minds set” is phroneō, the key word of the letter again: their mindset is earthly, the opposite of the mind of Christ (2:5). That last phrase is the diagnosis, and it is quieter than the others, which makes it the more searching. It does not describe an act but an orientation: where the mind settles when nothing is demanding its attention. Not what you would say your priorities are. What you think about in the ten minutes before sleep. That is the thing Paul is weeping over, and it is far more ordinary than the phrase enemies of the cross leads us to expect.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians cannot enjoy food or earthly gifts. God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). It means those gifts must not become gods.

Can a true Christian be an enemy of the cross? A true believer can fall into serious sin for a time, as David and Peter did, and must be called to repent. But Paul is describing a settled way of life: people whose god is their appetite and whose end is destruction. Those who live that way, whatever they profess, show that they do not belong to Christ (1 John 3:6–10). That is why Paul weeps rather than shrugs. If you are troubled by this, the trouble is a good sign; enemies of the cross do not grieve over their sin. Turn to Christ now, and keep turning.

What if the people I look up to let me down? Some will, because every human model is flawed, and some who seemed strong will fall. That is why Paul points through himself to Christ. Choose models whose lives are cross-shaped, not merely gifted or successful, and watch how they handle failure as well as success. When a model falls, grieve, learn, and do not let it shake your faith in the one they were pointing to. And remember that you are someone’s model too.

In a sentence. Join together in following Paul’s example, brothers and sisters, and just as you have us as a model, keep your eyes on those who live as we do. For, as he has often told you before and now tells you again even with tears, many live as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their destiny is destruction, their god is their stomach, and their glory is in their shame. Their mind is set on earthly things.

On a Tuesday. Who are you watching and imitating? Choose models who walk the way of the cross, and make time this month to spend with one of them. Then notice where your own mind settles in the ten minutes before sleep tonight, and give those minutes to Christ.

For worship. Christ wept over Jerusalem, and his apostle wept over the enemies of the cross, because the heart of God does not delight in the destruction of the wicked. The cross that some despise is the only hope of the world, and the Saviour who hung there still calls the self-indulgent to come and find in him what their appetites never gave them. He alone can satisfy the hunger that every false god feeds and never fills.

verseByVerse.quote: But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,

But our citizenship is in heaven. “But.” The hinge of the chapter. Against minds set on earthly things, Paul sets a single fact about where his readers actually belong. The noun is politeuma, commonwealth, homeland, and it is the sister of the verb Paul used back in 1:27 when he told them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel. He planted the seed there; here is the flower. A politeuma was a body of citizens resident in a foreign place, holding the rights and duties of a homeland they might never have seen.

A colony of heaven. And every reader in Philippi lived inside that arrangement. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with discharged legionaries and granted the standing of Italian soil, governed by Roman law. Its citizens were intensely proud of it; the charge against Paul in that very city had been that he was advocating customs “not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice” (Acts 16:21). Paul takes the proudest fact about their city and tells them it is a picture of something truer: you already know what it is to live in one place and belong to another. Now transpose it. Your capital is not Rome. The church is a colony of heaven on earth.

Not evacuation. Which corrects the usual misreading of this verse. Citizenship in heaven is not a promise of evacuation, and it is not permission to disengage. A Roman colony was not a group of homesick expatriates waiting for a boat. It was Rome’s presence on the frontier, established precisely so that the distant capital would be visible where it otherwise was not. Paul is not telling them to withdraw from Philippi. He is telling them what they are doing there.

And from it we await a Savior. The verb (apekdechomai) is a strong compound: to await eagerly, expectantly, as in Romans 8:19–25. And the title is chosen with care. Sōtēr, saviour, and kyrios, lord, were both claimed by Caesar; the emperor was hailed as saviour and lord. In a colony full of retired soldiers who had sworn an oath to him, Paul says quietly that the Saviour and Lord is someone else, and he is the one we are watching the road for.

The Lord Jesus Christ. He will come from heaven, as the emperor might visit a colony to rescue it. A colony always expects a visit from its king. The question this verse asks is not whether you believe he is coming, but whether anything in the way you live this week would only make sense if he were.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have no responsibilities on earth. Colonists served the empire where they lived. Believers serve Christ where they are, as citizens of heaven.

Should Christians care about their country, vote or serve in public life? Yes, but as citizens of heaven first. Paul used his Roman citizenship when it served the gospel (Acts 16:37; 22:25), and he told Christians to pray for those in authority and to seek the good of their society (1 Timothy 2:1–2; Romans 13:1–7). Love your neighbour, work for justice, vote with a conscience shaped by Scripture, and serve where you are called. But do not put your ultimate hope in any party, leader or nation, and do not let earthly loyalties outrank Christ. When the two conflict, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Will we live in heaven for ever? Our citizenship is in heaven now, and believers who die go to be with Christ there (1:23). But the final hope is not a disembodied existence. Christ will come from heaven, raise the dead, and make all things new: a new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–4). The capital comes down to the colony. God will dwell with his people, in resurrected bodies, in a renewed creation, for ever.

In a sentence. But our citizenship is in heaven. And we eagerly await a Saviour from there, the Lord Jesus Christ,

On a Tuesday. Look at your diary, your bank statement and your browsing history, and ask which city they would suggest you belong to. Then do one thing this week that only makes sense if Christ is really coming back: a gift, a reconciliation, a word of witness, a habit given up. Pray for your country and its leaders by name, as a citizen of a better one.

For worship. Christ is the true Saviour and Lord, and every Caesar is a passing shadow. He has a commonwealth that no army can conquer and no time can wear out, and he has made us its citizens by his blood. He reigns now in heaven, and he is coming from there to rescue his colonies and bring them home. We wait for him not as frightened subjects but as a bride waits for the bridegroom, with our eyes on the road.
verseByVerse.note: Philippi’s citizens were proud to be citizens of Rome; believers belong to a heavenly commonwealth.

verseByVerse.quote: who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.

Who will transform our lowly body. The chapter’s last great sentence, and it takes the hymn of chapter 2 and turns it on us. There, Christ was humbled and then exalted. Here, we are: he will transform our lowly body. “Transform” (metaschēmatizō) is to change the form, the outward state. “Our lowly body” is literally the body of our humiliation, and the word is the noun behind he humbled himself in 2:8. Paul is not sneering at the body. He is naming what everyone over forty already knows: these bodies are in a humiliated condition, weak, ageing, sick and dying (2 Corinthians 4:16; 5:4). They tire, thicken, fail, forget, and are finally laid in the ground. Anyone who has watched a strong parent become unable to manage a staircase knows exactly what phrase Paul has chosen, and knows he has not exaggerated.

To be like his glorious body. “Like” is symmorphos, conformed, and it is built on morphē again, the same root as the form of God in 2:6 and becoming like him in his death in verse 10. The pattern completes: he took our form so that we might share his. The resurrection body will be like Christ’s risen body: imperishable, glorious, powerful (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; 1 John 3:2).

Transformation, not escape. And against the humiliated body, the promise is not escape from the body but its transformation. This matters, and the church has often got it wrong. The Greek world around Philippi mostly held that salvation meant the soul getting free of the body, which was the problem. Paul says the body is not the problem and will not be discarded; it will be changed. The same body, made glorious, as Christ’s risen body was recognisably his own, still bearing the marks of the nails (John 20:27), and yet transfigured. This is also the full answer to the enemies whose god is their belly: the body is not to be worshipped, but it is not to be despised either. It has a glorious future.

By the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself. Then the guarantee, and Paul does not leave the promise hanging on sentiment. It is the same power by which Christ will rule all creation (Psalm 8:6; 1 Corinthians 15:27). The argument is from the greater to the lesser. The energy that will one day bring the entire created order under Christ’s feet, every hostile power, death included, is the energy that will be applied to your body. If he can do the first, the second is not going to strain him. No death, decay or disease can resist him.

Where the chapter has been going. Set that beside where the chapter began. Paul opened by throwing his pedigree out with the kitchen refuse and closes by promising that the humiliated body will be made like the body of glory. In between he told them not to set their minds on earthly things. This is why. Not because earthly things are unreal, but because they are not where the story is going.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become divine. We will be glorified humans, like Christ in his humanity, never sharing his deity. It does not mean the present body is worthless, either: it is the seed of what will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:36–38).

What about bodies that were destroyed, cremated or lost at sea? The resurrection does not depend on the condition of the remains. The God who made the first body from the dust can raise it from any dust. The power that subjects all things to Christ is not limited by fire, sea or decay (Revelation 20:13). Christians may differ on burial and cremation as a matter of practice and witness, but no believer’s resurrection is in any doubt because of how their body was laid to rest.

What does this mean for someone who is disabled, ill or ageing? It means your present weakness is not the last word about you. The body of humiliation will be raised in power and glory, free from pain, disease and decay. Every limitation sin brought into the world will be undone. That does not make present suffering small, and you are free to grieve it and to seek every help now. But you may also hope, concretely and bodily. Many disabled believers have said that the first face they will see with perfect eyes, and the first steps they take on perfect legs, will be towards Christ. The New Testament does not tell you the body does not matter. It tells you the body matters so much that God intends to raise it.

In a sentence. Who, by the power that enables him to bring everything under his control, will transform our lowly bodies so that they will be like his glorious body.

On a Tuesday. When your body aches or fails, or when you sit beside someone whose body is failing, say this verse aloud: he will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body. Then care for the body you have, with rest, food and medicine, as a gift to be stewarded until he comes.

For worship. Christ is risen, and his risen body is the pattern of ours. He has power to subject all things to himself, and with that power he will raise every one of his people from the dust and clothe them with glory like his own. The body that was laid in weakness will be raised in power; the eyes that closed in death will open on his face. Death will be swallowed up in victory, and the one who took the form of a servant will share his glory with servants who were never worthy of it. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.

4.title: The Peace That Passes Understanding: Rejoice, Pray, and Be Content
4.overview:
The last chapter gathers the letter’s threads into practice. First, a quarrel: two women who had worked hard beside Paul, Euodia and Syntyche, have fallen out, and Paul begs them by name to agree in the Lord, asking a trusted friend to help. Then a cluster of commands for a church under strain: rejoice in the Lord always; let your gentleness be known; do not be anxious about anything but pray about everything, and God’s peace will stand guard over your hearts; fill your minds with whatever is true, honourable and lovely; and practise what you have seen in Paul.

Finally Paul thanks them for their gift, carried by Epaphroditus. He does so delicately: he is grateful, but he has learned to be content in plenty and in want, because he can face anything through Christ who strengthens him. Their gift is a fragrant sacrifice to God, and God, who owns everything, will supply every need of theirs in Christ. He closes with doxology and greetings, including from believers in Caesar’s own household.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Stand Firm, and Two Women Who Cannot Agree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Drawing the threads together, Paul calls the church he loves and longs to see, whom he calls his joy and his victor’s wreath, to hold their ground in the Lord. Then he names a painful problem: two women, Euodia and Syntyche, who had worked hard beside him for the gospel, have fallen out. He pleads with each of them to be of one mind in the Lord, and asks a trusted colleague to help them make peace, reminding everyone that these women, like Clement and his other co-workers, belong to God’s registered people.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Christian Unity Actually Rests On

The appeal to these two women shows where the Reformed tradition has always located the ground of unity: not in agreement on every point but in a shared life in Christ — one Lord, one Spirit, one book of life. That is why Paul can ask for reunion before the dispute is settled, and without ever telling us what it was. A congregation whose unity rests on consensus will fracture at the first serious disagreement; a congregation whose unity rests on Christ can carry real friction without breaking.

Note also the pastoral restraint. Paul does not adjudicate, does not rebuke, and does not pull rank — the verb is parakalo, I beg. He repeats it for each woman so that neither is cast as the offender. And he ends not with a warning but with election: whatever they are currently doing to each other, their names are written in heaven, and that is the deeper fact about them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: These were not marginal figures. They had “laboured side by side” with Paul — the same athletic word he used in 1:27 for a team striving together — and the Philippian church had begun among women at a riverside prayer meeting (Acts 16:13), so they had very likely been in it from the first day. Their falling out mattered enough for an imprisoned apostle to address it by name in a letter he knew would be read aloud to everyone.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, my beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, my beloved.

Meaning first. Philippians 4 brings the letter’s themes of joy, unity and partnership to a close in a burst of practical exhortation and warm thanks. First, Paul urges the church to stand firm, and pleads with two women who had laboured with him, Euodia and Syntyche, to agree in the Lord (vv. 1–3). Then come some of the best-loved commands in Scripture: rejoice in the Lord always; let your gentleness be known; do not be anxious, but pray about everything with thanksgiving, and God’s peace will guard your hearts; think about whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely and commendable; and practise what you learned from Paul, and the God of peace will be with you (vv. 4–9). Finally, Paul thanks them for their gift. He has learned the secret of contentment in plenty and in want, because he can do all things through Christ who strengthens him. Their gift is a fragrant sacrifice to God, and God will supply all their needs according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus (vv. 10–23). A letter that began with grace ends with grace, and everything between is held inside it.

Therefore. The question is what the word reaches back to, because the answer sets the tone. The last thing Paul said was that our citizenship is in heaven and that Christ will transform the body of our humiliation into the likeness of his body of glory, by the power that can subject all things to himself (3:20–21). Therefore stand firm. The command to hold the line is not a demand for grit. It rests on a promise about how the story ends, and men hold ground far better when they know the outcome of the war.

My brothers, whom I love and long for. Count the endearments: my brothers, whom I love, whom I long for, my joy, my crown, my beloved. Five in a single verse, and beloved twice, once at each end, so that the command sits inside affection like a stone in a fist of wool. Paul is about to name two women in a public letter, and he builds the setting first. “Long for” (epipothētoi, deeply missed) picks up the ache of 1:8, where he yearned for them with the affection of Christ. This church is dear to him.

My joy and crown. “Crown” is stephanos: not the royal diadem but the wreath of leaves handed to the victor at the games, or a festive garland. Paul has just described himself as a runner straining for the prize (3:14); here he tells this congregation that they are the wreath. On the last day the Philippians will be Paul’s reward and joy, the evidence that his labour was not in vain (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20). When he stands before Christ, what he will have to show for nearly thirty years of shipwreck and flogging and argument is a handful of churches, this one among them. People are the prize. He has no other.

Stand firm thus in the Lord, my beloved. “Stand firm” is stēkō, as in 1:27, a military word for a line that holds when it is pushed. And the little word thus reaches backwards and gathers the whole letter: stand firm like that, with eyes on the coming Saviour, in the citizenship of heaven (3:20), in the one Spirit and the one struggle (1:27), in the Christ who has already laid hold of you (3:12). In the Lord: not in your own strength.

The seam inside. And here is why the verse matters where it stands. The instruction to hold the line comes immediately before the naming of a quarrel between two church members. Paul evidently thinks the two things are the same subject. A congregation does not usually break because a persecutor smashes it from outside; it breaks along a seam that opened inside it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s salvation depended on them. They are the joy of his ministry, not the ground of his acceptance. His standing is Christ’s righteousness (3:9); his crown is the people he served.

What does standing firm look like in an ordinary week? It looks less like heroism and more like staying put. Keep meeting with your church when you are tired or disappointed. Keep holding to the gospel when you hear clever voices that would add to it or take from it (3:2). Keep obeying in the area where temptation presses hardest. Keep loving the believers next to you in the line, especially the difficult ones. And do it in the Lord: by praying, by remembering what he has promised, and by leaning on the people beside you. A line holds because each person stays where he is and trusts the one next to him.

In a sentence. So then, Paul’s brothers and sisters, you whom he loves and longs for, his joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, dear friends!

On a Tuesday. Tell a fellow believer this week, in plain words, what they mean to you in the Lord: a note, a message, a sentence after church. Then encourage them to stand firm in whatever they are facing. Affection said aloud is one of the ways a line is held.

For worship. Christ has a crown made of people. He ran the race set before him, for the joy of a people redeemed, and on the last day he will present them faultless before the presence of his glory with great joy. If an apostle could call a small, quarrelling church his crown, how much more does the Saviour delight in the people he bought with his blood. He loves them, he longs for them, and he will hold them firm until he comes.
verseByVerse.note: The “crown” is the victor’s wreath awarded at the games.

verseByVerse.quote: I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord. Yes, I ask you also, true companion, help these women, who have labored side by side with me in the gospel together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord. Yes, I ask you also, true companion, help these women, who have labored side by side with me in the gospel together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.

I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche. Two names, and one of the very few places in the New Testament where a congregational quarrel is reported with the parties named. Euodia and Syntyche have been read in public assemblies for two thousand years because they fell out. Their quarrel was serious enough to reach Paul in prison, and it threatened the church’s unity (2:1–4). See how gently Paul does something so exposing, and how much he refuses to do. He does not say who is right. He does not summarise the dispute, or hint at it, so that we do not know to this day what it was about. He does not rebuke, threaten, or invoke his apostolic authority. The verb is parakalō, I appeal, I urge, I beg, and he uses it twice, once for each woman, so as not to take sides. Neither is addressed as the problem and neither is lumped in with the other. No one reading the letter aloud could tell which of them Paul thought had started it.

To agree in the Lord. Literally, to think the same thing (to auto phronein) in the Lord, and it is the exact phrase from 2:2 and the mind of 2:5. He is not asking them to reach the same conclusion about whatever it was. He is asking them to have the same mind, which is Christ’s, and that mind is described in the hymn: not grasping, counting the other more significant. The ground of reunion is not the settling of the argument. It is a Lord they both already have.

Yes, I ask you also, true companion. Then he does something churches are notoriously bad at: he brings in a third party. The true companion is unnamed; some suggest Luke or Epaphroditus, or a leader of the church. The word is syzygos, yokefellow, one of a pair of oxen pulling together, and it may well be a man’s actual name, Syzygus, with Paul punning that he is a true Syzygus. Either way, the point stands. Reconciliation is not left to the two who are stuck. Someone trusted is asked, publicly, to get involved and be a peacemaker. Most quarrels in most congregations are left to sort themselves out and therefore harden. Paul assigns it to a named person and puts the assignment in a letter everyone will hear.

Help these women, who have labored side by side with me in the gospel. And before anyone can start thinking of these two as troublemakers, he tells the church who they are. “Laboured side by side” (synathleō) is the same athletic word he used in 1:27 for striving together as a team, contending alongside like athletes. These were not troublemakers but valued gospel workers, front-rank workers. Women were prominent in the Philippian church from the start: it began among women at a riverside, with Lydia (Acts 16:13–15), and these two had very likely been in it from the beginning. Even faithful servants can fall out.

Together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life. That is where Paul leaves them, and the placing is everything. The book of life is God’s register of his people, the citizens of heaven (Exodus 32:32; Daniel 12:1; Luke 10:20; Revelation 20:12, 15). Their names are written there: they are God’s elect, eternally secure. Two women in a public dispute, and the last thing said about them is that their names are written in heaven. Their quarrel is real, it is damaging, and it is worth an apostle’s intervention from prison, and it is not the truest thing about them. People whose names are in the same book should be able to agree. That is how a church should learn to see people it is currently exasperated by: the disagreement is a fact, the register in heaven is a deeper one.

Where Christians differ: can names be erased from the book of life? Some read Revelation 3:5 and Exodus 32:33 as showing that names once written can be blotted out, so believers may be lost. Verdict: the book of life records those chosen by God before the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8; 17:8). Christ promises that he will never blot out the names of those who overcome (Revelation 3:5), and all true believers overcome (1 John 5:4). The names of God’s elect are written permanently. This is the security in which Paul can speak of his fellow workers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conflict among believers is unimportant. Paul addresses it publicly and urgently. It means believers who quarrel must be reconciled, with help from others.

What does this say about women’s ministry? Paul honours these women as fellow workers who laboured side by side with him in the gospel; their work was real and valued. He does not say what it was, and nothing here suggests they were elders or preached in the church’s gathering, which Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:2). Women served the gospel in many ways in Paul’s churches, in hospitality, teaching other women and children, supporting the mission and speaking of Christ, and they still should. A church that does not value and thank its women workers as Paul did has not understood him.

I am at odds with someone in my church. Should others be involved? Begin privately. Go to the person yourself, humbly, owning your part first, and try to be reconciled (Matthew 5:23–24; 18:15). If that fails, ask one or two wise, trusted believers to help, as Paul asked his true companion: not to take sides, but to help you both think the same thing in the Lord. Avoid recruiting supporters, which only hardens a quarrel into a faction. Paul named Euodia and Syntyche because their quarrel was already public and affecting the church. Most disagreements can and should be healed long before they reach that stage.

How can I know my name is in the book of life? Not by trying to read heaven’s register, but by looking to Christ. Everyone who trusts him as Lord and Saviour has been chosen in him (Ephesians 1:4), and Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20). If you are trusting Christ, your name is there, written before the foundation of the world. And the evidence grows as you follow him: love for his people, desire to obey, grief over sin. If you are not yet trusting him, the invitation is open today.

In a sentence. Paul pleads with Euodia and pleads with Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord. Yes, and he asks you, his true companion, to help these women, since they have contended at his side in the cause of the gospel, along with Clement and the rest of his co-workers, whose names are in the book of life.

On a Tuesday. If you are at odds with a fellow believer, remember that both your names are in the book of life, and take the first step towards them this week: a call, a coffee, an apology for your part. And if you can be a peacemaker between others, do it, gently and without taking sides.

For worship. The Lord writes names in his book and does not erase them. Before the world began he chose a people for himself, and he wrote among them a businesswoman, a jailer, two quarrelling women and a man called Clement whom history otherwise forgot. He is the God of peace, who reconciled rebels to himself by the blood of his Son, and he is able to reconcile his children to one another. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God, because they are like their Father.
verseByVerse.note: The “true companion” is unnamed; some suggest Luke or Epaphroditus. The book of life is God’s register of his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Rejoice, Do Not Be Anxious, and Mind What You Dwell On
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to rejoice in the Lord always, and to let their gentleness be known to all, because the Lord is near. Instead of being anxious they are to bring every need to God in prayer with thanks, and God’s peace, beyond understanding, will guard their hearts and minds in Christ. They should fill their minds with whatever is true, honourable, right, pure, lovely and admirable, and put into practice what they learned and saw in Paul. Then the God of peace will be with them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Anxiety and Its Remedy
